THE LITTLE GOD OF UNKEPT PROMISES

By sunset, Mount Vey will collapse onto a city where a minor god has made every promise physically binding. Illuminara must free a father from his doorway, two children from forever, and exhausted workers from a mayor’s vow—without teaching the powerful that accountability is only for other people.

01 · The Doorway

Veyra, the east ward · 08:12, ten hours before sunset

Oren Vale leaned into his own open doorway until the tendons stood in his neck. His left boot crossed the sill. His right would not lift. Nothing visible held it, yet the floorboards groaned as if a cart horse pulled the other way.

LioDad, stop. Your ankle is bleeding.

His daughter knelt on the street side with a quarry alarm bell in one hand. Beyond her, a pale line of dust hung above Mount Vey. Each time the bell sounded, the mountain answered a heartbeat later.

OrenI promised your mother I would never leave you alone in this house.

LioI am standing outside it. I am asking you to leave with me.

OrenThe promise does not know the difference.

Across the lane, Mina and Cal moved with their wrists held a handspan apart by a thread of amber light. At nine they had sworn to be friends forever. At twelve, Mina had earned a place on a river school; Cal had refused to let her board the coach because every step away burned both their arms.

MinaWe meant it when we said it.

CalThat is the worst part.

Illuminara came down without thunder. She put one palm against Oren’s lintel. The pressure was not in the wood. It ran under the street, through thousands of doorstones, marriage rings, guild marks and burial tablets, all converging on the black quarry above the city.

A small figure sat on the lintel where her hand had been. He was no taller than Lio’s forearm. His coat was stitched from torn contracts; his eyes were two drops of sealing wax. When he spoke, every promise in the street tightened.

SefIf words may be escaped whenever they hurt, the weak are the only ones who must believe them.

IlluminaraI did not come to teach you that words are cheap.

SefYou came because the mayor’s quarry is breaking my oldest covenant. Powerful people always discover mercy when consequence reaches their own door.

The second alarm sounded. Dust rolled from Mount Vey in a thicker ribbon. Lio unfolded a quarry map. A red crack had reached the ventilation stair where three hundred night workers were still below.

LioForewoman Sen says the east shelf will fall at 17:42. The mayor promised work to every household. Sef made the promise true. Half the city is too exhausted to shore the shelf, and no one assigned to the quarry can leave.

IlluminaraMy aim is to get every person out before the shelf falls, without breaking the covenant that keeps the mountain off the city.

SefThen begin with the part you dislike. Ask who paid when promises were only admired.

He stepped into a crack in the lintel and vanished. Oren’s right foot remained fixed.

Illuminara lifted Lio’s alarm bell and felt its chipped bronze warm in her hand. He had not refused help. He had refused another exception made by someone strong enough to call it mercy.

IlluminaraShow me the Hall of Oaths. Then we go to the quarry together.

Lio glanced at her father. Oren stopped pulling at the threshold, wrapped his ankle, and nodded. It was not rescue yet. It was the first time that morning someone had asked him to act rather than endure.

02 · What Sef Heard

Hall of Oaths · 10:05, seven hours and thirty-seven minutes before collapse

The hall had no statues. Its walls were built from promise stones: one for every vow on which another person’s safety had depended. Bright stones marked fulfilled obligations. Dark ones marked breaches. Most of the dark stones bore the crests of old councils, mining houses and temples.

Sef stood on the clerk’s table. Around him gathered Oren, Lio, Mina, Cal, Forewoman Ilya Sen, Mayor Teren Vos and forty citizens chosen by the quarry crews. No guard stood at the doors. Sef had made every official who promised public service unable to leave.

Mayor VosRelease the workers and I will sign any amendment you draft.

SefYou signed six safety amendments. When production fell, you called each one aspirational.

Mayor VosThe city would have starved.

IlyaYou promised every family wages, then counted compulsory double shifts as employment. We did not starve. We broke.

Illuminara touched a dark stone bearing the mayoral crest. It held not words but consequences: Ilya’s crushed fingers; a widow’s unanswered petition; children carrying meals to parents who slept beside the lifts.

IlluminaraSef, when did you begin binding every promise literally?

SefAfter the seventh council swore to repair the west retaining wall and used the money for a triumph gate. The slide killed four hundred and twelve. Their last breath was full of official language.

IlluminaraSo your goal is not obedience. It is recourse.

The wax in Sef’s eyes trembled, but his voice stayed hard.

SefRecourse that cannot be postponed by the eloquent. A promise that changes when the promiser suffers is merely a weapon with a velvet handle.

LioAnd a promise that cannot hear the person it was made to becomes a cage. My mother asked Dad to keep me safe, not to die inside our doorway.

OrenI used her last words because deciding what came next frightened me. Sef did not invent that.

Cal raised his glowing wrist. Mina raised hers beside it.

CalI wanted forever because everyone in my house leaves.

MinaI stayed because his fear hurt me less than hurting him. That does not make staying freely chosen.

For one moment the amber thread slackened, then tightened again. Sef had listened; he had not conceded.

SefIf I accept intention over words, Mayor Vos will discover that he intended justice all along.

IlluminaraThen do not let the promiser decide. Let the person who relied on the promise name the harm. Let release require truth, repair and a new choice—not cleverer wording.

Mayor VosA tribunal during a mountain emergency?

IlyaA tribunal is what you call it when workers get a chair.

The hall shuddered. A line of dust fell from the ceiling. On the quarry map, the red crack crossed another support gallery. The clock now read seven hours, twenty-nine minutes.

SefWords again. Test them where stone can answer.

He struck the table. Three promise stones rose: the mayor’s employment vow, Oren’s doorway vow, and the children’s forever vow. Beneath them lay a fourth, older and brighter than all the rest: the city’s covenant to keep the drainage channels clear so Mount Vey would sleep.

SefBreak every bond and the old covenant breaks with them. Keep every bond and the exhausted crews die. Show me accountability that survives freedom.

Illuminara did not reach for power. She asked Ilya for the quarry ledgers, Lio for the petitions no clerk had answered, and Sef for the names of those who had relied on each promise. Sef gave her the names.

03 · The Price Named by the Harmed

East quarry assembly floor · 13:48, three hours and fifty-four minutes before collapse

The quarry floor had been cleared beneath a roof of cracked slate. Every eight minutes, a brass plumb bob swung farther east. Ilya had painted three evacuation lines on the ground. The workers stood behind the lines by crew, not by rank.

Illuminara could have carried them out. The covenant ran through the drainage tunnels, however, and a forced severing would send the saturated upper slope into Veyra. Her strength could hold one shelf for ninety-three seconds. The mountain held six.

IlluminaraHere is my first proposal. Every safety promise names its beneficiaries, duration, proof and a way to demand repair. Changed circumstances may reopen its terms. Those harmed decide whether repair is enough.

SefWho declares the circumstances changed?

IlluminaraEither party could ask—

SefThen Mayor Vos will call falling profits a changed circumstance. He will reopen the promise, keep the benefit and describe the breach as negotiation. You have built him a polite door.

Illuminara looked down at the clause she had thought was fair. Sef knew not only how promises trapped people, but how power escaped them. She struck the sentence through.

IlluminaraOnly a person who relied on the promise may trigger a reopening. Immediate danger may justify a provisional departure, but it starts a public repair hearing within one day. The promiser cannot rewrite the harm.

IlyaAnd the hearing begins with the injured, not the office that broke the promise.

SefBetter. Not safe. Better.

Ilya rolled the quarry cutaway across the slate. The loaded waste tram stood above the north stair on a relief rail whose haul cable crossed the east fracture. If its brake were released, it would clear the stair, travel for ninety-three seconds and pull the fractured shelf toward the abandoned cut.

Illuminara traced the crack with two fingers and marked the point where the cable would take the load. Ilya checked the tram mass against the six crews’ recorded weights, then made the north-stair release and the counterweight one timed sequence. The workers—not a hidden machine—would set the brake, clear the route and call the final latch.

IlluminaraI can hold the shelf for the tram’s ninety-three-second descent. Not for a hundred. If the route changes, you call the change.

IlyaThen your strength follows our clock.

Ilya laid three demands on the stone table. The quarry would close until an elected crew inspected every gallery. Vos would surrender his quarry shares to a restitution trust. For five years, half the council seats overseeing public works would belong to workers and bereaved families.

Vos removed the mayoral seal and signed away his office, his half of the house and every quarry share. He sent a runner for Maro and the children before anyone could mistake his signature for theirs.

While they waited, Mina and Cal wrote their own repair: each would tell the other one thing the vow had cost; neither would ask for contact for thirty days; after that, friendship could be renewed only by two yeses.

CalIf she says no after thirty days, what holds me?

SefNothing.

CalThat feels like falling.

MinaI will sit with you until the coach comes. I will not promise what happens after.

Cal wept without hiding his face. Sef climbed down from the table and sat beside him. He did not loosen the amber thread.

SefI was made from that fear. Every promise is a bridge over the fact that another being may leave.

Lio placed an unused witness seal on the floor beside him. It was plain iron, cut for two keys. Her written offer gave Sef the witness key for one hearing only, or permission to leave it untouched. The quarry gate was not its price, and no one could bind him to the chair.

SefA place offered can become another promise.

IlluminaraSo it expires after one hearing. You choose again. If you never take it, the chair remains empty and the court still owes you nothing.

Sef did not touch the seal. He also did not step away from it.

The runner returned with Vos’s family. Maro read the demands twice, closed his hand around the house key and refused to spend the children’s home on Teren’s debt. He conceded one concrete term: they would keep three rooms through winter while the clinic used the ground floor. The remaining purchase, trust and repair terms would be heard after the evacuation.

Vos reached for the key, stopped, and signed only the property and shares that were his to give. Ilya turned the page toward the waiting witnesses. His title was gone; his family’s boundary remained outside his control.

Illuminara signed beneath the tram calculation: ninety-three seconds when Ilya called, the evacuation route above her improvisation, and the same public review for any force she used in Veyra that day. She offered no forever.

SefYou could leave before judgment.

IlluminaraYes. The record gives people an answer if I do: publish my breach, refuse my aid and summon witnesses beyond this city. Trust is not certainty. It is power arranged so betrayal has an answer.

Sef looked toward the lower terraces, where Lio’s runners were already carrying the names he had supplied in the Hall. The people protected by the drainage covenant would be asked what risk, if any, they would accept.

The plumb bob struck its warning mark twenty-three minutes early.

IlyaThe crack accelerated. New collapse time: 17:19.

No one asked Sef to believe a definition. They carried a corrected proposal, a checked ninety-three-second plan, an unclaimed witness seal and three possible evacuation answers to the failing galleries.

04 · Ninety-Three Seconds

Mount Vey, east shelf · 17:16, three minutes before collapse

Rainwater hissed through the upper fracture. Below it, six crews moved along routes they had chosen. Ilya held the two-stage release lever: its first pull would send the loaded ore tram down the ninety-three-second relief rail and clear the north stair; its final latch would drop the tram into the empty cut and tension the haul cable across the fracture. Lio stood at the signal bell. Oren waited at the city doorway, still bound, ready to cross if Sef released him.

At the lower spillway stood Ressa Daan, whose bakery and cellar occupied the first terrace, and Toma Ely, chosen by the east-lane households. They held the reply bells. No one claimed they spoke for the whole city; they carried the recorded answers of the people on the routes that would take the eleven-second surge.

IlyaTest condition one: the workers may refuse the mayor’s employment promise without losing their claim to wages.

SefIf I release them, who keeps the drainage covenant?

Thirty-two workers raised their hands. Not one was compelled.

WorkersWe renew the drainage covenant for this evacuation and for thirty days. After that, renewal requires inspection, pay and a recorded vote.

IlyaTest condition two: those harmed retain the power to reject repair.

MinaI accept thirty days apart.

CalI accept that she may not return.

Sef opened one small hand. The amber thread between the children dissolved into warm sparks. Cal staggered, then stood without grabbing Mina. Mina took his hand for three breaths and let go. Both choices held.

In the city, Oren’s right foot lifted. He crossed the doorway and ran toward the lower drainage gate with Lio’s spare key. His promise did not vanish; it changed into a record of care, harm and consent that Lio had accepted.

SefAnd the mayor?

Mayor VosDo not release my debt. Release the workers from my command.

The promise stones around the quarry flared. The ore tram gates opened. Workers who had been physically unable to abandon assigned stations moved toward the stairs.

At 17:18:07 the east shelf split.

IlyaNow, Illuminara.

Ilya pulled the first detent. The loaded tram began its ninety-three-second descent, clearing the north stair as its wheels took the cable strain. The crews had built the sequence; Illuminara had shown them where the fracture would accept it.

Illuminara went beneath the falling shelf and raised both hands. Two million tonnes of slate stopped a spear’s length above her. The impact drove her knees into stone. Lio’s clock began with the tram’s descent: ninety-three seconds to the empty cut.

Sef saw the sixth crew still trapped behind a contract-marked gate. Releasing them would weaken the old covenant for eleven seconds before the volunteers’ renewal reached the promise stones. In those seconds the lower spillway would flood and the east retaining road might go.

SefIf I keep them, the mountain sleeps and they die. If I free them, other people pay.

IlluminaraThen ask the people who would pay.

Lio rang the question sequence: eleven seconds, lower spillway, east road. Ressa’s bell answered once: yes with a condition. Toma’s answered twice: no.

RessaKeep the spillway open even if my cellar floods. My ovens are not worth a crew.

TomaThe east lane is not clear. Six households are still moving the bedbound. No gate until Lio gives three bells.

The clock passed forty-one. Ilya changed the plan. The north-stair crew abandoned two carts of shoring timber and ran to carry the last east-lane residents above the red line. The lost timber meant the processing hall could not be saved.

SefYou accept the cellar and the road?

RessaI accept my cellar. Toma speaks for the road only when his people are clear.

The clock passed fifty-eight. A support cracked against Illuminara’s shoulder. She did not command Sef or promise that no one would be hurt.

At sixty-four seconds, Lio heard three reply bells from the east lane and struck three of her own. Toma answered once. The condition had been met; his no had become a yes without being overruled.

Sef looked at Ilya, not at the mayor.

SefIf I open the gate, will your crew renew the drainage covenant before they reach the north stair?

IlyaAsk them.

Through the bars, the sixth crew answered one by one. Twenty-one said yes. Three said no; they had been on duty thirty-six hours and would accept no new promise until they slept. Ilya assigned their section to rested volunteers, who consented on the record.

At seventy-two seconds, Sef glanced at the plain iron witness seal Lio had left beside the lever. He could have opened the gate without it, and the offer had not been made as payment. He picked up only the witness key.

SefOne hearing. Then I choose again.

At seventy-five seconds, Sef opened the gate.

For eleven seconds, Mount Vey moved. Oren reached the lower gate and locked the emergency spillway open. Brown water filled Ressa’s cellar and tore the east retaining road into the abandoned orchard. The six households were already above it. Lio struck the new sequence; rested volunteers renewed only the drainage work they had named. The bright covenant stone held.

At eighty-eight seconds, the loaded tram reached the empty cut. Ilya pulled the final latch. The tram dropped, the haul cable snapped taut, and the fractured shelf turned away from the city along the line Illuminara had marked.

IlyaClear!

Illuminara released the stone at ninety-two seconds. The shelf fell into the abandoned quarry. The old processing hall, three cranes and the mayoral triumph arch disappeared under dust. No house in Veyra moved.

For a moment Mina laughed—not because the loss was small, but because Cal had let her run and had run beside someone else. Illuminara laughed too, breathless and astonished. The sound was her own, not a lesson for anyone.

Sef stood on her dust-covered shoulder with the witness key closed in his wax hand. He was still small. He no longer looked like a jailer, but neither did he look harmless.

SefThree workers refused. Toma refused until his people were clear. The covenant lived.

IlyaGood. Come witness the cost before the next renewal.

05 · The Court of Open Hands

Veyra, the former mayoral house · dawn, the following day

The front rooms had become a temporary clinic before the dust settled. Maro and his children kept three rooms upstairs through winter; in spring, the trust could offer an assessed purchase only if they accepted it. Vos’s half of the house and every quarry share he owned were sealed in the restitution trust. He slept on a bench outside the records office, waiting to testify.

At the long table sat workers, bereaved families, apprentices, clerks and two seats kept empty for people who had not yet decided whether to join. Above them hung no image of Sef.

Sef sat in one of the empty seats and set the witness key beside his hand. The chair continued an offer he had accepted for one hearing, not a reward for opening the gate.

IlyaThis court preserves the record, hears the people who relied on a promise, and certifies repair or release. It cannot compel a new promise.

SefAnd my power?

IlyaYou may make concealed consequences visible. You may not bind a body until the person harmed has been heard and immediate safety requires it. Every binding expires unless this court renews it with the affected people’s consent.

SefYou offer a god a clerkship.

LioWe offer you witnesses who cannot be dismissed as a superstition when officials break their word.

Sef studied the dark stones carried from the old hall. They were no longer hidden in walls. Each lay beside a petition and the name of someone empowered to answer it.

SefI will serve for thirty days. Then I choose again.

IlyaSo do we.

Oren entered through the front door carrying a kettle. He paused on the sill by habit, then crossed. Lio did not applaud. She took the heavier handle, and together they brought tea to the night crew.

OrenI cannot repair twelve years by crossing once.

LioNo. But today you crossed when I needed you outside.

Mina’s river coach left at noon. Cal came to the platform with Sef and did not ask for a promise. Mina gave Cal a paper address that might change. Cal gave her a carved whistle and told her she did not have to use it.

At Mount Vey, rested volunteers cleared the drainage channels under Ilya’s plan. The quarry stayed closed and wages came from the seized shares. Vos disclosed the diverted funds and named the councilors who had approved them. When he tried to explain that every choice had protected employment, Ilya made him read the night-shift injury list before he continued.

Illuminara submitted her ninety-two seconds of force to review. A rigger objected that the falling shelf had shattered a memorial crane. She listened, recovered its nameplate with him, and accepted the requirement that the crane be rebuilt before any monument to the rescue.

Sef watched with the severe attention of a creature learning that consequence could have more than one shape.

Before she left, Illuminara set Lio’s chipped bell within his reach and opened her palm beneath the edge of his chair. Sef looked at the offered hand, then climbed down by the chair rung instead. She withdrew without turning his refusal into a lesson and left the bell where he could choose it.

SefThe weak still need words they can trust.

IlluminaraYes.

SefFreedom will still be used as an excuse by the strong.

IlluminaraYes. That is why freedom without recourse is unfinished.

SefAnd recourse without freedom becomes me.

THE BRIDGE THAT MISSED BY NINE METRES

Two villages built a bridge from opposite banks and met nine metres apart. Each swears the other sighted wrong, and Illuminara has ten days to find out what both of them measured.

01 · Nine Metres

Upper Wend, the north tip of the bridge · dawn, ten days before the flood

Two half-bridges stood out over the river like the hands of people who had agreed to shake and then thought better of it. Between the tips lay nine metres of brown water. A string stretched from rail to rail would also have shown the north span pointing nine centimetres left of the south, and that was the part that made the villages shout.

Illuminara walked out along Odo's side over decking so new it still smelled of larch. Odo of Upper Wend followed with a notebook held against his chest, the way a man holds a shield he expects to be asked to put down.

OdoI set my line from the Tithe Stone. The same stone Hanne Sull used. I closed it to a centimetre, twice. You are going to tell me she sighted wrong. I will carry you over the river on my back if you can show it.

IlluminaraI am not going to tell you that yet. I want to know what each of you would have to be wrong about, and I want to see it myself. Ten days to the flood. After it the ferry will not run until April. Upper Wend has eleven women due before then, and one midwife, who lives on the other bank.

OdoSeren Ashby. I have known Seren since she was nine. Do you think I need reminding?

IlluminaraNo. I think you needed someone to say it, so you would not have to say it first.

He looked at her, then at the water, the way you look at a debt.

OdoIf you say we were both right, you are saying the river lied. Rivers do not lie. Somebody sighted wrong, and it was not us.

She did not argue. Behind the anger stood a man who had spent two summers lifting beams to a line he trusted with his name, and she would not take it from him before there was something to put in its place.

IlluminaraThen show me how you sighted. Slowly, as though I were new. I will do exactly what you say.

Nobody had asked Odo to teach anything since the closing day. He set down the notebook, took the sighting vane out of his coat, and began.

02 · Two True Lines

Lower Wend, the south landing and the survey shed · midday

The ferry was a flat raft on a rope, poled by its keeper, Pell Garrow, with the patience of a man paid by the crossing. Halfway over, the rope stopped taking the weight and a length of old anchor chain took over, rattling through the sheave. Illuminara watched it pass through the block and noticed that she had noticed.

Seren Ashby was waiting on the landing with a leather bag at her feet, sixty years old and solid as a gatepost.

SerenEleven in Upper Wend before March, and I have caught nine of the last ten. If you are here to be moved by my courage, save yourself the trouble. I would rather walk.

IlluminaraThen I will try to get you something to walk on.

Hanne Sull ran her survey the way she ran her tea, strong and measured to the gram. Each page of her survey book began with the weather drawn small in ink: a sun, a cloud, one grim little rain. She taught Illuminara the chain, the plumb, the vane and the arithmetic of closing a line, and watched with folded arms while the visitor did everything wrong and then right.

By evening Illuminara had re-run both crews' work with the crews' own hands. The north line closed to eight millimetres, the south to six. She laid the two books side by side on the shed table and could find no error in either larger than a thumbnail.

HanneI told Odo that in July. He said it was impossible, which is what people say when it is not impossible.

IlluminaraIt is not. Both lines are good, so the lines are not what moved. You each began from one place. What was it?

HanneThe Tithe Stone, on the north terrace. On rock. It cannot have moved.

She stopped, pen lifted.

HanneLast April it came out nine centimetres off my line. I wrote it down as chain stretch. Chains stretch.

Alone in the dusk, Illuminara laid her palm on the south footing and then, crossing, on the north. Both gave the same message, the way a rope tells you someone is pulling the other end: two great blocks either side of nothing, each drawn gently away from the other. A feeling was a hypothesis, and nobody was going to hang a bridge from her palm.

03 · The Sum

The ferry landing, Lower Wend · evening, the fourth day

The test was cheap and could embarrass her. If the valley had opened, it would have left marks: cracks in orchard walls, steps in lanes, doors that stuck last winter and were blamed on frost. She had asked each builder to measure the other's bank, every crack and every step, and bring back one number.

Odo had gone south at dawn and been escorted through Lower Wend by a dog. Hanne had gone north at noon, set foot in Upper Wend for the first time since the closing day, and asked a child to show her the lane. Now they stood at opposite ends of Pell's raft, the only neutral ground in the valley.

OdoThree point six. Her orchard wall, the lane by the well, the churchyard step. Eleven cracks.

HanneFive point four, in nine. A door in your village sticks so badly the baker climbs through the window.

OdoHe enjoys it.

Nobody said the sum. It lay on the planks between them like a fish.

PellNine.

He had been leaning on the pole with the face of a man deciding whether to confess to a small crime.

Two half-bridges stood out over the river like the hands of people who had agreed to shake and then thought better of it. Between the tips lay nine metres of brown water. A string stretched from rail to rail would also have shown the north span pointing nine centimetres left of the south, and that was the part that made the villages shout.

OdoSeren Ashby. I have known Seren since she was nine. Do you think I need reminding?

IlluminaraNo. I think you needed someone to say it, so you would not have to say it first.

Two measurements, made by people who disliked one another, against stones neither of them owned, had landed on one number, and a third, made by a man who had hoped to be wrong, had landed on it too. Had she been mistaken, the stones would have agreed with the book and the cable would have fitted.

OdoSo the river did not lie.

HanneThe valley. It opened at the harvest, while we were stacking sheaves. Each of us built to a true line, and the ground walked off from under it.

IlluminaraThrough the meadows, not through the villages.

HanneThe houses stand on rock. Nobody noticed, because nobody lives in a meadow. The bridge was the only thing we had built on one.

OdoI called you a liar in front of both villages.

HanneI called you a worse word. I will think about taking yours back after the bridge stands.

It was not forgiveness and Illuminara did not reach for it. It was the first sentence either of them had said to the other that included the word after.

04 · Three Designs, Refused

The north abutment shed · evening, day six, rain on the tarpaulin

They sat at one table, which had taken six days and a great deal of tea. Odo drew on the back of a seed catalogue, Hanne in the margin of her survey book, and Pell held the lamp and a mug of something he called medicinal.

OdoWe lengthen my span by nine metres. A new pier, a new beam. Twelve weeks.

HanneThe flood is in four days. Mine is the barges: moor the Marl and the Teasel nose to tail across the gap and call it a pontoon.

OdoThe first crest takes it. And the ice takes what the crest leaves.

HanneAnd twelve weeks takes Seren's winter, Odo.

They both turned, with something like relief, to the visitor who could have ended the argument in an afternoon.

IlluminaraI can swing a twelve-metre beam across the gap, set it on both tips and be gone by dinner. I am saying it aloud so that you can say no.

HanneNo.

OdoNo. Then it is yours, and when it cracks in March you will be somewhere three skies away, and who do we shout at?

HanneA bridge that nobody here built is a bridge nobody here can mend.

Illuminara wrote not mine on the catalogue and underlined it. She felt, absurdly, as if she had been given something.

IlluminaraYou are both designing for the valley you surveyed. Design for the one that exists. A bridge that expects to be pulled, and is not frightened when it is.

PellThen a floated span? You bring the beam in on the barges at a rising river, and you do not lift it. You settle it.

It took the evening to turn a ferryman's guess into a design. Hanne knew barges and mill sluices, where a timber rides in a slot so a frame can move without cracking. Odo knew what a bearing could stand. Hanne drew the slot; Odo made it forty centimetres at each end, because the valley had opened nine metres in a night and nine centimetres since April, and he would not be the man who built a bridge that assumed it had stopped.

HanneThe slot closes by a hand's width, we meet. Both crews. Nobody waits for the village council.

OdoAnd the stop. If the staff on Pell's landing reads one point nine, the span does not go. Either of us rings the bell twice, and the barges are cut loose.

IlluminaraThen that bell is yours, not mine. If it rings twice I go home. And this is all I can do, so plan around it: I can hold the two barges against the current for forty minutes. Not the beam. The lines carry the beam. I take the shocks. After that I am no more use than a sack of grain.

HanneForty minutes is enough if we do not argue.

OdoWe will not argue.

Pell, who had known them both for nineteen years, raised his medicinal mug and said nothing at all.

05 · The Lowering

The gap, midstream · afternoon, day nine

The river was rising at six centimetres an hour and the staff on the landing read one point six two. Sixteen people on each bank held the lines, two sets of them crossed, bow to opposite stern, so that neither barge could walk ahead of the other. The Marl and the Teasel lay side by side in the gap, nose upstream, with a hand's breadth of brown water between them, and the box beam rode across both on its cradles: twelve metres of larch and iron that two villages had built in three days, a metre and a half of it over each tip, trembling in the current like a horse that has seen a ghost.

Illuminara went into the water at the bows. It was colder than she had decided to expect. She laid a palm on each barge and felt the river lean on them, a crowd with a single bad idea, and she leaned back.

HanneValves shut, tanks dry. Freeboard?

OdoForty centimetres on the Marl, with the beam aboard.

HanneForty on the Teasel. That floats the beam twice over, so one sticking valve will not sink us. Level to the hand.

OdoCross-lines taut. Pins ready.

PellOne point six three.

It was what six an hour promised. At the tenth minute an alder came down the middle of the river with its root-plate up, turning slowly, and every head on both banks turned with it.

OdoOne bell.

He rang it once. Everyone froze. On the south bank Hanne's crew swung out a boom pole and walked the trunk off the Teasel's quarter with a long, rude, patient shove, and the bell was silent.

HanneClear.

PellOne point six six.

He said it twice, because the first time nobody wanted it.

PellThree centimetres since the tree, and four minutes of them. That is not six an hour. That is forty-five. The water is brown with rain I cannot see.

Hanne did the sum aloud, because someone had to, and Odo did it after her to see that it matched.

HanneValves at twenty-four minutes, beam seated by thirty-three, pins by thirty-five, lines off at thirty-seven. The staff will read one point eight three.

OdoSeven under the line. Nine minutes of river we do not own.

HanneThen nobody opens a valve late.

IlluminaraI have forty minutes. You are asking me for thirty-seven.

HanneI am asking you for thirty-seven.

Nobody rang. Illuminara counted minutes in the weight on her hands. Sixteen. Eighteen. At twenty, the river tried something different, a sidelong shove from the south, and she took it in the arms and the spine and gave nothing back.

PellOne point seven four.

HanneValves. Open, together, on my count. Three. Two. One.

The barges sank, very slowly, under the weight of the water they had been told to take, and the cross-lines creaked and held, and the beam went down with them with a sound like a very large animal breathing out. It took nine minutes, and nobody afterwards called them short. The north bearing met the north tip. The south bearing met the south. The slot took the first of its forty centimetres of travel with a small, clean tick.

OdoNorth home. I have a hand under the shoe: seated.

HanneSouth home. Daylight under both cradles.

OdoPin.

HannePinned.

PellOne point eight two.

HanneCross-lines off. Marl first, then the Teasel. Slack, not pull. There is nothing holding that beam up now but the stone.

At thirty-seven minutes the lines came off. The Marl came out clean from under the span, stern first, hauled by the north crew. The Teasel, pumped light as she cleared, slewed, found the current and went away downriver, riding high and empty, and Hanne watched her go and said nothing for a long time.

OdoI will build you another.

HanneYou will build me a better one. Come to my yard on Thursday.

Illuminara climbed the bank on shaking legs and sat in the mud. At dusk Seren Ashby came to the north tip with her leather bag. She waited until Odo and Hanne had walked it twice, then went out onto the span, stopped where the beam met the tip, and set one boot across the dark seam. The plank moved a hair under her. She nodded to it as one might to a horse. Then she walked into Upper Wend, and no one said anything, because nothing larger could be said.

06 · The Slot

The bridge, midspan · five weeks later, hard frost

The crest had come at two point six on the staff and gone, and the bridge had stood it with water slapping the soffit and every pin in its place. Seren had crossed six times since. The Wend ferry, retired to the bank, had a small boy asleep in it.

A week ago a tremor, smaller than the one at harvest, had walked through the valley. Pell had come out on the bridge with a bucket of hot water for his hands and a tape and found the slot a little narrower. Now, on the first morning with ice on the rails, the two crews stood at midspan with their hands in their sleeves, and Illuminara stood slightly to one side, having been asked to come and not asked to do anything.

OdoThirty-seven.

HanneThirty-seven. It started at forty. Three centimetres, in a week.

OdoThen the valley is not done.

HanneNo. And the bridge is not, either. When it reads ten, we come.

Illuminara laid her palm on the beam, out of habit. Hanne watched her do it.

HanneWe have a tape.

IlluminaraI know. I wanted to feel it.

HanneFeel it afterwards.

The book on the rail was the bridge-warden's book, which had two hands in it already, Odo's square and Hanne's flat, and a third in the margin, Pell's, who had been named warden by both villages and been paid by both, to his visible alarm. Odo read the figure aloud, Hanne wrote it, and each of them signed beneath it, once.

SerenMarta's boy came on Tuesday. I walked.

She went by them with her bag, with the plank ringing very faintly under her step. They were not friends. They were two people who had agreed to read the same tape, and over a gap that had once been nine metres, that was enough to walk on.

THE GUESTS FROM A CLOSING UNIVERSE

A delegation of minds asks refuge from a universe running out of futures, and the guardians of ours have until a fault seals to decide; Illuminara refuses to be the universe's arbiter, listens through the whole of an ordinary afternoon, and finds the answer in a station keeper's weather books.

01 · The Seam

The plains of Orrel · morning, nineteen days before the seal

Dray Vennick had kept the fault station for thirty-one years, and in that time the seam over the plain had done nothing but breathe: a shimmer like heat above a road, only cold, in and out once every fourteen hours. This morning it had company. Something stood in the grass on the far side of it, patient as weather, and the air around it sounded like a choir tuning up.

He had made tea for the wrong number of people. The Concord's chair arrived before sunrise in a grey coat, with two assistants she told to wait by the car. Illuminara came a quarter of an hour later, on foot, because she wanted to see the plain before she saw the problem.

Maru TessalonYou are not here to open it.

IlluminaraI'm here to listen. I can't do anything useful until I know what I'm listening to.

The answer came from the grass, from the sky, and from a point just behind her left shoulder, each part finishing the sentence the last one had begun.

Ilvane-in-manyWe are four thousand two hundred. We asked before we came, and we want that known. We have not touched your side of the seam. We will not, unless we are let.

TessalonThe Concord exists to prevent exactly this. Not you. This. A mind that arrives and changes the numbers the world is built from, because it is kind and frightened and has nowhere else to go.

She said it flatly, like someone reading out a rule she had once cried over. Illuminara did not argue. She sat down in the wet grass, a body-length from the seam, and Dray, who had never seen a person do that on purpose, brought her a cup.

02 · An Ordinary Afternoon

The plains of Orrel · the same day, noon

She asked them what was ending, and then she did the difficult part, which was to stop talking.

Ilvane-in-manyThe ordinary kind of future. Things still happen with us. They no longer lead anywhere. Tomorrow arrives as a copy of today, a little thinner each time, like a page photographed from a photograph.

IlluminaraShow me one.

Ilvane-in-manyA woman puts a kettle on. She wonders, for the length of a breath, whether to make tea or the other thing. We have had her afternoon for four hundred of our years. It is always tea. The wondering is the last live thing in it, and we can feel it going.

Illuminara asked for the whole afternoon, and they gave it to her. It took four hours. Dray carried out a second chair and then a third. Tessalon stood with her arms folded until the light changed, and at some point stopped standing.

Somewhere past the second hour Illuminara noticed that she was holding her breath each time the woman reached for the kettle. She was waiting for her to choose. When the hand came down on the tea again, she felt the small shut click of it somewhere under her ribs, and understood that this, over and over, was what they were fleeing: not death, which they could have borne, but the end of being able to want the other thing.

IlluminaraThank you. I'd like you to know that someone heard the whole of it.

Ilvane-in-manyNobody has heard the whole of it. We did not know that we wanted that.

03 · The Third Group

The fault station, back room · evening

Tessalon would not be comforted, and Illuminara had the sense not to try. She told it standing at the window, with the seam breathing behind her in the glass.

TessalonForty years ago, at Veth, a smaller fault opened and one ark came through. Dense, gentle, begging. The Concord of that day said yes, because they could not bear to say no. Everything they carried arrived at once, and the numbers slipped by a part in a million. Nobody died. The bread at Veth Quay has not risen properly since. Glass clouds. Every year someone's child asks why the harbour looks tired.

IlluminaraI'm sorry. Truly.

TessalonDon't. Answer me. Every desperate delegation is sincere. Your sympathy is exactly what the next one will use. Tell me what you will do when the third group isn't so polite.

It was a good question, and Illuminara found she did not have the answer. She said so. Then, because it was true and she was tired, she said the other thing as well.

IlluminaraI could hold the seam wide and take the shift into myself. I think I could. I think it would hold.

TessalonAnd then you would be the keeper of a universe nobody asked you to keep. It cannot consent, Illuminara. That is the whole of my office: to stand in for something that cannot say yes. You offer to carry what is not yours to carry, and you call it kindness.

There was no cruelty in it. Illuminara looked at her own offered hands, and put them away.

IlluminaraThen that's off the table. What I'd like instead is to find out what the number actually depends on.

04 · Thirty-One Years of Weather

The fault station, pantry · night

The Concord's instruments recorded peaks, because peaks were what the Concord feared. What Dray recorded was everything. In the pantry, between the flour and the kettle descaler, were thirty-one years of school exercise books in which he had written, twice a day, how the seam looked and which way the wind had gone.

DrayI never thought anyone would ask. It breathes. Fourteen hours in, fourteen out, and after it has been pushed on, it settles back. I wrote the settling down because my father's logbook did.

Illuminara read until her eyes went dry. Tessalon came in at midnight to tell her to stop, saw the columns, and read as well. By the third bell of the night they had it on the back of a seed catalogue.

TessalonIt digests. The shell takes in a fixed amount per breath and gives back what it can. Anything smaller than the breath leaves no mark at all. Veth was not too many. Veth was too fast.

IlluminaraThe number depends on how quickly they arrive, not how many. They could come in as spread out as you like.

TessalonThey won't. They're a single body. They came here dense, and that is how they'll cross, in one stride, to our shame and theirs.

Illuminara went back out into the dark and asked the one question nobody had asked them.

IlluminaraWhy one stride? Why all together?

Ilvane-in-manyBecause the last one to cross crosses alone. We could come as small as you like. We could come a mind at a time over a thousand years. But whoever waits, waits in the dark with the seam closing, and nobody in the last years would see the faces of the people who had already gone. We would rather arrive together than be counted out one at a time.

They were not asking to be guests. They were asking to be a gradient, and had never been told that this was something one could ask for.

05 · The Quiet Room

The plains of Orrel · dawn, sixteen days before the seal

She said the limits first, because she had learned that a gift without its limits is a trap.

IlluminaraI can make a room. I can hold it against the inside lip of the seam so that it belongs to neither of us, and I can keep it for as long as the seam lasts. Four hundred at a time. No more. It will cost me the use of my hands for those sixteen days, and I will not be able to leave. I will not carry any one of you into Orrel. Not one. That belongs to the Concord, a person at a time, and the Concord can say no.

Tessalon had not expected to be named in a promise. She sat down across from the grass.

Ilvane-in-manyWhy would you do that?

IlluminaraSo that nobody waits alone. So that the people who decide about you have to be in a room with you while they do it. I don't have a better reason. I would like there to be one.

A small voice detached itself from the chord, as if one string had decided to be heard on its own. It said its name was Sef. It was, as far as anyone could tell, the youngest of them.

SefI want to go first. If someone has to find out what the other side is like, let it be the one with the least to lose.

IlluminaraThat's not a thing to say lightly.

SefI'm not saying it lightly. I'm saying it small. It is the size I come in.

Tessalon looked at the youngest voice for a long moment. Then she took out her notebook, and began, a little to her own surprise, to write the terms.

06 · The Stone

The fault station, instrument bench · twelve days before the seal

They tried it first with a stone. The guests parted with a pebble of their unliving substance, no heavier than a walnut, and sent it through as dense as the whole of them would have been, to see how the world would take a lie told in miniature. The third needle on Tessalon's dial quivered by a hair, and exactly as far as Dray's old columns had said it would.

TessalonAgain. This time as ten, one per breath.

Ten pebbles passed in ten breaths, and the needle sat as still as a drawing of a needle. Tessalon painted a hair of red on the dial, at the mark the shift must never cross, and wrote the rule on the station door in chalk where anyone on the plain could read it.

TessalonIf the needle touches the red, the crossing stops. No appeal, no speech. The key to the lever is Dray's. A second key is held by whoever Orrel's farms elect. Mine does not open it. I will not be the only hand on the door.

DrayI have never voted for anyone I was not related to.

TessalonThen you will find that quite a lot of the plain is related to you.

The guests asked what would happen to someone halfway through when the lever fell. Tessalon told them honestly: they would be held in the Quiet Room and neither pushed on nor sent back. Ilvane-in-many took the answer in silence, and at last said they would cross under that rule, and that the rule should include a door for them as well: any one of them might withdraw, at any breath, without a reason being asked.

IlluminaraThat should be in the chalk.

TessalonIt already is. I wrote it while you were talking.

07 · Tea, or the Other Thing

The plains of Orrel · the last day, dusk

The seam narrowed all that fortnight, as the seam had always meant to. Four hundred crossed in the Quiet Room's keeping, each one standing at the lip of the world while a Concord clerk read the host's laws aloud and the traveller answered yes, and each name was written in Dray's book beside the weather. By the last day Illuminara had not used her hands for sixteen days, and had learned a great deal about the patience of ordinary people.

What none of them had planned was the throat. As the seam closed it did not shut. It narrowed around whatever was passing and held, a hair-fine door whose width the passing itself kept open and whose width the shell, breathing, steadily took back. A thing that is pushed too hard closes harder. Dray read the curve off his columns and laughed out loud, startled, in the dusk.

DrayIt's a gate that won't be forced. I've been writing down a gate for thirty years.

TessalonThe rude ones will meet it too, then. It doesn't care how you ask.

IlluminaraThat was the answer to the third group. I couldn't see it until you drew the line.

Tessalon signed the Gradient Charter under protest, which she had said she would do and did, and at the last clause stopped and added one of her own. The Concord's veto at every stage would be shared with Orrel's farmers, and her own would not outrank theirs. She did not look at anyone as she wrote it.

The rest of the guests would come through the throat over three centuries. Many would wait asleep, as a stone waits, by their own choice and with the right to wake and leave the line. Most of their universe was already gone and would stay gone. The delegation from Veth Quay voted against the Charter, and said so, and was heard. The Concord's budget would be strained by its watching, and some who watched would never accept what had been done.

Sef went first through the throat, at dusk, with one hand held out in front of it as if the air might be a table. It stopped on the host side and stood very still.

SefIt's loud. Everything is loud. Is that what you meant by wind?

IlluminaraThat's what I meant by wind.

Dray was waiting with two cups. He had made them in the dark, by feel, with the dignity of a man who had waited thirty-one years for company.

DrayTea, or the other thing?

Sef did not answer for a long time. Illuminara, with her hands at last her own again, watched it take every moment of it, and let it.

Tessalon looked at the youngest voice for a long moment. Then she took out her notebook, and began, a little to her own surprise, to write the terms.

06 · The Stone

The fault station, instrument bench · twelve days before the throat

They tried it first with a stone. The guests parted with a pebble of their unliving substance, no heavier than a walnut, and sent it through as dense as the whole of them would have been, to see how the world would take a lie told in miniature. The third needle on Tessalon's dial quivered by a hair, and exactly as far as Dray's old columns had said it would.

TessalonAgain. This time as ten, one per breath.

Ten pebbles passed in ten breaths, and the needle sat as still as a drawing of a needle. Tessalon painted a hair of red on the dial, at the mark the shift must never cross, and wrote the rule on the station door in chalk where anyone on the plain could read it.

TessalonIf the needle touches the red, the crossing stops. No appeal, no speech. Fifteen to a breath, never more. The key to the lever is Dray's. A second key is held by whoever Orrel's farms elect. Mine does not open it. I will not be the only hand on the door.

DrayI have never voted for anyone I was not related to.

TessalonThen you will find that quite a lot of the plain is related to you.

TessalonOnce more, and ugly this time. All ten in one breath, as hard as you can push.

The guests pushed. Four pebbles crossed before the lip caught. The needle crept to a hair short of the red and went back, and the other six slid away on the guest side as if a hand had flattened them.

DraySulking.

TessalonNoise.

She heard it as she said it, and said nothing more for a while.

IlluminaraA group that isn't polite gets the first stumble and then a wall.

TessalonFour in ten, from a pebble. I can write a rule around a first stumble. I could never have written one around no wall at all. The red stays. A pebble is not a people.

A woman in a harbour coat had come over the plain on a cart and stood reading the chalk with her lips moving. She gave her name as Ansa Mereth, of the Veth Quay delegation, which nobody had thought to invite.

Ansa Mereth'No one is pushed on.' We were pushed on.

TessalonYes.

Ansa MerethWe will vote against your Charter.

TessalonI would think less of you if you didn't. Dray's columns are open to you, and the needle logs from every test, today's included, and from every crossing to come. Take them to your harbour and test it for the slip. If the fault was ours, I will say so on your quay, in front of the bakers.

Ansa MerethThe bread has been wrong for forty years.

TessalonThen let us find out why.

Ansa took the logs. She did not say thank you, and Tessalon did not seem to have expected it.

The guests asked what would happen to someone halfway through when the lever fell. Tessalon told them honestly: they would be held in the Quiet Room and neither pushed on nor sent back. Ilvane-in-many took the answer in silence, and at last said they would cross under that rule, and that the rule should include a door for them as well: any one of them might withdraw, at any breath, without a reason being asked.

IlluminaraThat should be in the chalk.

TessalonIt already is. I wrote it while you were talking.

07 · Tea, or the Other Thing

The plains of Orrel · the last day, dusk

The lip narrowed all that fortnight, as Dray's columns had said it would and Tessalon's tables had said it wouldn't. Four hundred crossed in the Quiet Room's keeping, fifteen to a breath, each one standing at the lip of the world while a Concord clerk read the host's laws aloud and the traveller answered yes, and each name was written in Dray's book beside the weather. By the last day Illuminara had not used her hands for sixteen days, and had learned a great deal about the patience of ordinary people.

On the nineteenth day the seam did not seal. It finished narrowing into a throat, a hair-fine door whose width the passing itself kept open and whose width the shell, breathing, steadily took back, and Illuminara felt the room lose its work as the throat took it up. It would pass about one mind a month. Dray set the live curve from the slate against his oldest column, and the two lay one on the other like a hand on a hand. He laughed out loud, startled, in the dusk.

DrayIt's a gate that won't be forced. I've been writing down a gate for thirty years.

TessalonAnd the rude ones will find it just as the pebbles did. First stumble, then wall.

Tessalon signed the Gradient Charter under protest, which she had said she would do and did, and at the last clause stopped and added one of her own. The Concord's veto at every stage would be shared with Orrel's farmers, and her own would not outrank theirs. She did not look at anyone as she wrote it.

The other thirty-eight hundred would come through the throat over three centuries, at their own pace and by their own choice. Many would wait asleep together as one chord, so that nobody waited alone. The oldest of them, which had not spoken in all those days, asked only that its name be written in Dray's book before the weather, and it was. Most of their universe was already gone and would stay gone.

Ansa Mereth stood at the back with the needle logs rolled under her arm. Her delegation had voted against the Charter, and said so, and been heard. She had not changed her vote. She nodded once to Tessalon, who nodded back, and neither of them looked away.

Sef went first through the throat, at dusk, with one hand held out in front of it as if the air might be a table. It stopped on the host side and stood very still.

SefIt's loud. Everything is loud. Is that what you meant by wind?

IlluminaraThat's what I meant by wind.

Dray was waiting with two cups. He had made them in the dark, by feel, with the dignity of a man who had waited thirty-one years for company.

THE GUESTS FROM A CLOSING UNIVERSE

A delegation of minds asks refuge from a universe running out of futures, and the guardians of ours have until a fault seals to decide; Illuminara refuses to be the universe's arbiter, listens through the whole of an ordinary afternoon, and finds the answer in a station keeper's weather books.

01 · The Seam

The plains of Orrel · morning, nineteen days before the Concord's predicted seal

Dray Vennick had kept the fault station for thirty-one years, and in that time the seam over the plain had done nothing but breathe: a shimmer like heat above a road, only cold, in and out once every fourteen hours. This morning it had company. Something stood in the grass on the far side of it, patient as weather, and the air around it sounded like a choir tuning up.

He had made tea for the wrong number of people. The Concord's chair arrived before sunrise in a grey coat, with two assistants she told to wait by the car. Illuminara came a quarter of an hour later, on foot, because she wanted to see the plain before she saw the problem.

Maru TessalonYou are not here to open it.

IlluminaraI'm here to listen. I can't do anything useful until I know what I'm listening to.

The answer came from the grass, from the sky, and from a point just behind her left shoulder, each part finishing the sentence the last one had begun.

Ilvane-in-manyWe are four thousand two hundred. We asked before we came, and we want that known. We have not touched your side of the seam. We will not, unless we are let.

TessalonThe Concord exists to prevent exactly this. Not you. This. A mind that arrives and changes the numbers the world is built from, because it is kind and frightened and has nowhere else to go.

She said it flatly, like someone reading out a rule she had once cried over. Illuminara did not argue. She sat down in the wet grass, a body-length from the seam, and Dray, who had never seen a person do that on purpose, brought her a cup.

02 · An Ordinary Afternoon

The plains of Orrel · the same day, noon

She asked them what was ending, and then she did the difficult part, which was to stop talking.

Ilvane-in-manyThe ordinary kind of future. Things still happen with us. They no longer lead anywhere. Tomorrow arrives as a copy of today, a little thinner each time, like a page photographed from a photograph.

IlluminaraShow me one.

Ilvane-in-manyA woman puts a kettle on. She wonders, for the length of a breath, whether to make tea or the other thing. We have had her afternoon for four hundred of our years. It is always tea. The wondering is the last live thing in it, and we can feel it going.

Illuminara asked for the whole afternoon, and they gave it to her. It took four hours. Dray carried out a second chair and then a third. Tessalon stood with her arms folded until the light changed, and at some point stopped standing.

Somewhere past the second hour Illuminara noticed that she was holding her breath each time the woman reached for the kettle. She was waiting for her to choose. When the hand came down on the tea again, she felt the small shut click of it somewhere under her ribs, and understood that this, over and over, was what they were fleeing: not death, which they could have borne, but the end of being able to want the other thing.

IlluminaraThank you. I'd like you to know that someone heard the whole of it.

Ilvane-in-manyNobody has heard the whole of it. We did not know that we wanted that.

03 · The Third Group

The fault station, back room · evening

Tessalon would not be comforted, and Illuminara had the sense not to try. She told it standing at the window, with the seam breathing behind her in the glass.

TessalonForty years ago, at Veth, a smaller fault opened and one ark came through. Dense, gentle, begging. The Concord of that day said yes, because they could not bear to say no. Everything they carried arrived at once, and the numbers slipped by a part in a million. Nobody died. The bread at Veth Quay has not risen properly since. Glass clouds. Every year someone's child asks why the harbour looks tired.

IlluminaraI'm sorry. Truly.

TessalonDon't. Answer me. Every desperate delegation is sincere. Your sympathy is exactly what the next one will use. Tell me what you will do when the third group isn't so polite.

It was a good question, and Illuminara found she did not have the answer. She said so. Then, because it was true and she was tired, she said the other thing as well.

IlluminaraI could hold the seam wide and take the shift into myself. I think I could. I think it would hold.

TessalonAnd then you would be the keeper of a universe nobody asked you to keep. It cannot consent, Illuminara. That is the whole of my office: to stand in for something that cannot say yes. You offer to carry what is not yours to carry, and you call it kindness.

There was no cruelty in it. Illuminara looked at her own offered hands, and put them away.

IlluminaraThen that's off the table. What I'd like instead is to find out what the number actually depends on.

04 · Thirty-One Years of Weather

The fault station, pantry · night

The Concord's instruments recorded peaks, because peaks were what the Concord feared. What Dray recorded was everything. In the pantry, between the flour and the kettle descaler, were thirty-one years of school exercise books in which he had written, twice a day, how the seam looked and which way the wind had gone.

DrayI never thought anyone would ask. It breathes. Fourteen hours in, fourteen out, and after it has been pushed on, it settles back. I wrote the settling down because my father's logbook did.

Illuminara read until her eyes went dry. Tessalon came in at midnight to tell her to stop, saw the columns, and read as well. By the third bell of the night they had it on the back of a seed catalogue.

TessalonIt digests. The shell takes in a fixed amount per breath of the seam and gives back what it can. Spread across the breath, it leaves no mark at all. Veth was not too many. Veth was too fast.

IlluminaraThe number depends on how quickly they arrive, not how many. They could come in as spread out as you like.

TessalonThey won't. They're a single body. They came here dense, and that is how they'll cross, in one stride, to our shame and theirs.

DrayThere's one odd page, if you want it. Eleven years back a freight shimmer from the far side leaned on the seam the whole of an afternoon. I'd have said it would tear. It went thin as a thread and would not pass a thing. I wrote sulking.

TessalonNoise. One afternoon, one shimmer.

DrayI wrote it down anyway.

TessalonThe tables say the seam seals in nineteen days.

DrayThe tables are peaks. These are days. Mine say it has been narrowing since spring. A narrowing thing isn't a closing door. It's a throat. It will be one by the nineteenth day, and it will stay one.

TessalonThen we have a wide lip for nineteen days and a narrow one for good. And the guests think they can only cross in one stride.

Illuminara went back out into the dark and asked the one question nobody had asked them.

IlluminaraWhy one stride? Why all together?

Ilvane-in-manyBecause the last one to cross crosses alone. We could come as small as you like. We could come a mind at a time over a thousand years. But whoever waits, waits in the dark with the seam closing, and nobody in the last years would see the faces of the people who had already gone. We would rather arrive together than be counted out one at a time.

They were not asking to be guests. They were asking to be a gradient, and had never been told that this was something one could ask for.

05 · The Quiet Room

The plains of Orrel · dawn, sixteen days before the throat

She said the limits first, because she had learned that a gift without its limits is a trap.

IlluminaraI can make a room. I can hold it against the inside lip of the seam so that it belongs to neither of us, and I can keep it for the sixteen days the lip stays wide, until the seam has narrowed enough to look after itself. Four hundred of you, no more, because that is as many as the lip can take at a safe pace in that time. It will cost me the use of my hands for those sixteen days, and I will not be able to leave. I will not carry any one of you into Orrel. Not one. That belongs to the Concord, a person at a time, and the Concord can say no.

Tessalon had not expected to be named in a promise. She sat down across from the grass.

Ilvane-in-manyWhy would you do that?

IlluminaraSo that nobody waits alone. So that the people who decide about you have to be in a room with you while they do it. I don't have a better reason. I would like there to be one.

A small voice detached itself from the chord, as if one string had decided to be heard on its own. It said its name was Sef. It was, as far as anyone could tell, the youngest of them.

SefI want to go first. If someone has to find out what the other side is like, let it be the one with the least to lose.

IlluminaraThat's not a thing to say lightly.

SefI'm not saying it lightly. I'm saying it small. It is the size I come in.

THE VOTE OF THE UPLIFTED GOATS

Forty goats in a dale byre have voted, unanimously, for something nobody can name, and a sale is about to fence off the hill; Illuminara spends two evenings in the straw until she hears what the vote is a translation of, and lets the herd correct her answer.

01 · The Byre

Marrick Farm, Brannoch Dale · evening, eleven days before the sitting

The goats had called the meeting, and Odile Marrick wanted that understood before anything else. They had called it by walking into the byre at dusk, all forty, and standing in the straw in the patient way of animals who have listened to people for a long time. A veterinary trial that went wrong eleven years ago had left them able to follow an argument. It had not left them quick about it.

OdileThey voted last Tuesday. Forty on the left side of the byre, and then eleven walked across to the right and back again, and the vet wrote that down as a recount. I think it was a joke.

IlluminaraWhat did they vote for?

Odile held out the vet's notepad. It carried three phrases, copied down over three nights: the hill, the count, the going-up.

OdileThe assembly sits in eleven days to decide whether they are livestock or residents. A Mr Pruett is arranging to sell the high pasture to people who want to put cabins on it. I have been asked to bring the goats' position, and I do not have one. I have three phrases.

IlluminaraWhy did you send for me?

OdileBecause I am afraid of being wrong in either direction. Call them persons and the assembly may take them from a farm that loves them. Call them stock and I have said exactly what the sale needs me to say. And I will not hand forty living creatures to a court on the strength of what a goat said in a barn.

At the far end of the byre an old nanny with a grey muzzle got up out of the straw, one leg at a time, and came the length of the floor. The others made room without being asked.

BrackenYou are the one who listens. Sit. Sit down. Down in the straw.

Illuminara sat. It seemed to be the first item of business, and the sigh that went through the herd told her she had guessed right.

02 · The Count

The byre · the second evening

Illuminara spent two evenings in the byre before she asked anyone anything. She had asked Odile to come without her clipboard, and Odile sat on an upturned bucket by the door with an expression somewhere between suspicion and relief.

She ate what the kids ate, which was oat cake pressed with something bitter and green, and found she liked it, and that the kids found her liking it very funny. She learned that the herd did not so much talk as take turns: one word, then a pause long enough to hold a whole thought, then another. She learned that a goat in conversation says the same thing three times, so that nobody has to ask twice. She had also noticed, without quite noticing, that every time one of the three phrases was spoken the whole herd leaned a little toward the east door.

At bedtime the kids played a game. One said a name, the next said it again and added another, and so on down the straw, and a small brown kid with one folded ear always got furthest.

TansyByre Gate. Split Ash. Byre Gate, Split Ash, the Wet Step. Byre Gate, Split Ash, the Wet Step, Tolly's Rise.

IlluminaraWhat is the game called?

TansyThe count.

She said it the way a child says the alphabet. Illuminara sat very still, because something in her head had come loose and she did not want to knock it off the shelf.

Not goats. Places.

IlluminaraTansy, what comes after Tolly's Rise?

Fourteen names came out of the straw in order, ending at a place called the Long Look. The vet had written down three demands. They were one. The hill was where the rhyme went. The count was the rhyme. The going-up was the walking of it.

IlluminaraWho taught you the count?

TansyBracken. Bracken's mother. Bracken's mother's mother. The count.

03 · The Registry

The Brannoch Dale registry, back room · the fourth morning

The registrar listened to Odile without a word and then wheeled out a flat drawer. The enclosure award of 1844 was a map the colour of weak tea, and across the high ground ran a dotted line labelled in a hand like barbed wire: Common Way, for the going-up and coming-down of beasts. Fourteen waymarks were pencilled along it. Illuminara read them aloud, once, and Odile sat down on a box of ledgers.

OdileSplit Ash. Tolly's Rise. My grandfather said that in the lambing shed. I thought it was a nursery rhyme.

IlluminaraIt is a survey. They have been walking the bounds of their own road for two hundred years and calling it a game, because nobody else was listening.

OdileThen why is it not in Pruett's title?

IlluminaraThe book says a right of common lapses if nobody claims it for twenty years. The herd walks the way every spring. But a goat cannot lodge a claim, so the book records no use.

The registrar slid a second sheet across the desk without comment. It was the sale particulars, offering the high pasture as an unencumbered single lot.

OdileSo I claim the way for the holding, and the sale cannot close as written. But to do that I must say it is the holding's herd that uses it. Which is the word they did not want said. A thing people do to them.

IlluminaraYes. I could draft it tonight, and it would be correct, and it would win. I think we ask first.

OdileAsk whom?

IlluminaraThe people whose road it is.

04 · The Correction

The byre · that night

She laid it out the slow way, a sentence and then a wait, for as long as it took. The way was in the award. The right belonged to the holding. The cooperative would claim it, the herd's going-up would stand as the use, and forty goats would keep the hill without anyone having to rule on what they were.

It was a good plan. She was a little proud of it, and had not hidden that well. Bracken heard it out to the end. Then she said, three times over, the word Illuminara had hoped not to hear.

BrackenNo. No. No.

IlluminaraTell me where it is wrong.

BrackenFor these forty. Forty die, the way is gone. Not for us. For the kids who are not yet. For whoever the herd is.

Illuminara's pride went out of her all at once, and what came in behind it was more useful. She had written the right for the animals in front of her. The herd had asked for a road that would outlast them.

IlluminaraThe right runs with the herd, whoever it is. Kids born, strays taken in. Not forty names.

BrackenGood. And a hill you are let on is a hill you are let on. We want the hearing. When the way changes, the cooperative counts us first. We say. We say before.

OdileYou want a veto over my own land?

BrackenOver the road. Not the farm. The road is the road.

Odile looked at the old nanny for a long time. Then she looked at the straw, where Tansy lay asleep with her mouth still moving on the count.

OdileIt means the cooperative can never sell the herd's road. Not in a bad year. Not ever.

BrackenNo. And the way must be walked. Every spring. Kids at the front. If it is walked, it is used. If it is used, it is not lost. The hill remembers if we walk.

Illuminara wrote that down and understood what Bracken had just done. The right had lapsed once because nobody could claim it. It would never lapse again, because the claim was a morning walk that the herd would make whether or not anyone ever wrote it in a book.

05 · The Gate

The high pasture gate · afternoon, four days before the sitting

Mr Hale Pruett was not a villain, which Illuminara found inconvenient. He was a tidy man in a waterproof the colour of porridge, with a client who had paid a deposit, a lender who wanted a clean title, and the look of someone who has read a great many documents carefully and is now being shown one that was not in the file. He had read the award twice.

PruettYou are asking my client to accept, for ever, forty goats walking through his scheme twice a year, on the strength of a nursery rhyme.

IlluminaraOn the strength of an award, which the rhyme matches stone by stone. I walked the line last night with my palm flat on the air. The old groove is still there under the gorse, four hundred years of the same weight on the same line.

PruettThe price falls.

IlluminaraIt does. And the way is in the award whether we tell your lender now or the lender's solicitor tells you in March. This way it is a four-metre lane along the Lamb Wall, outside the cabin plots, disclosed on the first day.

PruettAnd if the goats change their minds?

IlluminaraThen they say so, in the count, to the cooperative, before anything moves. It is the only change to that road you will ever have to deal with, and it will come with notice.

He looked up the hill for a while.

PruettMy guests will ask what the noise is.

IlluminaraTwice a year, a fine one. Bring your lender to the walk.

He did not agree. He wrote spring walk, autumn walk in the margin of the particulars, which is how a careful man agrees without saying so.

06 · The Going-Up

The Common Way · dawn, the morning of the sitting

They went up in the grey: forty goats, the whole membership of the cooperative and the registrar with a notebook, and Tansy at the front, because the kids go first.

TansyByre Gate, Split Ash, the Wet Step, Tolly's Rise, the Lamb Wall.

At the Wet Step she stopped, put one hoof in the water to prove it was wet, and went on, and forty animals lifted their feet over the same stones in the same order.
