Ilse BrannockAlways in a gap. I called it the small hours because that was the gap we kept giving it.

Ilse BrannockFour-oh-five. Shift change. The ring goes quiet for twenty minutes while the crews swap.

IlluminaraThe size follows the loudness before the gap. The timing follows the gap itself. If there is an intention here, the least extravagant account is not anger. It is turn-taking: something raising its voice over a crowd, then waiting not to be overwritten. But the same trace could still come from a rotating spot, a precursor that suppresses our band, or chance.

Ilse BrannockSay what you want to do.

IlluminaraMove the gap. Fill four-oh-five with ordinary traffic, open a new gap at seven, and write every prediction before we touch the switches.

Ilse BrannockThe exchange monitor shares the band. A precursor could fool it.

IlluminaraWhat does not share it?

Ilse BrannockThe old bolometric plate. Hard wire, separate clock, nothing in the exchange band. Rourke wanted it scrapped.

IlluminaraThen it stays. And you present the test. I will not borrow nine years of your listening and call it my discovery.

Ilse looked at the double-underlined question in her ledger. Hope is not evidence, Illuminara thought. But shame can hide evidence for years if nobody makes room for the person carrying it.

Ilse BrannockI will present it if the envelope contains the ways I may be wrong.

IlluminaraPut them first.

03 · The Case for Flight

Council chamber · Day 1, 18:00

Vance opened the session by reading the clock aloud: fifty-nine hours, ten minutes. Then she gave the floor to Rourke, who stood with his hands behind him, like a man giving evidence in a trial he hoped to lose.

Pell RourkeThe dangerous dawn alignment on Day Four, ordinary traffic, one point three of rating. Our two requested test gaps may draw smaller responses before it. If they do, that is new behavior, not the seventh and eighth members of the old sequence. It may strengthen the case for turn-taking, or mean the experiment itself is increasing the hazard.

Teodora VanceThat's the case for flight, and I will make it myself so nobody thinks I haven't. Evacuations fail when they start late. A star that changes because we ask it to is not automatically safer than a star that does not.

Gideon FarrowWho pays if we flee from a weather event? The ice is my guild's wages and the ring's drinking water. It can't be that nobody may ask whether the star is just a star.

Teodora VanceNobody has forbidden it. Dr. Brannock?

I have three rivals: a spot rotating every twenty-four-point-one hours, a lull caused by a precursor rather than chosen by us, and chance.

Teodora VanceHow much chance?

Ilse BrannockI preserved the clustering in the nine-year record and shuffled ten thousand pairs of gaps with the same widths and traffic levels. Seven pairs caught bursts in both timing windows and both amplitude bands. Seven in ten thousand is not zero. It is also not an argument I would throw away.

Dov AchterbergA calculation built from the same ledger that suggested the question. And your windows are fifty minutes wide.

Ilse BrannockYes. Which is why the spot and precursor predictions are sealed beside ours. If the spot fires at the old hour, we lose. If the exchange band fails while the independent plate stays quiet, we lose. If one requested result misses, we write miss before we explain anything.

IlluminaraAt four-oh-five tomorrow we fill the usual gap with ordinary traffic. At seven we pause the exchange net for twenty-two minutes. The independent plate remains live. We repeat with a shorter gap after the next dusk peak. The council writes the stop conditions.

Gideon FarrowWhat does the pause cost my traders?

IlluminaraTell the room what they need to keep.

Gideon FarrowThe settlement hour. Move around it and I will sell the test to the guild. I won't sell a permanent blackout.

Dov AchterbergNor should he. A scheduled silence is a scheduled vulnerability. Medical calls, collision alarms, smugglers who know when nobody is looking. If the proposed cure requires fourteen thousand people to become deaf on a timetable, I prefer the ferries.

Illuminara turned toward him rather than back to the lectern.

IlluminaraThen the test must preserve an emergency carrier outside the crowded band, and any lasting arrangement must be movable. Nadim, can that be done without contaminating the plate?

Nadim OyelaranA narrow red channel, hard-limited to alarms and medical speech. The plate won't see it. For a lasting window, the Chair could choose within a ninety-minute band and announce it fifteen minutes ahead.

Teodora VanceNoted. My cancel line: any requested burst over nine-tenths, any burst outside both registered windows, any failure of the independent plate, or any failure of the red channel. The ferries are fuelled tonight and manifests cut. A trigger starts loading within one hour; completing it still takes twenty-six. Nobody edits that sentence afterward.

04 · The Gap Moves

Communications office, exchange net · Day 2, 06:52

At four-oh-five the old gap had been filled, and the Wick had said nothing. The exchange band stayed clean; so did the independent bolometric plate. Ilse had been awake since the previous morning and sat very straight in a chair she had not chosen.

Nadim OyelaranSealed envelope is in the council log. Rotation said four-oh-five, which did not happen. Precursor said the exchange band would fail there while the plate remained quiet, which did not happen. Turn-taking says seven, within twenty-five minutes, between half and seven-tenths of rating.

At seven the exchange net went quiet. Kitchens went on, ferries stayed fuelled, and the red emergency carrier whispered with two medical calls and one collision alarm. The trading floor stopped for twenty-two minutes as fourteen thousand people agreed to leave a space.

The hard-wired plate drew a flat line, then a flat line, and then a sharp stroke at seven-oh-two. The network monitor followed a fraction later. The long shoulder on the decay was the mark Ilse had drawn in her ledger for nine years.

Ilse BrannockFifty-eight hundredths on the plate.

Nadim OyelaranInside timing and amplitude. Red channel never dropped.

Nobody cheered. Illuminara held Ilse's elbow only after the older woman reached for her.

Ilse BrannockOne.

IlluminaraOne.

The second requested gap came at twenty-two thirty on the same day, after a smaller dusk peak. A weak rise appeared on the exchange monitor eleven minutes before the pause. Dov, watching from the council feed, called it a precursor. The hard-wired plate stayed level.

At twenty-two thirty-six the Wick flared. The registered amplitude band ended at forty hundredths. The plate climbed to forty-one.

Dov AchterbergOutside the envelope.

Ilse BrannockBy one hundredth. It is a miss.

Nadim OyelaranThe early rise was our own carrier leaking into the exchange monitor. It is absent from the plate. That defeats the precursor claim, but it does not put the amplitude back inside the envelope.

Pell RourkeAnd two requested responses in sixteen hours are faster than the old forty-four-hour background. If we are causing them, that matters more than whether we have taught the sun manners.

Illuminara studied the two traces and did not rescue her prediction.

IlluminaraRecord the timing hit, the amplitude miss, the failed precursor rival and the faster cadence. Then stop opening gaps until the council decides what the faster cadence means.

Ilse BrannockYou wanted a second night.

IlluminaraI wanted an answer that could tell us no. This one has.

05 · Forty Hours

Council chamber · Day 2, 23:10

Clock hour forty found the chamber full. On the wall were four lines, none softened: OLD-GAP SILENCE; FIRST REQUEST HIT; SECOND REQUEST TIMING HIT / AMPLITUDE MISS; REQUESTED CADENCE FASTER THAN BACKGROUND.

Teodora VanceNobody in this room gets to call that two clean predictions. Dr. Brannock, what survives?

Ilse BrannockThe rotating-spot prediction failed at four-oh-five. The precursor prediction failed on the independent plate. In ten thousand paired shuffles, seven matched both timing and amplitude; ours matched both timings but only one amplitude. The data still prefers schedule-response. It does not prove a mind, and the faster cadence may be a cost of asking.

Dov AchterbergThen stop asking and load the ferries. The experiment changed the thing we feared.

Pell RourkeOr exposed that it was already waiting for gaps we happened to give it. The Day Four burst remains the dangerous one. With the dusk cap and the parasol turned before dawn, my median is eight-tenths. Without them, one point three.

Dov AchterbergMedian. Your upper edge?

Pell RourkeNine-tenths. At the cancel line.

The two numbers stayed between them. Vance looked not at Illuminara but at Ilse.

Teodora VanceIf we stay, what do you ask the Wick to do?

Ilse BrannockNothing beyond what the dangerous burst may do anyway. One bounded silence at dawn, three pulses from our cutter, then no second request. If the flare comes in the window and under the line, we learn whether leaving room changes the load. If not, the manifests are already cut.

Gideon FarrowThe dusk cap costs the guild its best settlement of the quarter. We will take it once. Not daily, and not without the loss entered beside the science.

Dov AchterbergAnd no fixed daily blackout. The red channel stays open. Any later window moves inside the ninety-minute band, fifteen minutes' notice, renewed by vote each day. Security may cancel it without your permission.

Nadim OyelaranI can enforce that in hardware. Trade carrier dark; red carrier live; plate independent. Six signatures to change it.

IlluminaraThat is better than what I brought you.

Teodora VanceIt is safer because the people paying for it changed it.

Vance kept one hand on the written cancel line.

Teodora VanceThe ferries stay fuelled. Loading starts within one hour if the plate crosses nine-tenths, the flare leaves the window, the red carrier fails, or security calls the silence unsafe. Anyone may take a berth now. We attempt one bounded exchange at dawn. Dov's moving-window amendment and Farrow's cost ledger are part of the motion.

The vote passed seven to four, not nine to two. Dov voted no. His amendment passed eleven to zero.

Afterward the reply was designed in the communications office. Nadim had the forty-metre ice-cutting array. Ilse had her ledger open to the rising edge of the first requested flare.

Nadim OyelaranI can give it a beam. I can't tell you it will see it.

Ilse BrannockThree pulses on the rhythm of its own rise. Then silence for as long as the pulses took. Heard, and your turn.

IlluminaraNo claim about what it means.

Ilse BrannockNo. Only a courtesy we can withdraw.

06 · A Turn at Four-Oh-Five

Calloway Reach, communications office and Rakel Quay · Day 4, 04:05

Under ordinary traffic the dangerous burst had been forecast at one point three of parasol rating. Farrow's dusk cap cost the guild its best evening of the quarter. Turning the parasol cost a month's thruster propellant and left Rakel Quay outside its full shadow. Rourke's registered range was seven-tenths to nine-tenths. Nine-tenths remained the line.

The Chair chose four-oh-five from the ninety-minute band and announced it fifteen minutes before. The red carrier stayed live. In the communications office Nadim held the beam trigger. On Rakel Quay his sister Kemi and two riggers waited beside the relay-mast breakers, because the model said the exposed masts would take the first side-load.

Kemi OyelaranRakel ready. You owe me two masts if your polite sun sneezes.

Nadim OyelaranPut them on Farrow's ledger.

Gideon FarrowThey are already there.

At four-oh-five Nadim sent three pulses. The trade band remained silent afterward. A medical call crossed the red carrier from nursery six; a child had swallowed a button. The silence did not make the ring helpless.

Four minutes passed.

The independent plate climbed.

Pell RourkePoint six. Point seven-two. Parasol taking thirty-one percent.

A second shoulder rose under the first.

Teodora VanceRead the plate, not the model.

Pell RourkePoint eight-six.

At Rakel, the first mast began to arc. Kemi cut its breaker before the automatic relay understood what was happening. The mast folded across an empty loading rail. The second leaned toward a fuel line.

Kemi OyelaranLosing west two. Clearing the line now.

She drove the quay tug into the mast's lower brace. Metal went down away from the fuel line, taking the tug's manipulator arm with it.

Nadim OyelaranKemi?

Kemi OyelaranStill expensive.

The plate touched eighty-nine hundredths. For twelve seconds its uncertainty band crossed the line, though the central reading did not.

Teodora VanceRourke.

Pell RourkeCentral reading below nine. Structure stable. My recommendation is hold, Chair. Your line says over, not near.

Vance's finger rested on the loading order. She could have called uncertainty a trigger. Nobody would have blamed her.

Teodora VanceHold. Kemi has the quay. Red carrier is live. If the central plate rises one hundredth, load.

It did not. The long shoulder fell through eight-tenths, then seven. The parasol held. Rakel lost two relay masts and one tug arm; no one was hurt.

In the decay, with Nadim's array still silent and the ring keeping the space it had promised, the independent plate drew three small steps.

Ilse BrannockThree. I have nine years and it has never made three.

IlluminaraDon't read it yet. We don't know that it's a reply.

Ilse BrannockNo. We know only that it happened after our three.

They did not repeat the request that night. The next day the council authorized one movable window, with the red channel and security veto intact, and required a fresh vote every seven days. Farrow entered the lost settlement, two masts, a tug arm and a month of propellant in the same ledger as the avoided evacuation. Dov signed the safety protocol and wrote beneath his name that he still believed they should leave.

Teodora VanceHe is allowed to be wrong in the record, if he is wrong.

IlluminaraSo are we.

Ilse closed her ledger, opened it again, and wrote on the next clean line in her small upright hand: Four-oh-five. We stopped. It knocked.

THE STAR THAT ONLY SPOKE IN FLARES

A ring habitat of fourteen thousand has seventy hours to decide whether its star is attacking it, and the only evidence that it is not is a silence nobody had thought to measure.

01 · Seventy Hours

Calloway Reach, Ring Council chamber · Day 1, 06:10

The clock on the chamber wall read 70:00:00. Someone had put it there so that it would be read aloud, and nobody had. Outside the long window the ring turned slowly under a red sun the size of a coin, with fourteen thousand people on its inner face, and the room smelled of cold tea and of a council that had not slept.

Illuminara had come aboard three weeks earlier on an ice tender, hired by the Rakel cooperative to model how heat and light loaded the cutting quays. She was in the chamber because her models were the only ones nobody had yet argued with. She stood at the back, beside the water jug.

Teodora VanceThe Wick has thrown six dangerous bursts in eleven days. In nine years of records it threw about one a month. Eleven days is two hundred and sixty-four hours; six bursts in that time is one every forty-four, and that is not a fluctuation I can fold into the background. They cluster after our evening traffic peaks. The next natural alignment is due at about four in the morning on Day Four. Under ordinary traffic the shield office forecasts one point three times the rating of our parasol. Ferries need twenty-six hours to finish loading, and I will not cut a two-hour margin out of a ring's lives. The order has to go out by hour forty-two.

Pell RourkeThe parasol takes one burst. I will not promise it takes that one.

IlluminaraWhat does leaving cost?

Teodora VanceRakel. Everything we mine. A ring that leaves carries eight months of water, and after that it's a very large cup.

Vance was sixty and square-shouldered, with the habit of putting the worst number first so that no one could accuse her of hiding it. She turned from the window to face the back of the room.

Teodora VanceDon't tell me it's talking. We have no way to know it is speaking at all, and you are asking fourteen thousand people to stay under a possible weapon on the strength of a pattern. If I'm wrong about the weapon we lose the ice and a year. If you're wrong we lose the ring.

IlluminaraI won't tell you it's talking. I haven't seen enough to say so, and you would be right not to believe me if I did. I'd like your dock-clock traffic log, Dr. Brannock's flare record, the specifications of every detector, and the room until the evening session.

Teodora VanceThe council sits at eighteen hundred. At eighteen hundred I put the evacuation to a vote.

IlluminaraThen I'll bring you something you can test before you vote.

Vance looked at the clock and then at her. Curiosity did not soften her face; it made the responsibility in it more exact.

Teodora VanceTest it with what? We have sixty-nine hours and fifty-one minutes.

02 · Nine Years of Margins

Ring observatory, Brannock's office · Day 1, 09:30

Ilse Brannock kept the flare record in a ledger as well as on the network, because the ledger could not be edited by anyone who disliked it. Nine years of the Wick filled it, night by night, in a small upright hand with questions in the margins. A few were underlined twice.

Ilse BrannockYou're the ice woman with the thermal models.

IlluminaraToday I'm the ice woman who read your flare record. It's very clean. Who keeps it?

Ilse BrannockI do. Nobody else wanted to. A flare is a flare.

IlluminaraYou don't think so.

Ilse put a hand flat on the ledger as one might on a sleeping animal.

Ilse BrannockI showed this to two people. One laughed, kindly, which was worse. I said the Wick grows louder when we do. After every busy evening the next burst is larger by about the same fraction. A star's flares don't care about our trade. I knew how it sounded, so I stopped saying it.

IlluminaraAnd the timing?

Ilse BrannockAlways in a gap. I called it the small hours because that was the gap we kept giving it.

Illuminara laid the traffic log over the flare record on the glass table. The observatory clock and dock clock were three minutes apart. Nobody had held the records together because the exchange net carried private trade.

She slid one trace by three minutes. The bright marks dropped into the troughs of the traffic like coins into a purse.

Ilse BrannockFour-oh-five. Shift change. The ring goes quiet for twenty minutes while the crews swap.

IlluminaraThe size follows the loudness before the gap. The timing follows the gap itself. If there is an intention here, the least extravagant account is not anger. It is turn-taking: something raising its voice over a crowd, then waiting not to be overwritten. But the same trace could still come from a rotating spot, a precursor that suppresses our band, or chance.

Ilse BrannockSay what you want to do.

IlluminaraMove the gap. Fill four-oh-five with ordinary traffic, open a new gap at seven, and write every prediction before we touch the switches.

Ilse BrannockThe exchange monitor shares the band. A precursor could fool it.

IlluminaraWhat does not share it?

Ilse BrannockThe old bolometric plate. Hard wire, separate clock, nothing in the exchange band. Rourke wanted it scrapped.

IlluminaraThen it stays. And you present the test. I will not borrow nine years of your listening and call it my discovery.

Ilse looked at the double-underlined question in her ledger. Hope is not evidence, Illuminara thought. But shame can hide evidence for years if nobody makes room for the person carrying it.

Illuminara turned the ledger's pages back to the worst flares and forward to the Day Four forecast, and stopped. The test would tell them whether the star kept time. It would not shrink the burst already coming.

IlluminaraOne more thing, and it is a question about your own margins. If the size follows the loudness before the gap, then the Day Four burst is not fixed. It is being sized right now by what we do on the evening of Day Three. What happens to the flare after a quiet evening?

Ilse turned eight pages without looking for them. The smallest flares in the book were all there: the nights after the ring had gone dark for the harvest festival, when the trade band was nearly empty by dusk.

Ilse BrannockSmall. They're the smallest in the book. I put them down to the calendar.

IlluminaraThen the lever is the dusk peak, not the gap. If the council can cap one evening's traffic before the Day Four alignment, the parasol may meet something near eight-tenths instead of one point three. Pell will have to model it. I can't promise it. I can tell you which number to try to move.

Ilse BrannockI will present it if the envelope contains the ways I may be wrong.

IlluminaraPut them first.

03 · The Case for Flight

Council chamber · Day 1, 18:00

Vance opened the session by reading the clock aloud: fifty-eight hours, ten minutes. Then she gave the floor to Rourke, who stood with his hands behind him, like a man giving evidence in a trial he hoped to lose.

Pell RourkeThe dangerous dawn alignment on Day Four, ordinary traffic, one point three of rating. Our two requested test gaps may draw smaller responses before it. If they do, that is new behavior, not the seventh and eighth members of the old sequence. It may strengthen the case for turn-taking, or mean the experiment itself is increasing the hazard.

Teodora VanceThat's the case for flight, and I will make it myself so nobody thinks I haven't. Evacuations fail when they start late. A star that changes because we ask it to is not automatically safer than a star that does not.

Gideon Farrow rose from the guild benches. He was round and beautifully dressed and had been counting something in his head for the whole session.

Gideon FarrowWho pays if we flee from a weather event? The ice is my guild's wages and the ring's drinking water. It can't be that nobody may ask whether the star is just a star.

Teodora VanceNobody has forbidden it. Dr. Brannock?

Ilse stood. Her hands were steady on the lectern, and Illuminara, three rows back, saw her find the notes she had meant not to need.

Ilse BrannockI have nine years of flares, three instruments and three clocks. The timing sits in the quiet of our traffic, and the size follows the loudness before it. I have three rivals: a spot rotating every twenty-four-point-one hours, a lull caused by a precursor rather than chosen by us, and chance.

Teodora VanceHow much chance?

Ilse BrannockI kept the clustering and the one-a-month background of the nine-year record, and shuffled ten thousand pairs of gaps with the same widths and traffic levels. Seven pairs caught bursts in both timing windows and both amplitude bands. Seven in ten thousand is not zero. It is also not an argument I would throw away.

Dov AchterbergA calculation built from the same ledger that suggested the question. And your windows are fifty minutes wide.

Ilse BrannockYes. Which is why the spot and precursor predictions are sealed beside ours. If the spot fires at the old hour, we lose. If the exchange band fails while the independent plate stays quiet, we lose. If one requested result misses, we write miss before we explain anything.

IlluminaraAt four-oh-five tomorrow we fill the usual gap with ordinary traffic. At seven we pause the exchange net for twenty-two minutes. The independent plate remains live. We repeat with a shorter gap after the next dusk peak. And there is a second lever, which the ledger itself points to. The size follows the loudness before the gap, so the Day Four burst is being sized by the evening of Day Three. If the guild caps that one dusk peak, Pell's median should fall well below the parasol's rating. That is a prediction too, and it can fail. The council writes the stop conditions.

Gideon FarrowWhat does the pause cost my traders? And what does your cap cost them?

IlluminaraTell the room what they need to keep.

Gideon FarrowThe settlement hour. Move around it and I will sell the test to the guild. The cap I will price tonight, and the number will not be small: that dusk is my best evening of the quarter. I won't sell a permanent blackout, and I won't sell a permanent cap.

Dov AchterbergNor should he. A scheduled silence is a scheduled vulnerability. Medical calls, collision alarms, smugglers who know when nobody is looking. If the proposed cure requires fourteen thousand people to become deaf on a timetable, I prefer the ferries.

Illuminara turned toward him rather than back to the lectern.

IlluminaraThen the test must preserve an emergency carrier outside the crowded band, and any lasting arrangement must be movable. Nadim, can that be done without contaminating the plate?

Nadim OyelaranA narrow red channel, hard-limited to alarms and medical speech. The plate won't see it. For a lasting window, the Chair could choose within a ninety-minute band and announce it fifteen minutes ahead.

Teodora VanceNoted. My cancel line: any requested burst over nine-tenths, any burst outside both registered windows, any failure of the independent plate, or any failure of the red channel. The ferries are fuelled tonight and manifests cut. A trigger starts loading within one hour; completing it still takes twenty-six. Nobody edits that sentence afterward.

THE FIRE THAT KNEW HOW TO BURN

An eighty-one-year-old woman has lit forty-one small fires on a hill the fire service wants emptied, and the only way to prove she is right is to find the one place her map is wrong.

01 · Burns by the Wall

Sorrel Gate, upper terraces · 12:40

Smoke stood on the western ridge, six kilometres off and leaning toward them. The district had given Sorrel Gate until three o'clock. Illuminara had spent the morning walking the upper terraces with a tablet of creek gauges, which was what the regional water office had sent her to do, and she had stopped doing it at the first black patch.

There were forty-one of them now. Each was the size of a tablecloth. Each was still warm when she held her palm an inch above it. None lay in open grass. Every one lay on the sheltered side of a drystone wall or the lip of a terrace, and not one had crossed the stone.

Someone is counting the wind, she thought. Someone is lighting only where the wind has been refused.

Taavi Brandt came up the track with a drip torch hanging unlit from his belt and a young crew lead named Joss Marren a pace behind. He was fifty-odd and broad, with the stillness of a man who had learned to spend his words last.

Taavi BrandtSomebody has been lighting my hill since six this morning. Eleven fires I can account for. I'd put the rest on the same hand.

IlluminaraForty-one. I've walked them all.

Taavi BrandtThen you've walked forty-one places where a fire could have got away from a person. Constable Hale is at the church with an order for Ivet Corrandon. She's eighty-one, she won't open her door to my crews, and at dark I carry her down that road myself. I would sooner she walked.

IlluminaraLook at where they are, Chief. Not at who.

He looked, because he was fair and because she had said it quietly. He looked at the nearest patch and the wall above it, and for the length of a breath he said nothing.

Taavi BrandtCalder Fold. Nine years ago. I lit a backburn, lawful and signed, in a wind that behaved for four hours. In the fifth it veered and the fire took the track and then a barn, and there was a man asleep in the barn. Aldous Penn. Careful fires are the ones that kill people. The careless ones don't last long enough.

IlluminaraThen I won't argue that she's careful. I'll ask whether she's right, and look for an instrument that can answer without either of us having to believe anything. Let me speak to her first.

Taavi BrandtUntil two. At two the buses load, and she's on one or she's on my shoulder.

02 · What the Hill Was For

Corrandon cottage, kitchen · 13:15

The door was not locked. Illuminara knocked anyway, and a voice told her through the wood that it never was, that people simply believed it was, and that she could come in if she had the sense to wipe her boots.

Ivet Corrandon sat at the table with ash to the elbows, a match tin at her right hand and a blackthorn stick against her chair. Across her left palm ran a blister the width of a finger. She had the face of someone who had been right for a long time without anyone's help.

Ivet CorrandonYou're the water girl. They said a water girl was on my walls with a machine.

IlluminaraI'm a water-modeller. The machine is a tablet and mostly it counts creeks. May I sit?

Ivet CorrandonIf you've come to take me to the bus you can sit on the floor.

IlluminaraI've no authority to take you anywhere. I came to ask about the wall at the top of Pellam's field.

The old woman looked at her for some time. Illuminara took the clean cloth from the dresser while she waited and asked, with her eyes, about the hand. A question can wait and a blister cannot. Ivet let her do it, watching with open suspicion and then, slowly, with less.

Ivet CorrandonIn nineteen eighty-four a forestry man stood in this kitchen and told my Edrin the hill must not be burned, not by anyone, not ever, and he took the paper that said we could. Edrin was fined. He didn't speak for a week. Forty years we've lived under a hill with nothing to do but grow.

IlluminaraAnd you went on burning.

Ivet CorrandonSmall. At the end of the wet, on the lee of the walls. Edrin called it combing. A fire that comes over a ridge is hungry, and it eats everything between itself and the next thing to eat. Comb the lee of a wall black and the headfire reaches the stone, looks over, and finds nothing for its mouth. A wall with no black behind it is only a stack of stones.

IlluminaraThen why not tell the chief?

Ivet CorrandonHe lit a hill once and a man died. I read it in the paper. He'll hear old woman, and he'll hear liability, and he will not hear wall.

She said it without cruelty, as she might have given the weight of a loaf. Illuminara had been wrong about nothing in this kitchen so far, and she had the feeling that would not last.

Ivet CorrandonAnd you. Your machine has never smelled a slope at four o'clock. It's never stood where the air changes its mind.

IlluminaraNo, it hasn't. So tell me where your map is wrong. I would rather find that here than on the ridge.

Ivet CorrandonNowhere.

The silence went on long enough for the kettle to tick. Ivet looked at the dressed hand, and at the stick, and at the window.

Ivet CorrandonThe north. The gully above the Marrick cottages. I ran out of knee. Edrin never combed the gully. He said it burns itself. Then he never said another word about it, and I never asked.

Something turned over in Illuminara, quietly, like a key in a lock she had been leaning on for three weeks. The gully was the old stone leat, the flood channel she had modelled for the water office. Every storm she had run went down that cut like thread into a needle. Water finds it. So does anything else that wants to go downhill.

IlluminaraMrs Corrandon, would you tell me the order you burn in? Not the reasons. The order. I'll carry it to the chief as something he can test, with his own torch, on his own say.

Ivet CorrandonAnd if his test says I'm a fool?

IlluminaraThen a fool's mistake is corrected in thirty metres, instead of a village's in three hundred. Either way the hill is the winner.

03 · A Test He Could Stop

Sorrel Gate school, command post · 14:05

Two buses idled in the car park with their doors open. Brandt stood over a trestle table with the district map pinned under four stones, and he did not look up until she had laid her tablet on top of his county. Over his shoulder, Joss Marren was loading a hose reel and trying not to listen.

IlluminaraShe isn't lighting fires. She's combing the lee of every wall so a headfire has nothing to eat behind the stone. It's a firebreak drawn in fire. Forty years old, and the state forbade it for all of them.

Taavi BrandtThat's what she says.

IlluminaraIt's what the walls say. I read them as load paths, and a load path is an interpretation, and she could be right by accident. So I'm not asking you to believe her. I'm asking for one segment. Thirty metres of the east wall, your crew, your torch, your hose behind it. If the burn does not die at the lee by itself, you put it out and we've lost twenty minutes.

Taavi BrandtAnd if it dies by itself, I've learned about one wall. The headfire isn't one wall.

IlluminaraNo. But it's a way of turning a coincidence into a measurement. And I'd ask you to hold the second thing against it as well, because I think she's right about the walls and I'm afraid of the place she hasn't burned.

He took a long time. A bus driver coughed. Outside, a woman was counting children from the school into the first coach, name by name, getting each name right.

Taavi BrandtThen these are mine. The buses go at three, all of them, nobody comes off. Anyone not on a bus is crew or on a tanker. The wind goes southwest at about twenty to six, and if the ridge gauge shows a gust past thirty-five, or one ember lands across a wall, I put every flame out and I don't explain myself to you. And the woman stays where I can see her. Not in cuffs. At my shoulder.

IlluminaraShe'll want that. She'll want to be told what she's looking at.

Taavi BrandtHale takes her statement afterwards. She isn't pardoned. If this goes wrong at Calder's rate, I'll want it said that I heard her and chose it, not that she tricked me.

Ivet had arrived at the car park door without being noticed, which at eighty-one and with a stick took talent. She stood in the frame and heard the last of it.

Ivet CorrandonI never asked to be pardoned, Chief.

Taavi BrandtNo. I'm told you never asked anyone for anything. That's most of what's wrong with this.

04 · The Gully

East wall, then the gully head · 16:05

Joss Marren lit thirty metres of the lee at ten past four, with Brandt crouched at his elbow and Ivet in a borrowed folding chair on the track above, her stick across her knees like a sword she had decided not to draw. The flame crept three paces along the grass. It lay down against the stone and went out.

Nobody said anything. A second pass, a little further along: the same. Joss looked at his chief. Brandt put two fingers into the black and held them there.

Taavi BrandtCold.

Ivet CorrandonOf course it's cold. It had nothing to ask for.

Then the smoke from the last small patch did something that Illuminara had been waiting for and did not enjoy being right about. It did not lift. It slid sideways along the ground, thin and grey, leaning north, and went into the mouth of the gully above the Marrick cottages the way water goes into a drain.

IlluminaraChief, look at the smoke. That's my creek. The gully is the old leat, and it is the same shape for air that it is for water. When the wind goes southwest at twenty to six, the headfire won't come at the village over the walls she's combed. It'll come to the one place that has no black behind it, and the leat will take it straight down the cut and out over the top terrace.

Taavi BrandtInto the school and the Marrick cottages.

IlluminaraInto both. And it won't stop at the wall, because no one has burned anything behind that wall for forty years.

Ivet CorrandonEdrin said it burns itself.

IlluminaraWhen did he say it?

Ivet CorrandonThe year after the goats went. Hennie Marrick kept sixty goats on that cut and they ate everything to the clay. Edrin said what he saw. He didn't say the goats had been doing the burning for us.

It was the first time Illuminara had seen the old woman look surprised, and she did not look away from it, out of courtesy. Forty years of a rule that had been right on the day it was spoken.

Taavi BrandtI can't backburn it dry. Not with a headfire two hours out. Dry fuel in a cut that draws like that, I'd be lighting my own chimney.

IlluminaraThen don't burn it dry. The leat has a sluice at the head, and the creek is still running. Forty litres a second for the wet band, down the floor of the cut and over both banks, and a margin either side that your crew combs slow and downhill, Mrs Corrandon's way. A wet strip, a black strip, a wall. The fire has a river on one side and a stone on the other and nowhere to go but out.

Taavi BrandtDownhill. Not up. You said up in your notes.

IlluminaraI did.

Taavi BrandtUp and you're feeding it a ramp. Thirty years I've never lit upslope. Down, a flame has to work for every metre.

IlluminaraDown. Thank you. Then the sluice opens first, and the first torch can't light until the wet front has passed the third terrace. Eleven minutes a hundred metres. If it opens at ten past five, you light at twenty to.

The wheel at the sluice head had not turned since before Illuminara had been in the district. It took Joss and two of Brandt's volunteers and a length of scaffold pipe for a lever, and she stood by with her watch and counted them through it aloud, as one counts a woman in labour. At ten past five the stone throat filled and the cut began to talk.

05 · The Wind Comes Round

Ridge above the gully · 17:41

The wind turned a minute early.

It came off the west like a door opening in a long house, and the smoke that had leaned north for three hours stood up, thought about it, and leaned the other way. The ridge gauge on Brandt's radio read twenty-nine, then thirty-three. His crews were already in their lines: black behind every wall, a wet band shining down the bottom of the cut, a combed margin either side with the last embers of Joss's slow torch still ticking in it.

Taavi BrandtThirty-four on the gauge. One more and it's my line, and I stop everything. Nobody lights anything else. Everybody who's holding, hold.

The headfire arrived at six minutes to six. It did not come as a wave. It came as a noise, then as a colour on the underside of the smoke, then as a line of brightness across the whole west face of the hill with embers going over it like thrown seed. It reached the first wall. It looked over. Illuminara watched it do exactly what an old woman had said it would do, and find nothing for its mouth.

In the gully it was worse and better. The fire went down into the cut because the cut drew it, and met the wet band, and the wet band cooled it to a crawl; it tried both banks and found them combed and black. For forty minutes it hissed and leaned and spat at the stone. Then it ran out of road.

Not everything held. The two Marrick cottages at the north end of the cut lay beyond the strip, because there had been neither time nor water nor crew to carry the break that far, and a gust took an ember across the last wall at six-ten. Joss started toward the tanker.

Taavi BrandtNo. They're empty. Let them go.

Joss MarrenChief, they're Hennie's—

Taavi BrandtThey're stone and slates. Hennie's in the school hall with his dog. If I send one lad up that track and the wind veers again, I've done Calder in a new place. Let them go, Joss.

They went up like paper lanterns, one and then the other, and the whole crew watched them in a silence that Illuminara did not interrupt. Below them the village lay dark and standing. Three hundred roofs. A school with its windows reflecting something that was no longer a threat.

06 · What Remained

Corrandon cottage, kitchen · 21:40

Constable Hale took the statement at the kitchen table with her hat on her knee and was careful to write only what she was told. Ivet gave it with her bandaged hand flat on the wood. When it was done Hale put away her pen and said nothing about permits, because there was a chief in the doorway and it was his to say.

Taavi BrandtThe Marrick cottages are ash. The test burn was lit without a licence, on my say, against the district's written order. I'll answer for both. I'll answer, too, for the look I gave an old woman at midday.

Ivet CorrandonYou gave me a perfectly good look. I'd have given it to you.

Taavi BrandtMy report starts with your map and ends with my abort line. The review can read it in that order.

Ivet CorrandonThey'll fine me.

Taavi BrandtThey may. I'll stand beside you at the hearing and say what I saw on that wall. That isn't a pardon. I can't give you one.

Ivet CorrandonI don't want one. I want it taught.

Brandt turned his hat once in his hands. It was the nearest thing to hesitation the night had left him.

Taavi BrandtThen you'll teach my crews. Mine first, in the dry month, before any licence is argued over. The regional office can quarrel about the paper with a hillside that's still standing.

Ivet said nothing. Edrin's map lay open under the lamp, drawn forty years ago in pencil on the back of a seed catalogue: every wall of Sorrel Gate, each lee shaded. Illuminara drew one more line on it at the north, a thin blue cut with an arrow, and wrote beside it, in her small precise hand, leat and wet band, comb downhill. She turned the paper toward the old woman.

IlluminaraWould you sign it with his name as well? It's the part he never had time to finish.

Ivet took the pencil in her bandaged hand, and wrote, slowly and without once pressing too hard, Edrin Corrandon, and under it, and Ivet.

Car park wall, below the gully · 17:39

It came as a noise, then as a colour on the underside of the smoke, then as a line of brightness across the whole west face of the hill with embers going over it like thrown seed. In the gully it was worse and better. The fire went down into the cut because the cut drew it. Illuminara kept her eyes on the head of the cut and on the two banks, as she had told him she would, and said what she saw aloud so that he could hear it.

IlluminaraSlowing. Banks clear.

The wet band took it to a crawl; it tried both banks and found them combed and black, and no flame stood on either one for longer than it took to be seen. For forty minutes it hissed and leaned and spat at the stone. Then it ran out of road.

Not everything held. The two Marrick cottages lay forty metres beyond the fence where the break ended, exactly where she had marked the edge of her water, and there had been neither time nor crew to carry it further. A gust took an ember across the last wall at ten past six. Joss started along the wall toward the tanker parked at the foot of the Marrick track.

Taavi BrandtNo. They're empty. Let them go.

Joss MarrenChief, they're Hennie's—

Taavi BrandtThey're stone and slates. Hennie's in the school hall with his dog. This wall is the line, and that track is the wrong side of it. If I send one lad up it and the wind veers again, I've done Calder in a new place. Let them go, Joss.

They went up like paper lanterns, one and then the other, and the whole crew watched them in a silence that Illuminara did not interrupt. Below them the village lay dark and standing. Three hundred roofs. A school with its windows reflecting something that was no longer a threat.

06 · What Remained

Corrandon cottage, kitchen · 21:40

Constable Hale took the statement at the kitchen table with her hat on her knee and was careful to write only what she was told. Ivet gave it with her bandaged hand flat on the wood. When it was done Hale put away her pen and said nothing about permits, because there was a chief in the doorway and it was his to say.

Taavi BrandtThe Marrick cottages are ash. The test burn was lit without a licence, on my say, against the district's written order. I'll answer for both. I'll answer, too, for the look I gave an old woman at midday.

Ivet CorrandonYou gave me a perfectly good look. I'd have given it to you.

Taavi BrandtMy report starts with your map and ends with my abort line. The review can read it in that order.

Ivet CorrandonThey'll fine me.

Taavi BrandtThey may. I'll stand beside you at the hearing and carry your map in with me, with the gauge log and the times, and say what I saw on that wall and in that cut. That isn't a pardon. I can't give you one. It isn't a promise they'll adopt anything, either.

Ivet CorrandonI don't want a pardon. I want it taught.

Brandt turned his hat once in his hands. It was the nearest thing to hesitation the night had left him.

Taavi BrandtThen a trial, not a promise. Two of your walls first, my crews, in the dry month, my gauge in my hand and my line on the radio. The regional office can quarrel about the paper with a hillside that's still standing.

Ivet said nothing for a while. Edrin's map lay open under the lamp, drawn forty years ago in pencil on the back of a seed catalogue: every wall of Sorrel Gate, each lee shaded.

Ivet CorrandonThen I'll say what I'm giving, since you've said what you are. I don't light alone again. I light with your crew at my elbow, and when you call your signal my torch stops, and I won't need telling twice. And the gully goes on the map, in ink. Edrin said it burns itself. It burned itself because Hennie's goats kept it bare, and when the goats went nobody wrote the date on the rule. I want the date on it.

Illuminara drew one more line on the map at the north, a thin blue cut with an arrow, and wrote beside it, in her small precise hand, leat and wet band, comb downhill; one hill, one wind, one day. She turned the paper toward the old woman.

IlluminaraWould you sign it with his name as well? It's the part he never had time to finish.

Ivet took the pencil in her bandaged hand, and wrote, slowly and without once pressing too hard, Edrin Corrandon, and under it, and Ivet.

The Guest Too Large for the Universe

A visitor from outside the cosmos is bending the stars of the Hesper cluster, three armed powers are turning their keys, and Illuminara has to find out whether what looks like an attack is a birth, in a way none of them has to take on trust.

01 · The Nine Clocks

Command deck, Kerrel's Anchor · Day one, 06:10

Nine clocks hung on the forward bulkhead, and no two of them agreed.

The Kerrel Assembly kept them there on purpose, one for each inhabited system that still sent timing, so that its officers could see at a glance how far the sky had come apart. The spread was four minutes now. Yesterday it had been ninety seconds. Beyond the viewport the stars of the Hesper cluster sat a hair out of place, as though someone had jogged the table they stood on.

Commander Maren Vask met Illuminara at the lock with a slate in each hand and no greeting.

Maren VaskYou have until ten-forty tomorrow morning. That is not my deadline. It belongs to the Triple Key. Kerrel, the Ussu Chorus and the Halcyon fleet each hold a third of a strike order, and all three keys are turned to ready. At ten-forty the thing in the outer reach is hit with everything the Reach owns.

Wren OdiraIt has not fired on anyone. I would like that said before anybody says invader.

Wren had come aboard ahead of her, as she always did, and was already doing what she did best, which was standing beside the loudest clock.

Maren VaskIt has taken the tide-songs from two Ussu brood-worlds. It cost a convoy its navigation for six hours. It is a body the size of a small moon, nobody can find its edge, and the sky bends where it sits. I do not need it to fire, Wren. I need it to stop.

IlluminaraThen I will ask what you would ask. What is it doing, in order, and when? Not what it means. The log.

Vask gave her the left-hand slate. Nine entries. Each was a pulse: the stars within a light-year swung a few arcseconds off their places, hung there for about forty minutes, and swung back. Illuminara let AC show her the lines of strain across the cluster, the way a map shows slope, and the strain agreed with the log. A long swell, then release, then a flat quiet.

She did not look at the swells. She looked at the gaps between them.

IlluminaraTwelve hours. Ten and a half. Nine and a bit. Each gap is seven-eighths of the one before it.

Maren VaskA decaying signal. Alarms do that. So does a fuse.

IlluminaraYes. A series that shrinks by a fixed fraction has a sum, and the sum is a date. The last gap was four hours forty-three. Seven times that is thirty-three hours. At about one tomorrow afternoon the gaps become shorter than the pulses themselves, and the pulses run together into one. Your Key turns two hours and twenty minutes before that.

Nobody on the deck said anything. One of the nine clocks ticked over, three seconds ahead of its neighbour.

IlluminaraIt is an ending or a beginning. I do not know which, and neither do you. Before anything else I want a way of finding out that none of us has to take on faith.

02 · Seven-Eighths

Operations hall, Kerrel's Anchor · Day one, 07:40

The delegates came by relay: three faces and one absence. Commander Vask for Kerrel. Iyo-Seven for the Ussu Chorus, who was seven bodies in a tide-tank and spoke by turns. Tally for the Halcyon fleet, a point of cold light on the table that answered in the flat, courteous voice of a machine that had decided long ago not to be liked.

Illuminara set two stories side by side and asked them to distrust both equally.

IlluminaraStory one. A being from outside our cosmos is in labour. The pulses are contractions, and the gaps shorten because that is what labour does. Between pulses the strain falls back to the same floor, because between contractions a body rests. Story two. This is an incursion wearing a mother's shape. The pulses are a charge, and the gaps shorten because the weapon is nearly ready. Between pulses the floor would climb, because a thing that is charging does not rest.

Maren VaskStory two is the one a mother's story is built to hide.

IlluminaraYes. That is why I am not asking you to believe either. I am asking you to predict. Each of you measures the pulses with your own instruments and writes down when the next one begins and how high the floor sits after it. Seal it. Nobody opens anybody's envelope until the pulse has come.

TallyKerrel keeps time by atoms, the Chorus by song, my fleet by ranging pulsars. Our errors are unrelated. If all three of us land together, it will not be because we copied one another.

Iyo-SevenWe add what the Commander has not said. Each pulse unmakes the songs of our young. We do not ask for pity. We ask that your test be quick.

The tenth pulse began at 08:07 and held the sky for forty minutes. Tally had sealed 08:06. The Chorus had sealed 08:09, Kerrel 08:05. Behind the swell the floor dropped back to exactly where it had dropped before, within the width of a pencil line.

Maren VaskOnce. A coin can land once.

IlluminaraA coin can. So we spend every pulse we have as another throw, and we write down now what would make us stop. If the floor rises more than three parts in a hundred of the peak, or a gap breaks the seven-eighths by more than a quarter of itself, the story is false and the Key turns. We write that while none of us is frightened. We will not be able to write it when we are.

Tally took the line and logged it without comment. After a moment so did Iyo-Seven, seven bodies nodding out of step. Vask took longest.

Maren VaskAnd while the coin is still in the air, you intend to go and ask the thing itself.

IlluminaraI intend to ask her what no instrument of yours can read.

Wren OdiraI'll keep the clock. I say your name at every hour. You answer, or I come in.

IlluminaraYou can't come into a window.

Wren OdiraWatch me find out.

03 · The Window

Tide-boat Long Patience, outer reach · Day one, 09:20

The Long Patience hung a light-year and a half from the guest, which was as near as the Ussu would take her. Distance did not help. Illuminara felt the thing out in the dark as a slow tilt in the floor of everything, a hill her body leaned away from.

She made the window the way she had made them before: a place where one consciousness could meet another without either being crushed, wide enough that the guest's size could not spill into her. The guest came into it as a long dim shoreline, warm at the far end, with something at the warm end turning over in its sleep.

AnomeiYou are small, and not afraid enough. Good. The others sent engines.

IlluminaraI am Illuminara. Are you hurting my cluster on purpose?

AnomeiI am hurting it by being. You are a room, and I was offered a closet. At the first door they closed a gate. At the second they sang me away. At the third they sent a fleet. I did not come for your stars. I came for what I carry.

IlluminaraTell me what you carry.

AnomeiA child. In your word, which is a poor word for it: soon.

The shoreline shivered. Out in the cluster, a swell began to build.

AnomeiI will tell you what I have told no one, because you asked and did not aim. If I am refused a place, I will bear the child where I stand. Its first breath will make a sphere of my home's law three light-years wide, and everything inside will become part of that law. It will not be malice. It will be a birth. I would do it, small one. I would rather be the thing you fear than watch my child die in a closet.

Illuminara did not soften it. She had learned long ago that the worst thing to do with a true threat was to make it smaller for the people who had to decide about it.

IlluminaraThen I will carry that sentence to three suspicious powers exactly as you said it. They need to know what refusing you costs. And they will believe the rest of what you tell them only if you have hidden nothing.

AnomeiYou will turn them against me.

IlluminaraPerhaps. Or they will find that you did not lie when lying would have helped you. Now. What must the room be? Do not say large. Tell me how.

Anomei had no measure for it in any language Illuminara could translate. But the swell was still rising, and Illuminara understood that she had been standing in the answer for three days. Each pulse was the child leaning on the walls of the room, and the lean grew by exactly as much as the wall was missing. She ran the peak through the strain map and the map drew a sphere around the guest: six-tenths of a light-year, growing to a little under one at the end.

Then she searched the charts she carried for a place that was empty to that radius and had stayed empty.

IlluminaraThere is a void at the cluster's edge. Dornrath. Nothing in it larger than a comet for nearly two light-years in every direction.

AnomeiAt the second door they spoke of it. They called it the ocean of nobody.

IlluminaraIt is not nobody's. Nine thousand people live on its rim, in the dark, on purpose. Asking them is the first thing I must do, and they can say no.

The shoreline went quiet for a long moment.

AnomeiThen you will ask them honestly, and I will have to wait for an answer from strangers about my child. I have never asked a stranger for anything.

Wren OdiraIlluminara.

IlluminaraHere, Wren. Hour one. Here.

04 · The Ocean of Nobody

The Quiet Rung, rim of the Dornrath void · Day one, 12:15

The Tenders lived in the dark because they had wanted quiet, and three generations had not talked them out of it. Nine thousand people on a ring of habitats lit by ice-farm glow; nothing but the far cold stars over the glass. Halcyon's probes had gone through the void in four hours and Tally read out the survey as flatly as a ledger: empty to 1.9 light-years from the centre, one dead comet, no traffic, no dust worth the name.

Elder Pell Auro heard it standing, one hand on the rail of her council balcony.

Pell AuroSo you have come to rent our dark.

IlluminaraI have come to ask for it. I cannot rent what is not mine, and you may refuse.

Pell AuroAnd if I do?

IlluminaraThen I go back to a table where three keys are turning and tell them to find another room. There is no other room. I will not pretend that costs you nothing to be asked.

Pell asked to see the pulses herself, and Tally threw the floor trace on the wall: the swells rising, the floor underneath staying flat as a table. Pell looked at it for a long time.

Pell AuroI have borne four children. The floor goes flat. Between, you rest. You have to.

TallyA Tender's testimony cannot be entered as a measurement.

Pell AuroNo. I am not a measurement. I am the owner.

Illuminara let that stand, because it was true, and because the Halcyon machine had just made the better argument for her without meaning to: whatever Pell believed, she was reading the same instruments as everyone else.

IlluminaraThere is a risk and I would rather say it than have you find it. I got the size of the room from the lean of the pulses. If I am wrong by a factor of two, the edge of her sphere meets your rim.

Pell AuroThen you are asking nine thousand people to stake their lives on your arithmetic.

IlluminaraI am asking you to check it. Have your own people do the sum. And hear the rest, which is that nothing so far tells us whether this is a mother or a weapon. Only the end of the series can. So the plan has to be one we would carry out even if the worse story is true.

She laid it out for the Elder and, by relay, for Vask and Iyo-Seven. The guest would come to Dornrath in five hops, each made only in the rest between pulses, while she was folded small and could do nothing but travel. The three fleets would hold at three light-years with the Key still turned. The cancel conditions were already sealed. If the story broke, they would strike a mother or a weapon in the middle of an empty ocean, with nothing of theirs and nothing of the Tenders' within the reach of what she could do.

Pell AuroThe inner ring. Eight hundred of us live nearest the void. They go to your Kerrel transports for the day, with their children and their animals.

Maren VaskDone.

Pell AuroAnd afterward, whatever the sphere leaves in my sky, we sit at the table when it is decided what happens to it. Not as witnesses. As a hand.

IlluminaraAs a hand.

The Elder looked a moment longer at the flat line on the wall.

Pell AuroTell her the dark is lent. Not given.

IlluminaraI will tell her exactly that.

05 · Five Windows

The outer lanes · Day one, 15:33 to Day two, 01:30

The first hop opened at 15:33, the instant the twelfth pulse released the sky. The guest folded small, and for forty-four minutes the Ussu tide-boats sang a line of steady space from the outer reach toward Dornrath, and the thing that could bend the stars crossed two light-years without bending anything. Tally's probes ranged her the whole way. Vask's ships hung at the edges with their guns trained, and the guest had asked for them to be trained, so that no one could say she had come unwatched.

The second hop and the third passed the same way. At each pulse the three sealed predictions came in within a few minutes of each other and within a few minutes of the pulse. The floor stayed flat. Nobody called it proof. But Illuminara noticed, from the tide-boat, that the officers on the Anchor's deck had stopped saying story two.

The fourth pulse came eleven minutes early.

It came at 21:56 where all three predictions had said 22:07, and the sky tilted and held. On the Anchor's deck Vask's hand went to the Key before the thought did.

Maren VaskIt is early. It broke the series.

TallyIt broke it by nine per cent of a gap. The sealed limit is a quarter. The floor is flat.

Maren VaskSay it is not your guess, Illuminara.

IlluminaraIt is not my guess. It is in the tolerance we wrote down this morning, when nobody was frightened. I wrote it for exactly this minute. Please hold your hand where it is.

The hand stayed. The cost was real. The early pulse had shifted the whole series, and three instruments refit it on the spot. The last window, the one between the sixteenth and seventeenth pulses, shrank from fifty-seven minutes to forty-three. Anomei needed forty-nine to cross the final two light-years folded small. A flinch at either end would drop her into the sky of the Reach at full size, with the contractions less than an hour apart.

AnomeiI cannot do it faster.

Iyo-SevenThe Chorus can.

Seven bodies in a tide-tank, singing as one for the first time in Illuminara's hearing.

Iyo-SevenWe cannot move her. That is hers. But we can hold the strain steady along the last line so she need not bend around it. It will cost us the songs of two more broods. We choose it.

AnomeiWhy?

Iyo-SevenBecause we have lost songs to your pulses for three days, and not one of them has come at the same hour as the last. They come as a body that is trying not to hurt us. We have felt it. We know the difference between an engine and a creature that is trying.

The fifth hop opened at 00:42. It took forty-one minutes. At 01:23 the guest unfolded at the heart of the Dornrath void with two minutes to spare, and the sky of the Reach, for the first time in four days, did not tilt.

06 · The Cradle

Dornrath void, the Quiet Rung · Day two, 12:20

The last hours of the series were not measured in minutes. By noon the pulses had run together into one long swell with no floor beneath it, which the Key's cancel conditions did not forbid, because the sealed text said the floor would vanish when the gaps did. Eight hundred Tenders slept in Kerrel transports three light-years away. The three fleets held their positions at the edge of the void, as promised, with their keys turned. Wren sat in the lock of the last tide-boat with a Halcyon clock on one knee and a Kerrel clock on the other, and for the first time she did not say Illuminara's name every hour. She said it every ten minutes.

Wren OdiraIlluminara.

IlluminaraHere.

Inside the window the shoreline had become something Illuminara had no word for, a warmth the size of a world with a sharp, small pain at its centre. She did not do the birth. It was not hers. She did what a window was for: she held a place where Anomei could be as large as her labour needed and not be afraid of the size of it, and where the small one at the centre of that place could go on being small.

AnomeiI am afraid.

IlluminaraI know. Afraid is allowed. I am here.

AnomeiIf it goes wrong, say that you tried to tell them it was a mother.

IlluminaraIf it goes wrong, I will say that you told me the truth when it cost you. I will say that first.

The three sealed predictions of the end of the series came in at 12:41, 12:58 and 13:11. The swell ended at 12:58.

The child's first breath made a sphere of its home's law, and the sphere was nine-tenths of a light-year across at the edge. Tally measured it within a hair of Illuminara's number. It lay in the middle of the void with its edge a long way from the Rung, a warm bright pearl in the dark, and the strain on every star in the cluster let go at once like a held breath.

On Wren's knees, the Kerrel clock and the Halcyon clock, which had refused to agree for four days, ticked over together.

In the Anchor's command deck the nine clocks on the bulkhead were within a second of one another before Vask had finished turning her key back.

The Cradle Accord was settled by the end of the day, in the window, with the Elder, the Commander, Iyo-Seven and Tally all speaking to a mother who held her child in a sphere that nobody else could enter. The terms were exact, because the powers would not accept anything vaguer, and Illuminara, who had spent days making them say what would change their minds, did not ask them to. The sphere's edge would shrink as the child's body learned the law of this cosmos; Tally projected forty years before it dropped below the threshold at which the two could leave. Until then the Tenders would host them, the three powers would keep their instruments on the void, and the Tenders would hold a hand at every table. Messages could pass to the child's family through a single beacon, read by all four parties. No body could cross without the unanimous consent of all four.

AnomeiYou have put my family's door in four hands.

IlluminaraYes. I cannot promise any of them will turn it. I can tell you they chose to hold it, and that at the other three doors there was no hand to turn.

Anomei was silent for a long time. Then the shoreline softened, and what came into the window was not an answer but a name, which Illuminara translated as best she could. It meant something close to Hold.

Afterward, on the rim, Wren found her standing at the glass. Beyond it the dark was no longer dark; it had a small pearl in the middle of it, which would be there for forty years. The Tenders had lost their sky, and the Chorus had lost the songs of four broods that would not return. The powers would not forget the fear. None of that was small.

Wren OdiraYou didn't make them trust her.

IlluminaraNo. I made it so they didn't have to.

Wren OdiraCome and drink something hot.

Illuminara went.

03 · The Window

Tide-boat Long Patience, outer reach · Day one, 09:20

A body pressing on the sky should push the near stars hard and the far stars softly, falling away by a fixed rule. She laid the swings against the rule and asked what size of pressing thing would draw that curve. It came out as a core six-tenths of a light-year in radius at the first pulse and a little under one by the series' end. The child was leaning on the walls of the room, and the lean grew by exactly as much as the wall was missing.

It was an inference, and the weakest thing she had. She marked it so, and searched her charts for a place empty to that radius and a good deal past it.

IlluminaraThere is a void at the cluster's edge. Dornrath. Nothing in it larger than a comet for nearly two light-years in every direction.

AnomeiAt the second door they called it the ocean of nobody.

IlluminaraIt is not nobody's. Nine thousand people live on its rim, in the dark, on purpose. Asking them is the first thing I must do, and they can say no.

AnomeiThen I must wait for an answer from strangers about my child. I have never asked a stranger for anything.

Wren OdiraIlluminara.

IlluminaraHere, Wren. Hour one. Here.

04 · The Ocean of Nobody

The Quiet Rung, rim of the Dornrath void · Day one, 12:15

The eleventh pulse was still holding the sky when the Long Patience docked. The Tenders lived in the dark because they had wanted quiet, and three generations had not talked them out of it: nine thousand people on a ring of habitats lit by ice-farm glow. Tally read out Halcyon's survey as flatly as a ledger. Empty to 1.9 light-years from the centre, one dead comet, no traffic, no dust worth the name.

Elder Pell Auro heard it standing, one hand on the rail of her council balcony.

Pell AuroSo you have come to rent our dark.

IlluminaraI have come to ask for it. I cannot rent what is not mine, and you may refuse.

Pell AuroAnd if I do?

IlluminaraThen I go back to a table where three keys are turning and tell them to find another room. There is no other room. I will not pretend that costs you nothing to be asked.

Tally threw the floor trace on the wall: the swells rising, the floor underneath staying flat as a table. Pell looked at it for a long time.

Pell AuroI have borne four children. The floor goes flat. Between, you rest. You have to.

TallyA Tender's testimony cannot be entered as a measurement.

Pell AuroNo. I am not a measurement. I am the owner.

IlluminaraThere is a risk, and I would rather say it than have you find it. I got the size of the room from how the stars swung. If I am wrong by a factor of two, the fringe of her law meets your rim.

Pell AuroThen you ask nine thousand people to stake their lives on your arithmetic.

IlluminaraI ask you to check it.

Corin Daas kept the Rung's survey instruments, a slow-spoken man with ink to the wrists. He took the nine swings away for forty minutes and came back with a different number.

Corin DaasOne point three, at the end of the series. Not a little under one.

His fit leaned hardest on the nearest star, the bright one the charts called Wick.

IlluminaraWick is a double. Its suns circle each other in nine days and swing together, but the chart lists the pair as one mass. Take it out and fit the other eight.

He did, with his lips moving.

Corin DaasNought point nine seven.

IlluminaraThen I was a little low and you were a good deal high, and the double was the whole difference. Use your figure, not mine.

Pell AuroOn a void that is one point nine. And you still ask for the dark.

Illuminara laid the plan out for the Elder and, by relay, for Vask and Iyo-Seven. Nothing so far told them whether this was a mother or a weapon; only the end of the series could. So the plan had to be one they would carry out even if the worse story were true. The guest would come to Dornrath in five hops, each made only in the rest between pulses, while she was folded small and could do nothing but travel. The fleets would hold at three light-years with the Key still turned. If the story broke, they would strike a mother or a weapon in the middle of an empty ocean, with nothing of theirs or the Tenders' within reach.

Pell AuroNot enough. Your three powers hold three sealed envelopes. We will hold a fourth. Corin reads the core on our instruments at every hop, not Halcyon's. If his projection passes one point two, she does not come in, and your Key may do what it likes.

Maren VaskA fourth hand on the stop is a fourth hand that can stop it at the worst hop.

IlluminaraYes. It is also the only hand that belongs to the people nearest the harm. I would rather have a veto I cannot talk past than a yes I bought.

Vask looked at the flat line on the wall for as long as Pell had.

Maren VaskWrite it.

Pell AuroThe inner ring goes to your Kerrel transports for the day, with their children and their animals. And afterward, whatever the sphere leaves in my sky, we sit at the table when it is decided what happens to it. Not as witnesses. As a hand.

Maren VaskDone.

Pell AuroTell her the dark is lent. Not given.

IlluminaraI will tell her exactly that.

05 · Five Windows

The outer lanes · Day one, 15:33 to Day two, 01:30

The first hop opened at 15:33, the instant the twelfth pulse released the sky. The guest folded small, and for forty-four minutes the Ussu tide-boats sang a line of steady space toward Dornrath, and the thing that could bend the stars crossed two light-years without bending anything. Vask's ships hung at the edges with their guns trained, as the guest herself had asked, so that no one could say she had come unwatched. After each pulse Corin sent his projection to all four envelopes: nought point nine eight, nought point nine seven, nought point nine eight. The floor stayed flat. Nobody called it proof, but the officers on the Anchor's deck had stopped saying story two.

The fourth pulse came eleven minutes early.

It came at 21:56 where all three predictions had said 22:07, and the sky tilted and held. On the Anchor's deck Vask's hand went to the Key before the thought did.

Maren VaskIt is early. It broke the series.

TallyBy nine per cent of a gap. The sealed limit is a quarter. The floor is flat.

IlluminaraIt is not my guess. It is in the tolerance we wrote this morning, when nobody was frightened. I wrote it for exactly this minute. Please hold your hand where it is.

The hand stayed. That crisis was over, and had been paid for in advance. The other one was not.

The early pulse had shifted the series. Corin's projection crept to one point oh four, under the Tenders' line, and he initialled it aloud. But the last window, before the seventeenth pulse, had been fifty-seven minutes and was now forty-three, and Anomei needed forty-nine to cross the final two light-years folded small. A flinch at either end would drop her into the sky of the Reach at full size, with the contractions less than an hour apart.

AnomeiI cannot do it faster.

Maren VaskThen I close my ships along the line. If she falls out of the fold, I want something near enough to catch her.

Seven bodies in a tide-tank began to sing as one, for the first time in Illuminara's hearing.

Iyo-SevenNo. Your wakes are the noise we cannot hold. We cannot move her; that is hers. But we can hold the strain steady along the last line so she need not bend around it, and only if the line is empty. It will cost us the songs of two more broods. We choose that. You pay the other half: your ships stay where they are, and your guns come off the guest for forty-one minutes.

Maren VaskYou ask me to look away from the thing I was told to stop.

Iyo-SevenWe ask you to trust three other watchers. Tally still ranges her. Corin still reads her. You will see her, Commander. You will only not be pointing. We have lost songs to her pulses for three days, and not one has come at the same hour as the last. They come as a body that is trying not to hurt us. We know the difference between an engine and a creature that is trying.

Vask took longer than she had taken over anything that day. Then the guns came off.

The fifth hop opened at 00:42 and took forty-one minutes. At 01:23 the guest unfolded at the heart of the Dornrath void with two minutes to spare, and the sky of the Reach, for the first time in four days, did not tilt.

06 · The Cradle

Dornrath void, the Quiet Rung · Day two, 12:20

By noon the pulses had run together into one long swell with no floor beneath it, which the Key's cancel conditions did not forbid, because the sealed text said the floor would vanish when the gaps did. Eight hundred Tenders slept in Kerrel transports three light-years away. The three fleets held their positions at the edge of the void, as promised, with their keys turned. Wren sat in the lock of the last tide-boat with a Halcyon clock on one knee and a Kerrel clock on the other, and for the first time she did not say Illuminara's name every hour. She said it every ten minutes.

Wren OdiraIlluminara.

IlluminaraHere.

Inside the window the shoreline had become a warmth the size of a world with a sharp, small pain at its centre. Illuminara did not do the birth. It was not hers. She held a place where Anomei could be as large as her labour needed and not be afraid of it, and where the small one at the centre could go on being small.

Then the pain sharpened, and Anomei, who had never asked a stranger for anything, did what a body does in that pain. She reached outward.

On the Rung, Corin's projection went past one point two. Tally said so, flat as a ledger. At that radius the fringe of the law touched the glass where eight thousand Tenders were still asleep in their own beds.

AnomeiI cannot hold it in. It is going out of me.

IlluminaraThen do not hold it. Lean on me.

AnomeiYou are small. It will crush you.

IlluminaraI am a window. I am made of the thing you are afraid of spilling. Lean.

She had stood three days in the answer. Now she stepped into it. The hill she had always leaned away from came down on her, and she widened the window to take its weight. It was the first thing in the whole story that nobody had asked her to do and nobody else could have done.

Wren OdiraIlluminara.

Nothing answered. On Wren's knees the two clocks ticked, a hair apart.

Wren OdiraIlluminara.

IlluminaraHere.

It was very faint. Wren breathed out and went on counting.

The sealed predictions of the end of the series came in at 12:41, 12:58 and 13:11. The swell ended at 12:58. The child's first breath made a sphere of its home's law, and Tally measured the core at eighty-four hundredths of a light-year in radius, more than a tenth under Corin's projection and under hers. The difference, Illuminara knew, was the part of that first breath she had taken into herself. The fringe reached barely a light-year and a quarter, well short of the Rung. The sphere lay in the middle of the void, a warm bright pearl in the dark, and the strain on every star in the cluster let go at once like a held breath. On Wren's knees the Kerrel clock and the Halcyon clock, which had refused to agree for four days, ticked over together. In the Anchor's command deck the nine clocks were within a second of one another before Vask had finished turning her key back.

The Cradle Accord was settled that evening, in the window, with the Elder, the Commander, Iyo-Seven and Tally speaking to a mother who held her child in a sphere nobody else could enter. The sphere would shrink as the child's body learned the law of this cosmos; Tally projected forty years before the two could leave. Until then the Tenders would host them, the powers would keep their instruments on the void, and the Tenders would hold a hand at every table. Messages would pass to the child's family through one beacon, read by all four parties. No body could cross without the consent of all four.

AnomeiYou have put my family's door in four hands.

IlluminaraYes. And I will not leave it there. Any hand may refuse a crossing, but the refusal goes to the other three and to you with its reason, and it dies in a year unless that hand renews it with a new reason. A hand can keep a door shut. It cannot forget that it is shut.

Maren VaskTally will renew everything for ever. It is a machine.

TallyI will not renew a refusal I cannot justify. If I must write a reason every year, Commander, I will run out of reasons long before you do.

AnomeiA year is long.

IlluminaraA year is not for ever. I cannot promise any of them will turn it. I can tell you they chose to hold it, and that at the other three doors there was no hand to turn.

Anomei was silent for a long time. Then the shoreline softened, and what came into the window was not an answer but a name, which Illuminara translated as best she could. It meant something close to Hold.

Afterward, on the rim, Wren found her standing at the glass. Beyond it the dark was no longer dark; it had a small pearl in the middle of it, which would be there for forty years. The Tenders had lost their sky, and the Chorus the songs of four broods that would not return. The powers would not forget the fear. Where the hill had pressed on Illuminara there was a bruise she would carry for a while. None of that was small.

Wren OdiraYou didn't make them trust her.

IlluminaraNo. I made it so they didn't have to.

Wren OdiraCome and drink something hot.

Illuminara went.
