The districts chose: Kiru's stone buttress outside the graves; Belu's public plates with local keys; Sava's terraced anchors tied to the trench. Kemi's crew would supervise every old connection.

Adaeze signed beneath the three requirements and accepted the seam chair only until the rain. Venn signed last. One package went to tender at 10:27. It contained no single wall.

05 · The Seams

Aruwa hillside · Days 2 to 11

The road culvert went in first. Illuminara held the exposed load path while the crew seated the second arch. She released it after thirty-eight minutes, before mortar could lock a hidden dependence into the joint; the arch had to show it could carry itself. Mensah stopped work when the first bedding layer crossed its settlement limit. Kemi's crew rebuilt it.

Kiru curved its buttress around the burial field. Belu installed twelve public plates on ferrite ribs, each with a physical key. Sava drove terraced anchors and fitted removable gates where every terrace met the old trench.

Every seam needed three signatures: ministry inspector, district operator and a neighbouring crew. During the sixth-plate test Kemi closed the lower drain gate. The transfer needle climbed past eight and stopped at eleven percent toward Kiru.

Chief Engineer Lio MensahThe plate passes its own specification. The seam fails.

Sami DaroHold the gate there. Change the angle, not the reading.

Sami reset the plate by two degrees. Kiru's masons laid a sacrificial slip course while Kemi reopened the gate one notch at a time. The needle fell to six percent and decayed in seven minutes. All three crews signed the fault before they signed the repair.

On Day 9 Cadran offered a storm monitor with no control channel.

AdaezeCan the districts turn it off?

Sami DaroAt our office. Raw records remain ours.

AdaezeThen it may watch. It may not become the memory we cannot afford to lose.

By Day 11 the culvert carried twice the old peak, every log was public at the hospital and each module passed dry load. Adaeze refused the ministry's photograph until Kemi and all three operators stood in it.

06 · Rain

St. Orra Hospital and Aruwa hillside · Day 12, 03:20 to 18:40

Rain arrived three hours early and harder than forecast. The piezometers rose; ninety minutes later the slope markers answered. Water entered the Sava trench at the red house and struck the road culvert in a brown sheet. The throat held.

At 06:40 Kiru's seam alarm showed nine percent toward Belu. Sami Daro reduced plate six and Kemi delayed gate four until the pressure peak. The transfer stayed above the eight-percent cap. Ten sustained minutes exhausted the pin's rated endurance.

The passive link broke with a sound like a snapped spade handle. Belu separated from Kiru exactly as the standard required. Kiru's buttress carried alone, its sacrificial slip course grinding five millimetres.

The eastern Kiru marker began to move: one millimetre, then two. Nia Sorel's voice came through the hospital channel.

Nia SorelPaediatrics is ready to clear. Tell me whether the rate is still rising.

Kemi SolHold the wing. The marker slowed when gate four opened; the next reading decides.

Venn heard the ministry lawyer ask who would own an evacuation if the third reading rose.

Director Miro Venn, on the radioCadran can take the plates now. I can put one operator under the liability.

Sami DaroThen put my name under the local key. Belu stands alone.

He turned the key to safe angle. Kemi watched the white stone disappear beneath the trench.

Kemi SolGate four open. Terrace closed to the trench. Send it all to the culvert.

The third marker reading held at two millimetres, then fell. Nia kept the wing occupied. For fourteen minutes the districts carried separate loads while the culvert took their common water. Sami reset the plate at four percent. The broken pin could not be replaced before the rain ended, so the modules remained apart and joint inspections doubled.

Illuminara held the radio but gave no order. The rule was doing the work its critics had forced it to do.

At 18:40 the hospital remained open, nobody had evacuated, and no slope marker had moved more than four millimetres. Kiru's slip course was damaged, the pin was gone and shared reserve would stay unavailable until both were replaced.

Venn published the standard with the tracer test, the rejected bedding, the storm separation and the fault ledger attached.

AdaezeThree noes did not become a yes.

IlluminaraNo. They became the shape of what could be built.

Adaeze touched her daughter Illuminara's cheek, then went uphill to chair the inspection. At the school bend, Kemi painted the high-water mark beside seven years of colours. The new line was the darkest and the lowest.

ADAEZE'S THREE NOES

A ministry has twelve days to hold a failing hillside above a hospital, but Adaeze refuses its single elegant system three times—for the graves it would move, the dependency it would create, and the local design it would erase.

01 · Three Noes

Aruwa regional hall, hillside map room · Day 1, 08:10

The hillside above St. Orra Hospital had moved eleven centimetres in six days. On the ministry map it was one red crescent. On the ground it was three districts, four thousand homes, a school, a market and a burial field older than the road that divided it. The first heavy rain was due in twelve days.

Ministerial engineers had drawn one answer in blue: a continuous retaining curtain, forty-two load-field plates linked through a private control room, and a diversion channel cut straight across the slope. Every plate shared the load; if one failed, the others would carry it.

Illuminara's mother Adaeze sat with the three district chairs. She listened until the procurement director asked for assent.

AdaezeNo.

Director Miro VennMrs. Okafor, the graves can be reinterred with ceremony. Compensation is included.

AdaezeKiru's dead are not a line item to be lifted because your blue line is straight.

Venn turned a page. The control room would belong for twenty-five years to Cadran Systems, whose plates the ministry could procure in time.

AdaezeNo.

Belu would not put the ground beneath its houses behind a company's password and call that safety.

The drainage appendix cut across a stone trench Sava residents had built by hand after the last wet season. Chief Engineer Lio Mensah called it unlined, irregular and too small for the design storm. He was right about its size.

AdaezeNo. They measured every seep for seven years. Your survey calls their work an obstruction because it began after they finished.

IlluminaraAre those three refusals, or three requirements the plan has failed to meet?

Director Miro VennThey have the same effect. We lose the only package that can clear audit this week.

Illuminara closed the blue projection before its elegance became an argument by repetition.

IlluminaraGive me the residents' measurements, the hospital's water records and twenty-one hours. If the trench is local drainage, your curtain remains fastest. If it is carrying the hill, we have called the spine an obstacle.

02 · The Fourth Line

Sava district, contour trench · Day 1, 09:30

The trench was knee-deep, faced with mismatched stone and bent around breadfruit roots. Adaeze walked it with Kemi Sol, the mason who had marked the first seep, while Mensah's team set nine piezometers above and below it.

Kemi SolIt fills beneath the red house, then here, then at the school bend. Never the other way around.

Chief Engineer Lio MensahDepth is not source. A leaking hospital main could give you the same order.

IlluminaraThen we test both causes. Treated water carries chloride. Hillside seepage carries iron from the upper basalt.

On a stone she wrote two rival explanations and what each must predict at all nine wells.

Chief Engineer Lio MensahAnd if neither survives?

IlluminaraThe fourth line is 'we do not know,' and three districts do not build on it.

At 10:06 the three Kiru heads rose in order. Eight minutes later the wet line climbed one stone course beneath the red house, then another beside the sixth well. The school-bend head stayed flat while the masonry between it and the sixth well darkened. When Kemi opened the trench, the upstream heads and the wet courses fell in the same order.

Illuminara chalked the times onto the wall. The missing quantity was water, not load, and it left the measured path somewhere between the sixth well and the bend. That interval ran under the Belu laundry.

Kemi opened seven notebooks, each wet season in a different colour. The hospital main had been closed twice; the red-house-to-school sequence had continued. Each pressure rise also preceded the nearest slope marker's movement by roughly ninety minutes.

Kemi SolOfficials ask whether it is big enough. Nobody asks why it is here.

IlluminaraThree groundwater paths meet here. The throat is too narrow, but the collector is real. Drain the hill first; retain what remains.

The throat could not widen toward Kiru without approaching the graves. Illuminara pointed toward the road.

IlluminaraNow we find whether it can deepen the other way.

03 · Twenty-One Hours

Aruwa hillside and St. Orra plant room · Day 1, 11:00 to Day 2, 05:00

The hospital isolated its upper main. No well showed its chloride trace; iron rose in a fan from the basalt. Mensah abandoned the leaking-main explanation, but not his objection to making a regional spine from a village trench.

At noon Kemi released a measured tracer above Kiru. The middle wells should answer in order and the school bend last. If water scattered or bypassed the trench, the interface idea would fail before anyone signed it.

Two middle wells answered. The Belu well did not.

Director Miro VennOne silent well is enough. Three contractors will blame one another while the hospital slides.

Illuminara followed the groundwater interval she had chalked to the laundry floor. Adaeze looked at the old drain scar and remembered a cistern there, used during a nurses' strike.

Kemi SolIts clay pipe was sealed before I took the trench.

AdaezeMy mother drew water from its overflow after that.

They opened the laundry floor and found the cistern full, its pipe hidden below the well. Before a sensor was moved, Mensah wrote the branch test: the overflow must answer first, a temporary probe below the pipe must answer next, the silent well must stay flat and the school bend must rise last. If the bend rose before the probe, or chloride appeared, the branch was false.

Chief Engineer Lio MensahI accept no cistern until all four lines hold.

At 23:30 the overflow answered. The lower probe followed at 00:30; the Belu well stayed flat. At 02:00 the school bend rose last. Mensah signed beneath the prediction, then beneath his acceptance.

A road-side shaft found basalt falling away soon enough for a covered culvert twice the trench's measured peak. Proof loading left sixteen percent spare capacity after wet bedding settlement.

Chief Engineer Lio MensahThe residents found the collector. They did not size the throat.

Kemi SolWe had hammers, not your drill rig.

IlluminaraBoth facts belong in the design. The trench is the spine. The culvert is its new throat. Retaining work must meet it without owning it.

By dawn the first and third noes no longer opposed each other. The second still did.

04 · One Package

Ministry audit chamber · Day 2, 09:00

Venn gave them ninety minutes. Emergency law released money for one package, one accountable integrator and one acceptance test.

Director Miro VennI am defending a signature I can prosecute if the hospital is buried. Give me one throat to hold.

AdaezeThe districts refuse to become tenants of the remedy, not accountability.

Illuminara placed four pages on the table. They specified interfaces, not a wall: pressure delivered to the common spine, anchor exclusions around the graves, open sensors, manual safe states, public keys and joint inspection at every seam.

IlluminaraBuy one audited interface. Let three districts choose three compliant modules. The integrator owns the seams and the test, not their controls.

Chief Engineer Lio MensahWhere did you get eight percent?

Illuminara laid the road-throat proof sheet beside the settlement trace. Sixteen percent was the measured reserve after the bad bedding had taken its share.

IlluminaraNo seam may consume more than half the smallest passive reserve. The link pin is rated to creep under transfer above eight percent and part after ten sustained minutes. That endurance is in the metal, not a command. The drainage spine stays open when it separates.

Chief Engineer Lio MensahThen an inspector at any seam gets stop-work authority. Not a dashboard. A person.

Director Miro VennAnd every fault and override is public before the next shift. Liability cannot live in three private notebooks.

Illuminara crossed out two clauses and wrote both changes into the standard.

IlluminaraAgreed. They need not think as one system. They must fail without making a neighbour fail.

Hospital director Nia Sorel read the endurance clause twice.

Nia SorelCan this be inspected before the rain?

Chief Engineer Lio MensahIf excavation begins today and choices freeze by sunset.

The districts chose: Kiru's stone buttress outside the graves; Belu's public plates with local keys, operated by Sami Daro, who would hold the district's physical key; Sava's terraced anchors tied to the trench. Kemi's crew would supervise every old connection.

Adaeze signed beneath the three requirements and accepted the seam chair only until the rain. Venn signed last. One package went to tender at 10:27. It contained no single wall.

Sami DaroAt our office. Raw records remain ours.

AdaezeThen it may watch. It may not become the memory we cannot afford to lose.

THE VILLAGE THAT COULD NOT SLEEP

Fourteen wounded villagers need surgery before the pass closes, every anaesthetic the clinic owns brings the same fever, and the one thing the patients share is not in their blood.

01 · Fever

Nemea clinic, operating room · 14:40

The third patient began to burn forty seconds after the anaesthetic took. Dr. Corin Hale stopped the drip before the monitor had finished saying so, and the room filled with the sound of everyone breathing in. Bartek Lind, who drove timber trucks and had been dug out of the cab of one that morning, lay rigid under the lights with a temperature climbing a degree every four minutes.

Osvin Pike, seventy, and Tomas Ketter, who tended the upper kilns, had burned the same way an hour before, one after the other. Both had been packed in ice and both had lived, and neither could be put under again. Illuminara had come up the pass with the first relief convoy and had been given a stool in the corner and a promise that she would be told if she was needed. She was needed now. She watched Hale pack the man in ice, and she did not speak until his temperature turned.

Corin HaleThat is the third. Same fever, three different people, and every agent I own does it. It is malignant hyperthermia or something that wears its face. It runs in families, and I have the dantrolene for two bodies, not fourteen.

Pelagia RuskThese are not families. I have the parish books. Eleven of the fourteen are Nemea people and they came here from three different valleys across a hundred years. Nobody in this clinic is anybody's cousin.

Corin HaleThen it is bad luck three times, and I do not operate on bad luck.

Dr. Rusk had run the village clinic for thirty years and was wearing the same cardigan she had been wearing when the mountain came down. She laid the list on the counter: fourteen names, four who could wait a night, ten who could not. A ruptured spleen. A pelvis. A girl of nine with a femur through the skin.

Nell Brandt, on the radioNemea, Brandt. Pass closes to freezing rain at twenty hundred. I can lift at seventeen and at nineteen, three stretchers a lift. That is six of fourteen. Tell me which six.

Pelagia RuskEight stay behind with an anaesthetic that fevers them.

Nell Brandt, on the radioThen six, and I will pray for the eight.

Illuminara took the list from the counter and read it as she read a load path, looking for the place where the weight did not go where it should. It took her a long minute. Then she asked Dr. Hale for the three charts, and the times on them.

02 · The Order of the Fevers

Nemea clinic, ward corridor · 15:05

She laid the charts side by side on the floor of the corridor, where the light was best. Beside the three reactions she set the two earlier ones from the first-aid post: a hiker named Sana Moreau, splinted with a sedative at noon and perfectly well, and a fourteen-year-old called Ilo Vell, sedated at one o'clock with a fever that had come and gone on its own.

IlluminaraYou said it runs in families. Then it would not care where a person slept. Look at it as a gradient and not as a yes and a no. Osvin Pike reacted worst, and he has sat beside an upper-village hearth every winter day for seventy years. Tomas Ketter reacted next. He lives at the kilns. Bartek reacted after him. He has slept two nights at the inn. Ilo reacted least, and he came home from the valley school yesterday evening. Sana reacted not at all. She has been on the ridge for three days and has not been indoors in Nemea once.

Corin HaleA gradient by hours indoors. That is a coincidence of five.

IlluminaraIt is five out of five, and it has a direction. A gene cannot count nights. Something in the houses can. What is in the houses that is not in the valley?

Nobody answered. Down the corridor a woman in a burned shawl, who had been sitting with her injured husband for six hours, lifted her head. This was Marta Vell, who kept the village's resin kilns, and she had not been asked for anything yet.

Marta VellResin. Every house burns it. It has always been so; my grandmother's grandmother burned it. But it is not the old resin, not since the dry autumn.

Pelagia RuskWhat do you mean, not the old resin?

Marta VellThe upper kilns ran short. We stretched the cakes with bark off the scorched slope, the one that came down today. Dark cake. The houses below the church burn the pale stock still, because they were slow to buy. The kiln houses and the upper houses burn dark.

Illuminara had not known that, and could not have known it, and she said so out loud, so that everyone in the corridor heard what the missing piece had cost to find.

IlluminaraThen I have a prediction, and I would like it written down before anyone is tested. If the dark cake is the cause, the more dark smoke someone has breathed, the slower the enzyme that clears this class of anaesthetic. We can measure that slowness in a drop of plasma in the blood-gas machine. Twelve minutes, no drug given to any patient. Marta, name me the fourteen houses and what each burns.

Corin HaleAnd if you are wrong, ten people wait on a hearth superstition.

IlluminaraIf I am wrong, the machine says so in twelve minutes, and we have lost less time than your next attempt would cost.

Hale looked at the three charts for a long moment. Then he went to find the plasma tubes.

03 · Twelve Minutes

Nemea clinic, laboratory corner · 15:20 to 16:15

She wrote the ranking in the clinic log in ink, with the time, and Rusk signed beneath it as witness. At the bottom: the fourteen names in the order the machine ought to give them, slowest to fastest, built from Marta's list of what each house burned and how long each patient had sat in its smoke. Sana Moreau went last, as the fastest of all.

The machine took two samples at a time. Hale fed it himself with a technician's care and a sceptic's face, and Illuminara stood behind the curtain and did not touch the controls. At minute twelve the first pair settled and the numbers came up. Osvin Pike, slowest by a margin that made the technician swear softly. Bartek Lind, next. The slopes came out in the order she had written. Pair after pair, they came out in that order, and the room went quiet, and the quiet had a texture it had not had at the third fever.

In the fourth pair the order broke. Osvin's grand-niece Ines lived in a pale-stock house below the church. By Marta's list and by Illuminara's ranking she belonged near the fast end. She stood fourth from the slow end.

Corin HaleThere. One in fourteen. Your hearth explains twelve and fumbles the other.

IlluminaraIt is wrong, and I am glad it is wrong, because a hearth that explained all fourteen would have been a story. Marta, where did she sit today?

Marta VellShe sat with Osvin. They carried him here from the slide at nine, and she has not left his bed.

Illuminara did not move for a moment. She had been looking at the houses, and the smoke she had been looking for had been in the room she was standing in.

IlluminaraDr. Rusk. What does this clinic burn?

Pelagia RuskThe big stove in the waiting room. The upper kiln sent down a sledge of cake at dawn, to keep the wounded warm. Dark cake. It is the only stove that heats all the beds.

There was a silence in which the hum of the machine was the loudest thing in the building.

IlluminaraThen every patient in this clinic is being dosed more every hour they wait. The longer we argue, the slower the enzyme gets. We are not waiting out a danger. We are feeding it.

On the screen the last pair settled. Sana Moreau, fastest of all, as written. The only fever in the room now was in Hale's face, and he was too honest a physician to hide that it was shame.

04 · The Stove

Nemea clinic, waiting room · 16:20

The stove stood at the end of the room like a low black animal, and a dozen faces turned from it to her as she came in. It was nine degrees outside the blanket line. Eight patients lay in shock with their feet toward the heat.

Pelagia RuskNo. If that goes cold, I lose the spleen and the girl to the chill before any anaesthetic touches them. You have found a poison and want me to put out the only fire.

IlluminaraI want you to change what the fire burns. Marta, how much pale stock is left below the church?

Marta VellForty cakes. It was to last the village until the thaw.

IlluminaraThen I am asking you for the winter, and I will not pretend that is small.

Marta did not answer for the time it takes to count forty cakes against a hundred houses. Behind her a man lying under a coat said something about his own hearth and what it had meant for four hundred years, and she said, without turning, that the hearth had meant it for the living.

Marta VellOpen the storehouse. But I want it written that the village gave it, and that the dark cake does not go to the lowlands to be sold. It goes in the river.

IlluminaraWritten, and I will sign it where the village can read it.

The stove changed its burn within the half hour. Two men from the kilns carried the dark cake out through the side door; Hale opened the high vents; and Illuminara put the second plasma set on the machine at minute forty, as she had said she would, so that nobody could say the plan had been decided before it was tested.

At minute forty the slopes had begun to rise. They rose unevenly, and Osvin Pike, who had breathed the most, had risen almost not at all.

Corin HaleTold you. He is the one it is in the blood for.

IlluminaraHe is also the one who has sat the longest in the smoke. Run him again at seventy. If I am wrong about him, I will be glad to learn it now.

At minute seventy the slope came up, slow and unmistakable. Osvin's was a washout, not a flaw. Hale took the sheet in both hands.

Corin HaleThen here is what I will do, and not one thing more. Whoever has risen past my line goes under the general. Whoever has not, I block, with the other chemistry, nerve by nerve, and I need each of them or their family to say yes with the numbers in front of them. The block takes me twice as long. I can do ten tonight with Dr. Rusk assisting.

Pelagia RuskTen, and the machine decides the order, not the clock.

Nell Brandt, on the radioThat leaves the two the block cannot reach. The spleen and the girl's leg. I lift at seventeen, two stretchers, and I want it noted that I am not waiting for you to be sure.

IlluminaraI do not need you to wait. I need you to carry them, and the machine will tell Dr. Hale who goes under the general while you are in the air.

Ilo Vell's mother would not sign for the boy's block until Hale put the plasma curve in her hands and showed her where he sat and where the line ran. She read it with a finger. Then she signed, and said that she did not understand a word of it, and that she understood the line.

05 · What the Pass Kept

Nemea clinic and landing field · 17:00 to 04:10

The helicopter lifted at 17:02 with the girl of nine and the man with the ruptured spleen, and went up into the beginning of the rain with its lights burning. Brandt radioed from the valley at 17:58 that they were down and handed over. The second lift at nineteen hundred stood on the pad unneeded, and she logged it that way, and told Illuminara afterwards that it was the best use of a flight she had ever made.

Dr. Hale blocked ten that night. He worked from the least recovered to the most, with Rusk's hands beside his, and each time the plasma line had said who should go under and who should not, and each time the family or the patient had said yes to the number. The four who had cleared his line went under the general in the early hours and woke without fevers. The block took twice as long and held, and Osvin Pike was the last man to be wheeled in, at three-forty, with his grand-niece asleep against the wall.

At 04:10 the last suture was in. In the waiting room the stove burned pale cake with its vents open, and nobody was cold, and nobody was feverish.

Illuminara stayed through the rest of the night because there was a log to finish. She wrote the protocol herself, in a plain hand, as Hale would use it and not as she would. A bench test, plasma and substrate, twelve minutes, no drug given. A line below which a patient was blocked, not put under. A pair of readings an hour apart for anyone who breathed smoke of unknown stock, because the slope moved and the machine could tell. Under it she wrote the name of the village that had given the winter, and the date, and Marta Vell signed it where the village could read it.

Pelagia RuskWhat does it cost us? Say the whole of it.

IlluminaraForty cakes of pale resin, which is the village's heat until the thaw. Dark cake does not burn indoors in Nemea again, and the kilns stand idle until someone finds what in the scorched bark does this. Two of the fourteen face long recoveries far from home. And the line on the sheet is provisional. It comes from fourteen people and one machine, and I would like it checked in a laboratory before anyone trusts it twice.

Pelagia RuskChecked. But it was right tonight.

IlluminaraIt was wrong once tonight, about Osvin's niece, and that is why it was right about the stove.

Rusk looked down the ward, where the patients slept in the pale light of the new fire. Then she asked Marta Vell to bring in forty cakes from the cold storehouse, and Marta, who had been awake for twenty-two hours, said she would bring them herself.

Pelagia RuskThese are not families. I have the parish books. Eleven of the fourteen are Nemea people and they came here from three different valleys across a hundred years. Nobody in this clinic is anybody's cousin.

Corin HaleThen it is bad luck three times, and I do not operate on bad luck.

Corin HaleRegional blocks avoid those agents, but the spleen and the girl's leg cannot be reached that way. For the others it is one nerve at a time, twice the work, and each patient or family must consent. I might finish eight before dawn if my hands hold.

Dr. Rusk had run the village clinic for thirty years and was wearing the same cardigan she had been wearing when the mountain came down. She laid the list on the counter: fourteen names, four who could wait a night, ten who could not. A ruptured spleen. A pelvis. A girl of nine with a femur through the skin.

Nell Brandt, on the radioNemea, Brandt. Pass closes to freezing rain at twenty hundred. I can lift at seventeen and at nineteen, three stretchers a lift. That is six of fourteen. Tell me which six.

Pelagia RuskEight stay behind with an anaesthetic that fevers them.

Nell Brandt, on the radioThen six, and I will pray for the eight.

Illuminara took the list from the counter and read it as she read a load path, looking for the place where the weight did not go where it should. It took her a long minute. Then she asked Dr. Hale for the three charts, and the times on them.

02 · The Order of the Fevers

Nemea clinic, ward corridor · 15:05

She laid the charts side by side on the floor of the corridor, where the light was best. Beside the three reactions she set the two earlier ones from the first-aid post: a hiker named Sana Moreau, splinted with a sedative at noon and perfectly well, and a fourteen-year-old called Ilo Vell, sedated at one o'clock with a fever that had come and gone on its own.

IlluminaraYou said it runs in families. Then it would not care where a person slept. Look at it as a gradient and not as a yes and a no. Osvin Pike reacted worst, and he has sat beside an upper-village hearth every winter day for seventy years. Tomas Ketter reacted next. He lives at the kilns. Bartek reacted after him. He has slept two nights at the inn. Ilo reacted least, and he came home from the valley school yesterday evening. Sana reacted not at all. She has been on the ridge for three days and has not been indoors in Nemea once.

Corin HaleA gradient by hours indoors. That is a coincidence of five.

IlluminaraIt is five out of five, and it has a direction. A gene cannot count nights. Something in the houses can. What is in the houses that is not in the valley?

Nobody answered. Down the corridor a woman in a burned shawl, who had been sitting with her injured husband for six hours, lifted her head. This was Marta Vell, who kept the village's resin kilns, and she had not been asked for anything yet.

Marta VellResin. Every house burns it. It has always been so; my grandmother's grandmother burned it. But it is not the old resin, not since the dry autumn.

Pelagia RuskWhat do you mean, not the old resin?

Marta VellThe upper kilns ran short. We stretched the cakes with bark off the scorched slope, the one that came down today. Dark cake. The houses below the church burn the pale stock still, because they were slow to buy. The kiln houses and the upper houses burn dark.

Illuminara had not known that, and could not have known it, and she said so out loud, so that everyone in the corridor heard what the missing piece had cost to find.

IlluminaraThen I have a working model, and I would like it written down before anyone is tested. A compound in the dark smoke may be tying up the same clearance pathway the anaesthetic needs, leaving a heat-driving metabolite faster than the body can remove it. That is a prediction, not a diagnosis.

Corin HaleAnd the blood-gas analyser does not measure enzymes.

IlluminaraNot directly. Mix each plasma drop with the clinic's clear test substrate. The analyser's oxygen sensor can read how quickly the substrate is consumed. If the dark cake is involved, the rate should follow hours in its smoke. Twelve minutes, no drug given to any patient. Marta, name me the fourteen houses and what each burns.

Corin HaleAnd if you are wrong, ten people wait on a hearth superstition.

IlluminaraIf I am wrong, the machine says so in twelve minutes, and we have lost less time than your next attempt would cost.

Hale looked at the three charts for a long moment. Then he went to find the plasma tubes.

03 · Twelve Minutes

Nemea clinic, laboratory corner · 15:20 to 16:15

She wrote the ranking in the clinic log in ink, with the time, and Rusk signed beneath it as witness. At the bottom: the fourteen names in the order the machine ought to give them, slowest to fastest, built from Marta's list of what each house burned and how long each patient had sat in its smoke. Sana Moreau went last, as the fastest of all.

The machine took two samples at a time. Hale fed it himself with a technician's care and a sceptic's face, and Illuminara stood behind the curtain and did not touch the controls. At minute twelve the first pair settled and the numbers came up. Osvin Pike, slowest by a margin that made the technician swear softly. Bartek Lind, next. The slopes came out in the order she had written. Pair after pair, they came out in that order, and the room went quiet, and the quiet had a texture it had not had at the third fever.

In the fourth pair the order broke. Osvin's grand-niece Ines, her left forearm splinted from the slide, sat on a stretcher beside his bed. She lived in a pale-stock house below the church. By Marta's list and by Illuminara's ranking she belonged near the fast end. She stood fourth from the slow end.

Corin HaleThere. One in fourteen. Your hearth explains thirteen and fumbles the other.

IlluminaraIt is wrong, and I am glad it is wrong, because a hearth that explained all fourteen would have been a story. Marta, where did she sit today?

Marta VellShe sat on that stretcher beside Osvin. They carried him here from the slide at nine, and she has not left his bed.

Illuminara did not move for a moment. She had been looking at the houses, and the smoke she had been looking for had been in the room she was standing in.

IlluminaraDr. Rusk. What does this clinic burn?

Pelagia RuskThe big stove in the waiting room. The upper kiln sent down a sledge of cake at dawn, to keep the wounded warm. Dark cake. It is the only stove that heats all the beds.

There was a silence in which the hum of the machine was the loudest thing in the building.

IlluminaraThen every patient in this clinic is being dosed more every hour they wait. The longer we argue, the slower the enzyme gets. We are not waiting out a danger. We are feeding it.

On the screen the last pair settled. Sana Moreau, fastest of all, as written. The only fever in the room now was in Hale's face, and he was too honest a physician to hide that it was shame.

04 · The Stove

Nemea clinic, waiting room · 16:20 to 17:46

The stove stood at the end of the room like a low black animal, and a dozen faces turned from it to her as she came in. It was nine degrees outside the blanket line. Eight patients lay in shock with their feet toward the heat.

Pelagia RuskNo. If that goes cold, I lose the spleen and the girl to the chill before any anaesthetic touches them. You have found a poison and want me to put out the only fire.

IlluminaraNot put it out. Change one grate at a time, keep the other dark grate burning until the pale side catches, and measure every bed through the change. Marta, how much pale stock is left below the church?

Marta VellForty cakes. It was to last the village until the thaw. I can put the bakery's hot soapstone under the two shock beds while the first grate catches, but the stones will not hold all night.

IlluminaraThen I am asking you for the winter, and your stones buy the swap time. I will not pretend either is small.

Pelagia RuskTemperatures every four minutes. If any bed loses half a degree before the pale side catches, the dark grate stays lit. That is my stop condition.

Marta did not answer for the time it takes to count forty cakes against a hundred houses. Behind her a man lying under a coat said something about his own hearth and what it had meant for four hundred years, and she said, without turning, that the hearth had meant it for the living.

Marta VellOpen the storehouse. But I want it written that the village gave it, and that the dark cake does not go to the lowlands to be sold. It goes in the river.

IlluminaraWritten, and I will sign it where the village can read it.

The staged swap began at 16:24. Two kiln workers banked the left grate and laid pale cake on the right while Marta slid hot soapstone beneath the two shock beds. Hale opened the high vents. At 16:44 the pale side held; no bedside reading had fallen more than two tenths of a degree. Rusk alone gave the word to empty the dark grate, and the full pale burn caught four minutes later.

Nell Brandt, on the radioThe spleen and the girl's leg are the two your blocks cannot reach. I lift at seventeen with those two, and I want it noted that I am not waiting for your assay.

IlluminaraDo not wait. Carry them. The next readings are for the twelve who remain.

At 17:04, forty minutes after the swap began and two minutes after Brandt lifted, Hale drew the second plasma set. Twelve minutes later the slopes had begun to rise. They rose unevenly, and Osvin Pike, who had breathed the most, had risen almost not at all.

Corin HaleTold you. He is the one it is in the blood for.

IlluminaraHe is also the one who has sat longest in the smoke. Draw him again at 17:34, seventy minutes after the swap began. If I am wrong about him, I will be glad to learn it now.

At 17:34 Hale drew the sample. At 17:46 the slope came up, slow and unmistakable. Osvin's was a washout, not a flaw. Hale took the sheet in both hands.

Corin HaleThen here is what I will do, and not one thing more. The two unreachable injuries are already in the air. I will block the eight urgent patients who remain, nerve by nerve, with consent and the numbers in front of them. The four who could safely wait will stay stabilised until their curves clear my line, and only then go under the general.

Pelagia RuskEight urgent blocks, four delayed generals, and the machine decides the order, not the clock.

Ilo Vell's mother would not sign for the boy's block until Hale put the plasma curve in her hands and showed her where he sat and where the line ran. She read it with a finger. Then she signed, and said that she did not understand a word of it, and that she understood the line.

05 · What the Pass Kept

Nemea clinic and landing field · 17:00 to 04:10

The helicopter lifted at 17:02 with the girl of nine and the man with the ruptured spleen, and went up into the beginning of the rain with its lights burning. Brandt radioed from the valley at 17:58 that they were down and handed over. The second lift at nineteen hundred stood on the pad unneeded, and she logged it that way, and told Illuminara afterwards that it was the best use of a flight she had ever made.

Dr. Hale blocked the eight urgent patients who remained. He worked from the least recovered to the most, with Rusk's hands beside his, and each time the plasma line had said who should be blocked and each time the family or the patient had said yes to the number. The four who had been stable enough to wait cleared his line in the early hours, went under the general and woke without fevers. The blocks took twice as long and held. Ines, her forearm dressed after her turn, fell asleep against the wall before Osvin Pike was wheeled in last at three-forty.

At 04:10 the last suture was in. In the waiting room the stove burned pale cake with its vents open, and nobody was cold, and nobody was feverish.

Illuminara stayed through the rest of the night because there was a log to finish. She wrote the protocol herself, in a plain hand, as Hale would use it and not as she would. A bench test: plasma and a clear substrate, with the oxygen sensor reading the consumption rate, twelve minutes, no drug given. A line below which a patient was blocked, not put under. A pair of readings half an hour apart for anyone who breathed smoke of unknown stock, because the slope moved and the machine could tell. Under it she wrote the name of the village that had given the winter, and the date, and Marta Vell signed it where the village could read it.

Pelagia RuskWhat does it cost us? Say the whole of it.

IlluminaraForty cakes of pale resin, which is the village's heat until the thaw. Dark cake does not burn indoors in Nemea again, and the kilns stand idle until someone finds what in the scorched bark does this. Two of the fourteen face long recoveries far from home. And the line on the sheet is provisional. It comes from fourteen people and one machine, and I would like it checked in a laboratory before anyone trusts it twice.

Pelagia RuskChecked. But it was right tonight.

IlluminaraIt was wrong once tonight, about Osvin's niece, and that is why it was right about the stove.

Rusk looked down the ward, where the patients slept in the pale light of the new fire. Then she asked Marta Vell to bring in forty cakes from the cold storehouse, and Marta, who had been awake for twenty-two hours, said she would bring them herself.

Nobody answered. Down the corridor a woman in a burned shawl, who had been sitting with her injured husband for six hours, lifted her head. This was Marta Vell, Ilo's mother and keeper of the village's resin kilns, and she had not been asked for anything yet.

Marta VellResin. Every house burns it. It has always been so; my grandmother's grandmother burned it. But it is not the old resin, not since the dry autumn.

Pelagia RuskWhat do you mean, not the old resin?

Marta VellThe upper kilns ran short. We stretched the cakes with bark off the scorched slope, the one that came down today. Dark cake. The houses below the church burn the pale stock still, because they were slow to buy. The kiln houses and the upper houses burn dark.

Illuminara said aloud that she had not known it and could not have known it.

IlluminaraThen here is the working model, written before we test it: something in the dark smoke may slow the same clearance pathway the anaesthetic needs. That is a prediction, not a diagnosis.

Corin HaleAnd the blood-gas analyser does not measure enzymes.

IlluminaraNot directly. Mix each plasma drop with the clinic's clear substrate and use the oxygen sensor to read consumption. If the dark cake is involved, the rate should follow hours in its smoke. Twelve minutes, no drug given. Marta, name the fourteen houses and what each burns.

Corin HaleAnd if you are wrong, ten people wait on a hearth superstition.

IlluminaraIf I am wrong, the machine says so in twelve minutes, and we have lost less time than your next attempt would cost.

Hale looked at the three charts for a long moment. Then he went to find the plasma tubes.

03 · Twelve Minutes

Nemea clinic, laboratory corner · 15:20 to 16:15

She wrote the ranking in the clinic log in ink, with the time, and Rusk signed beneath it as witness. At the bottom: the fourteen names in the order the machine ought to give them, slowest to fastest, built from Marta's list of what each house burned and how long each patient had sat in its smoke. Sana Moreau went last, as the fastest of all.

The machine took four samples at a time. Hale loaded it with a technician's care and a sceptic's face while Illuminara stood behind the curtain and did not touch the controls. At minute twelve the first run settled: Osvin Pike, slowest by a margin that made the technician swear softly, then Bartek Lind. Run after run, the slopes came out in the order she had written. When Hale loaded the fourth run, only two tubes remained. The room went quiet with a texture it had not had at the third fever.

In the fourth run the order broke. Osvin's grand-niece Ines, her left forearm splinted from the slide, sat on a stretcher beside his bed. She lived in a pale-stock house below the church. By Marta's list and Illuminara's ranking she belonged near the fast end. She stood fourth from the slow end.

Corin HaleThere. One in fourteen. Your hearth explains thirteen and fumbles the other.

IlluminaraIt is wrong. Good. A hearth that explained all fourteen would be a story. Marta—where did Ines sit today?

Marta VellShe sat on that stretcher beside Osvin. They carried him here from the slide at nine, and she has not left his bed.

Illuminara did not move for a moment. She had been looking at the houses, and the smoke she had been looking for had been in the room she was standing in.

IlluminaraDr. Rusk. What does this clinic burn?

Pelagia RuskThe big stove in the waiting room. The upper kiln sent down a sledge of cake at dawn, to keep the wounded warm. Dark cake. It is the only stove that heats all the beds.

There was a silence in which the hum of the machine was the loudest thing in the building.

IlluminaraThen the clinic is dosing every patient while they wait. The longer we argue, the slower the clearance. We are not waiting out the danger. We are feeding it.

On the screen the last pair settled. Sana Moreau, fastest of all, as written. The only fever in the room now was in Hale's face, and he was too honest a physician to hide that it was shame.

04 · The Stove

Nemea clinic, waiting room · 16:20 to 17:46

The stove stood at the end of the room like a low black animal, and a dozen faces turned from it to her as she came in. It was nine degrees outside the blanket line. Eight patients lay in shock with their feet toward the heat.

Pelagia RuskNo. If that goes cold, I lose the spleen and the girl to the chill before any anaesthetic touches them. You have found a poison and want me to put out the only fire.

IlluminaraNot put it out. Change one grate at a time, keep the other dark grate burning until the pale side catches, and measure every bed through the change. Marta, how much pale stock is left below the church?

Marta VellForty cakes. It was to last the village until the thaw. I can put the bakery's hot soapstone under the two shock beds while the first grate catches, but the stones will not hold all night.

IlluminaraThen I am asking you for the winter, and your stones buy the swap time. I will not pretend either is small.

Pelagia RuskTemperatures every four minutes. If any bed loses half a degree before the pale side catches, the dark grate stays lit. That is my stop condition.

Marta did not answer for the time it takes to count forty cakes against a hundred houses. Behind her a man lying under a coat said something about his own hearth and what it had meant for four hundred years, and she said, without turning, that the hearth had meant it for the living.

Marta VellOpen the storehouse. But I want it written that the village gave it, and that the dark cake does not go to the lowlands to be sold. It goes in the river.

IlluminaraWritten, and I will sign it where the village can read it.

The staged swap began at 16:24. Two kiln workers banked the left grate and laid pale cake on the right while Marta slid hot soapstone beneath the two shock beds. Hale opened the high vents. At 16:36 the girl's bedside reading had fallen four tenths of a degree. Rusk ordered the dark grate held for four more minutes; Marta shifted both hottest stones beneath the child and wrapped the exposed leg above the splint. By 16:44 the reading had recovered a tenth and the pale side held. Rusk alone gave the word to empty the dark grate, and the full pale burn caught four minutes later. While it caught, Rusk clipped a sheet to each flight stretcher with the dark-smoke hours and fever histories; Hale signed a request that the receiving anaesthetist hold the general until a clearance reading, or use a cooler regional option.

Nell Brandt, on the radioThe spleen and the girl's leg are the two your blocks cannot reach. I lift at seventeen with those two. The third stretcher space stays empty; nobody else is beyond the blocks, and I will not delay them to fill it. Note that I am not waiting for your assay.

IlluminaraDo not wait. Carry them. The next readings are for the twelve who remain.

At 17:04, forty minutes after the swap began and two minutes after Brandt lifted, Hale drew the second plasma set. Twelve minutes later the slopes had begun to rise. They rose unevenly, and Osvin Pike, who had breathed the most, had risen almost not at all.

Corin HaleTold you. He is the one it is in the blood for.

IlluminaraHe is also the one who has sat longest in the smoke. Draw him again at 17:34, seventy minutes after the swap began. If I am wrong about him, I will be glad to learn it now.

At 17:34 Hale drew the sample. At 17:46 the slope came up, slow and unmistakable. Osvin's was a washout, not a flaw. Hale took the sheet in both hands.

Corin HaleThen here is what I will do, and not one thing more. The two unreachable injuries are already in the air. I will block the eight urgent patients who remain, nerve by nerve, with consent and the numbers in front of them. The four who could safely wait will stay stabilised until their curves clear my line, and only then go under the general.

Pelagia RuskEight urgent blocks, four delayed generals, and the machine decides the order, not the clock.

Marta would not sign for her son's block until Hale put the plasma curve in her hands and showed her where Ilo sat and where the line ran. She read it with a finger. Then she signed, and said that she did not understand a word of it, and that she understood the line.

05 · What the Pass Kept

Nemea clinic and landing field · 17:00 to 04:10

The helicopter lifted at 17:02 with the girl of nine and the man with the ruptured spleen, and went up into the beginning of the rain with its lights burning. Brandt radioed from the valley at 17:58 that they were down and handed over: the receiving anaesthetist had read both sheets, run clearance readings and held each general until its line rose. The second lift at nineteen hundred stood on the pad unneeded, and she logged it that way, and told Illuminara afterwards that it was the best use of a flight she had ever made.

Dr. Hale blocked the eight urgent patients who remained. He worked from the least recovered to the most, with Rusk's hands beside his, and each time the plasma line had said who should be blocked and each time the family or the patient had said yes to the number. The four who had been stable enough to wait cleared his line in the early hours, went under the general and woke without fevers. The blocks took twice as long and held. Ines, her forearm dressed after her turn, fell asleep against the wall before Osvin Pike was wheeled in last at three-forty.

At 04:10 the last suture was in. In the waiting room the stove burned pale cake with its vents open, and nobody was cold, and nobody was feverish.

Illuminara stayed through the rest of the night because there was a log to finish. She wrote the protocol herself, in a plain hand, as Hale would use it and not as she would. A bench test: plasma and a clear substrate, with the oxygen sensor reading the consumption rate, twelve minutes, no drug given. A line below which a patient was blocked, not put under. A pair of readings half an hour apart for anyone who breathed smoke of unknown stock, because the slope moved and the machine could tell. Under it she wrote the name of the village that had given the winter, and the date, and Marta Vell signed it where the village could read it.

Pelagia RuskWhat does it cost us? Say the whole of it.

IlluminaraForty cakes of pale resin, which is the village's heat until the thaw. Dark cake does not burn indoors in Nemea again, and the kilns stand idle until someone finds what in the scorched bark does this. Two of the fourteen face long recoveries far from home. And the line on the sheet is provisional. It comes from fourteen people and one machine, and I would like it checked in a laboratory before anyone trusts it twice.

Pelagia RuskChecked. But it was right tonight.

IlluminaraIt was wrong once tonight, about Osvin's niece, and that is why it was right about the stove.

Rusk looked down the ward, where the patients slept in the pale light of the new fire. Then she asked Marta Vell to bring in forty cakes from the cold storehouse, and Marta, who had been awake for twenty-two hours, said she would bring them herself.

THE COMET'S SECOND TAIL

A comet grows a tail that walks upwind, nine thousand young shells of living plasma sit across the grain lane, and a claim holder keeps the key to a sweep that would sterilize them.

01 · The Comb

Oss Station, observation ring · Hour 0 of 40

Eleven days out, the comet Maren-Quill had grown a second tail, and the second tail was walking the wrong way. The first streamed from the sun as tails should. The new one crawled up into the solar wind, a thin violet braid shedding knots of charged dust that tumbled across the freight corridor like seeds across a road.

Sunniva AchterbergThose knots are alive, in whatever sense a field can be. They fold dust into shells, and inside each shell something keeps a heartbeat on the low radio band. Nine thousand shells, all young. And every shell scatters our navigation. A ranging beam comes out of that braid like light through frosted glass.

Ngozi FarrantArdent has a fix good to eighty metres, when the lane needs four. I carry nineteen hundred tonnes of grain, and my radiation margin lets me reroute exactly never.

Ibrahim TadesseLamentine's mills turn for eleven more days. The other four stations are not far behind. The lane closes for the perihelion in forty hours. Three convoys must cross before then, or my people eat the seed stock.

Dagny Voss, on the lineAnd the comet is mine, Councillor, under the Voss-Kane charter, down to the last gram of nickel. The charter lets a holder clear a hazard to navigation from her own claim. At Hour 12 I fire the comb. Forty minutes, and the lane is clean as glass.

Sunniva AchterbergAnd so is the nursery. A magnetic sweep tears every shell apart.

Dagny Voss, on the lineI read your paper, doctor. A pretty braid. Four hundred people draw wages from this claim, and they will not draw them from a braid.

Illuminara had stood at the window the whole time, watching the violet thread on the screen below the stars. Nobody had asked her opinion yet. She did not offer one.

IlluminaraNot the summary. The raw tracks. Every knot, every minute since the braid formed.

Sunniva AchterbergThat is two terabytes of scribble.

IlluminaraThen nobody has read it yet.

02 · The Beacon That Lost Its Clock

Oss Station, tracking bay · Hour 3

She read the tracks the way she read a face, looking for the place where the expected thing failed to happen. It took her an hour and ten minutes. She found it in a gap forty minutes wide.

IlluminaraBeacon nine lost its clock at 22:10 yesterday. Its phase wandered for forty minutes. Look at the knots in that stretch.

Sunniva AchterbergThey parted. Around the beacon, in a bubble. I took it for a sensor fault.

IlluminaraThey parted for exactly forty minutes and closed the moment the clock came back. You told the council the knots hunt the beams. A thing hunting beams would have swarmed the one that was shouting.

Sunniva AchterbergUnless they shun anything incoherent.

IlluminaraAnd they are not drifting at random. Every strand runs along the old guide rails, the magnetic edges laid down to keep the beams clean. The rails are the quietest, straightest edges in forty million kilometres.

Sunniva AchterbergThen we built them a road. And we invited them onto it.

Ngozi Farrant, on the lineThen cut the rails.

IlluminaraThen your ranging goes with them, the lane turns to static, and I do not know what a young shell does when its road becomes noise.

Sunniva AchterbergFracture. I would guess.

IlluminaraIt is a guess, and I would rather not learn the answer by being right. Suppose we offered something quieter, longer and cleaner than the rails, and led away from traffic.

Sunniva AchterbergYou are assuming they take offers.

IlluminaraI am assuming nothing. I want to see whether they decline.

03 · The Key

Voss-Kane platform, comb control · Hour 6

Dagny Voss kept the firing key on a cord around her own neck. Her engineer, Kemal Aydin, stood at the panel with his hands in his pockets, which Illuminara understood to be a courtesy.

Dagny VossYou have come to ask me to wait.

IlluminaraI have come to ask what would make you not fire.

Dagny VossA clean lane before Hour 12. Show me ranging lock to four metres, and I will not touch the key. I will also want to see the thing I am sparing. I do not break my own payroll over a diagram.

IlluminaraThen take the heartbeat. Dr. Achterberg can put it on this panel. While the shells are whole it is a single clean note. If they tear, it spreads into static. You will watch harm happen the moment it does, and you can fire the second you see it.

Kemal AydinWhich means you are handing her the right to stop you.

IlluminaraIt was always hers.

Dagny VossAnd if you are wrong, I want it on the record that I warned you, and that every hour I waited cost me a hauler contract.

IlluminaraIt will be on the record. The cost will be too.

Dagny VossThen do it. Hour 12 is when Kemal turns the comb. I will wait past it for as long as the lane is getting better and the heartbeat stays whole. The first time either one turns, he fires, and I will not be asked twice.

04 · Two Ribbons

Oss and Lamentine field arrays · Hour 8 to Hour 10 and a half

The first ribbon ran out from Oss, south and away from the lane: a faint coherent edge, drawn as cleanly as the arrays could draw it. The second ran from Lamentine across the corridor, a decoy and a control. Illuminara wrote her prediction in the station log before either went live. The knots would leave the rails for the outbound ribbon within ninety minutes. If they took neither, or the crossing one, she was wrong, and she wrote that too.

They did nothing for seventy minutes. On Voss's panel the heartbeat held one clean note, and Aydin counted the minutes aloud in a flat voice.

At 09:20 the knots moved. They did not take the outbound ribbon, and they did not take the crossing one. They settled on the seam where the two edges overlapped, a line nobody had drawn, running a hundred and forty kilometres along the lane's southern rail.

Sunniva AchterbergThey declined both.

IlluminaraNo. They chose the best edge in the sky, and I built it by accident. I had them picking between my offers.

Ngozi Farrant, on the lineMy fix just went to a hundred and twenty metres. Tell me that is the end of the bad news.

IlluminaraIt is the middle. I made the lane worse.

She said it once, at the volume she would have used for a measurement, and went back to the screen. It was 10:35.

05 · The Seam

Oss field array, control room · Hour 10 and 40 minutes

IlluminaraThe seam sits where the two ribbons are equal. Weaken the crossing one and the seam slides toward Lamentine's side, away from the rail. Strengthen the outbound one and it slides the same way. Slide it slowly and the knots may follow it, because it is still the best edge there is.

Sunniva AchterbergThe arrays can't hold their phase that precisely. They wander. Noise is exactly what the knots flee.

IlluminaraThen I will be the clock. I can feel which way each field is bending a breath before your instruments log it. I cannot move the knots, or the ice, or the shells. I can tell each of you which way you are drifting and by how much.

Ibrahim TadesseLamentine's array runs on the mill reserve. Drain it for this and the mill stays cold a day. Four thousand households will go without bread.

IlluminaraI will not pretend that is a small price.

Ibrahim TadesseTake it.

For forty minutes she called corrections over two channels, one voice to Oss and one to Lamentine, a few milliseconds ahead of what the instruments could see. The seam crept south. The knots flowed along it like seeds along a tide line.

At minute forty-one Voss's voice came over the speaker, level and dry.

Dagny Voss, on the lineThe heartbeat is broadening.

Illuminara did not argue the point. She said stop, and she held the arrays exactly where they were. Aydin's hand was on the comb, and no one in the room breathed.

Dagny Voss, on the lineTell me why I should not turn it.

IlluminaraBecause the pull outran the young. The elders came with the seam and the youngest could not keep the pace, and you are looking at the shells stretching. I should have set the slope slower. Give me twenty minutes of stillness. If the note does not narrow, turn the key.

For twenty minutes the seam did not move and the heartbeat did not settle, and then, a little at a time, it did. The laggards were catching up, and the braid closed behind them like a hand.

Dagny Voss, on the lineResume. Half the speed.

06 · Clean Glass

Oss Station and the lane · Hour 16 to Hour 31

By Hour 15 the seam lay two hundred kilometres south of the rail, and the braid lay with it, a long violet comma pointing away from the lane. Ranging lock came back in steps: eighty metres, forty, nine, four.

Ngozi FarrantFour. Four and holding. I said I would not enter above eighty metres, and I am entering at four on my own judgement, not because anyone told me it was safe. Ardent is in the lane.

Illuminara watched the scatter chart flatten on Oss's screen. The three convoys crossed one behind another, at half speed, through the narrow clean band, and the last of them cleared the closing line with nine hours to spare. The grain would reach the stations two days late. The mills of Lamentine would burn their reserves and turn again only when the first loaves arrived.

Voss came to the observation ring herself, with the key on its cord.

Dagny VossA season. The north face is still mine, but the south face is shut while the heartbeat band is active, and the charter will say so in writing. I have never signed away a season for a diagram.

IlluminaraIt stopped being a diagram when you could hear it.

Ibrahim TadesseThe new beacons will be paid for by every hauler on the lane. Nobody has agreed to that yet.

Sunniva AchterbergThey will have to. The next braid will not wait for a committee.

On the screen the heartbeat held its single clean note, and under it, new and faint, a second tone that had not been there before. Achterberg turned it up. Nobody could say what it meant, and Illuminara did not offer a guess. She asked, instead, that one ribbon be left on at a whisper through the season, and Voss, after a moment, nodded.

THE DAY WREN WAS RIGHT

A floating market of twelve hundred households has thirty days to meet a sanitation law it genuinely breaks, and the plan that would save it is wrong in the one way only Wren could see.

01 · The Clean Plan

Harbour Office quay, Sorrel Water · Day 3 of 30, 08:10

The Order was fourteen pages long and gave thirty days, and on the third morning Illuminara laid her answer across the Harbour Office counter on a single sheet.

Twelve hundred boat-households lived on Kettle Market. The Harbourmaster's Sanitation Order No. 14 said that after the fifteenth of November none of them could go on discharging into Sorrel Water, and the August samples had shown the Order was right. Illuminara's sheet showed a licensed pump-out barge, six fixed stops, a sensor in every tank and one monthly bill.

Cedric AldanaIt is the cleanest compliance plan anyone has put in front of me. Every vessel metered, every pump-out logged. I could sign it on a Friday.

Wren Odira came up the quay steps with smoke in her coat and river mud to the knee. She had spent three weeks sleeping on other people's decks. She read the sheet standing, twice, and set it down.

Wren OdiraIt will fail.

IlluminaraTell me where it breaks first.

Wren OdiraWherever the barge is when the string has moved. Kettle doesn't sit at six stops. It re-rafts on every ebb, boats slide to be near the boats they owe. Your stop six holds a hundred and forty hulls on Monday and sixty on Thursday. And you meter the tank. Whoever pays by the tank learns to keep it half empty and the hose long.

IlluminaraA meter that pays a family to leave the harbour dirty. I did not model that.

Wren OdiraYou modelled a machine. It's a rumour with a rota.

Illuminara did not defend the sheet. Wren has the shape of it. I do not yet have one fact that is worth more than her three weeks.

THE COUGH THAT FOLLOWED THE BELLS

Forty-one children cough every Sunday night in a mountain town that has spent five weeks blaming its doctors and its church, and nobody has asked which bell, which room, or what changed last winter.

01 · Forty-One Notebooks

Children's clinic, Ostrava Vell · Monday, 07:40

Ostrava Vell was a mountain town of four thousand people, one church with a tower too large for it, and, since the second week of September, forty-one children who coughed in the evenings.

Dr. Ilse Varga had taped her spirometry curves to the examination-room wall, one line to a child. Every line sagged on Sunday night and climbed back by Thursday, forty-one small tides.

Ilse VargaCultures, PCR, serology, three rounds. There is nothing in any of them. No virus I know keeps a calendar.

Judit Moravec, who chaired the town council, had come in with her coat on and meant to leave in it. Father Matej Hroch of St. Wenzel stood by the door with his hands folded in his sleeves.

Judit MoravecThe council wants the school shut on Wednesday. A closed school is a thing I can actually do. Tell me what else I can do by Wednesday and I will do that instead.

Ilse VargaI can tell you that it costs the fifteen-year-olds their exams in six weeks, and that I cannot promise it helps.

Matej HrochAnd while you are all looking for something to shut, leave the bells out of it. This town blamed them for the hail, the frost and the winter the cows failed. They were innocent every time.

Illuminara had been asked to read the evidence rather than the people. She stood a while before the curves, then before the map beside them, where each child was a pin in the street they lived on and the pins thickened toward the church.

IlluminaraEveryone has plotted the children by where they live. Has anyone plotted them by where they sleep?

Ilse VargaWhere they sleep is where they live.

IlluminaraUsually.

Nives Hadzic had come in with her coat still buttoned. She held out a school exercise book, soft at the corners.

Nives HadzicForty-one mothers, forty-one notebooks. You asked for them in week two, Doctor. I write down every cough and the hour. And Lenka does not fit. We are out on Spindle Road, past the cemetery, the farthest house from the tower there is. She coughs on Sundays like the rest of them.

Ilse VargaI set Lenka aside as an outlier.

Illuminara turned the pages. Saturday: to Baba's. Sunday: home at five. Sunday night: coughing, two hours.

IlluminaraWhere is Baba's?

Nives HadzicCooper's Lane. Right under the tower, near enough.

IlluminaraThen she is not an outlier. She is the one child you have who proves something. The cough follows the child and not the address, so it is not a house or a street, and probably not a germ going door to door. It is a room she slept in, and the room has a clock.

The doctors had asked what was in the children. Nobody had asked what was in the rooms.

Judit MoravecAnd the school?

IlluminaraTell me which of these children sleep there.

02 · Saint's Flour

St. Wenzel's tower, ringing chamber · Monday, 10:15

The ringing chamber smelled of rope and cold stone. Dana Kral had pulled the bells of St. Wenzel for thirty-eight years, as her husband had before her, and she watched the stranger look at the ropes instead of the bells and made ready to be annoyed.

IlluminaraI have one question, and I think nobody has asked it. Which bell is the heaviest, and when is it rung?

Dana KralEverybody asks which is loudest.

IlluminaraI am not asking about loud.

Dana KralOld Wenzel. Two tonnes and a hundred kilos. Four of us swing him, Sundays and feast days only. The little ones go from the keyboard, and the hour bells strike by the clock, every day of the week.

Matej HrochThere, you see. The hour bells strike every day and nobody coughs on a Tuesday.

IlluminaraI agree. So it is not the bells. It may be one bell, on one day.

She asked for a single stroke of the old bell. Hroch looked a long time at the rope, and allowed exactly one. Dana and three ringers swung Old Wenzel up from rest, and Illuminara went down to the ground chamber and stood on the flagstones at the west wall.

The stroke came through the tower like a blow to the bottom of a chair. She had never needed her ears for a bell. The tower pressed its weight into the stone, the stone passed it down, and she read where the paths ran. Under the west wall they stopped. There was one place where the rock no longer carried anything and only hung, a long emptiness with a thin roof, and it answered the stroke the way a drumhead answers a palm.

Something down there rings.

IlluminaraUnder this wall there is a hollow, wide and shallow, with a thin ceiling over it. When Old Wenzel strikes, the ceiling moves.

Matej HrochThe tower stands on rock.

Dana KralIt stands on the lip of the old adit. The miners' air shaft, bricked and boarded before my grandmother's time. Mind the floor by the lectern, it is hollow.

She pushed back her sleeve. Along the dark wool lay a fine white powder, like flour.

Piazza of St. Wenzel · Sunday, 11:00
