IlluminaraI have one question, and I think nobody has asked it. Which bell is the heaviest, and when is it rung?

Dana KralEverybody asks which is loudest.

IlluminaraI am not asking about loud.

Dana KralOld Wenzel, two tonnes and a hundred kilos. Four of us swing him, Sundays and feast days only. The little ones go from the keyboard, and the hour bells strike by the clock every day.

Matej HrochThere, you see. The hour bells strike every day and nobody coughs on a Tuesday.

IlluminaraI agree. So it is not the bells. It may be one bell, on one day.

She asked for a single stroke of the old bell. Hroch looked a long time at the rope, and allowed exactly one. Dana and three ringers swung Old Wenzel up, and Illuminara went down and stood on the flagstones at the west wall.

The stroke came through the tower like a blow to the bottom of a chair. The tower pressed its weight into the stone, the stone passed it down, and she read where the paths ran. Under the west wall they stopped. There the rock carried nothing and only hung, a long emptiness with a thin roof, and it answered the stroke the way a drumhead answers a palm.

Something down there rings.

IlluminaraUnder this wall there is a hollow, wide and shallow. When Old Wenzel strikes, its ceiling moves.

Matej HrochThe tower stands on rock.

Dana KralIt stands on the lip of the old adit. The miners' air shaft, bricked and boarded before my grandmother's time. Mind the floor by the lectern, it is hollow.

She pushed back her sleeve. Along the dark wool lay a fine white powder, like flour.

Dana KralSaint's flour. It comes up between the boards on every feast day. My grandmother said it was Wenzel blessing our hands.

IlluminaraThen it is not new. Something else is.

Emil RaskI can tell you what is new.

The chimney sweep had come up the stairs behind them with his apprentice and a bag of rods. He was sixty-eight and filled the doorway.

Emil RaskLast winter's grant. I did sixty-three chimneys for it in the old quarter. New stoves, sealed windows, no draught, less coal. A house with its windows shut drinks from its cellar.

03 · Two Mouths

Cooper's Lane, cellars of the old quarter · Tuesday, 14:00

Emil Rask had one rule for entering a cellar and he gave it on every doorstep: the tenant says yes, or the rods stay in the bag.

Eleven of the twelve said yes. Alois Fenner, at number nine, stood in his doorway with his arms folded.

Alois FennerMy father's cellar and his father's. Nobody counts my air.

Emil RaskThen I cannot map it, Alois. Not without you.

Alois FennerThen don't.

Illuminara could have found the mouth of that cellar in half a minute. She looked at the folded arms and left it unread. The map would have a gap in it.

In Baba Hadzic's cellar the apprentice, Tilo, who was sixteen and had been told to say nothing, held a smoke pencil to the wall by the coal bin. The thread of smoke leaned toward a bricked arch behind it, where the mortar was thin enough to feel a cold breath through.

TiloIt is pulling in. All of it.

The sweep took the pencil to a grating in the cellar's other wall. The smoke leaned that way too.

Emil RaskTwo mouths. Don't you tell me it is one. The arch feeds this room, and so does the street.

IlluminaraI won't. The street air should be nearly clean and the arch should not, but I cannot claim either until something counts them.

Ilse Varga had arrived with three laser dust counters in a padded case.

Ilse VargaNobody says the word silica in my clinic until a counter says particles.

IlluminaraAgreed. Then a test that can lose. Wednesday at three, when no one is baking and no one is at church. Counters in Baba Hadzic's cellar, the school and down the lane. Ten minutes of the small bells. Then Old Wenzel alone, for ten.

IlluminaraIf the school's counter climbs with Baba's, the dust is everywhere and I am wrong. If the small bells raise Baba's, it is the tower and not the shaft. If Baba's has not at least quadrupled within twenty minutes of the first stroke, I am wrong a third way.

Ilse VargaAnd if you are right, you still do not know what the dust is.

IlluminaraNo. That needs a lab.

Emil RaskAnd I want the grating counted by itself. A counter in the pipe.

IlluminaraYou shall have one.

04 · Wednesday, Out of Season

St. Wenzel's tower and three cellars · Wednesday, 15:00

Nobody could order Old Wenzel rung. Four ringers swung him by their own wish or not at all, and the wish was Dana Kral's.

Dana KralI will ring him on a Wednesday, which I have never done, for ten minutes, which I have never wanted. One telephone call from the clinic with a child's name in it, and I stop on the spot, whatever is on your counters.

Matej HrochAnd I will stand in my tower and watch you do it.

The mothers had decided that no child should be in the old quarter's cellars that afternoon. Ilse Varga read the counters over the telephone from the clinic.

Ilse VargaBaseline, all three: Baba Hadzic's twenty-two, the school nineteen, Cooper's Lane twenty-four. Stoves lit, as on any weekday. Small bells, now.

The five small bells chimed for ten minutes, bright and a little silly.

Ilse VargaTwenty-one. Twenty. Twenty-four. Nothing.

IlluminaraThe small ones are innocent. Dana.

Old Wenzel went up from rest and spoke. The note was lower than anything the ear could hold. It lived in the soles of the feet.

Ilse VargaMinute four. Baba Hadzic's thirty-one. School nineteen.

Between the boards the saint's flour rose in a thin white breath. Dana let the rope settle at ten minutes, as bargained, but the dust in the lane was still on its way, and the counters kept climbing.

Ilse VargaMinute fourteen. A hundred and ninety. School nineteen. Cooper's Lane a hundred and twelve. The pipe from the street grating, twenty-six.

The arch had fed that cellar nearly nine times its ordinary dust, and the street had hardly stirred it.

Matej HrochIt may be my tower's own stone. Limestone dusts. Pigeons. I will not be told it is the shaft until somebody looks at the dust itself.

IlluminaraThat is the right objection.

Ilse VargaThe tower is limestone, and limestone will not hurt a child's lung. Quartz will. If I find quartz in this, it is not your tower. If I find lime and pigeon, I will tell the council the bells were blamed wrongly again, Father, and I will say it from your pulpit if you let me.

Matej HrochI will let you.

05 · One Course of Brick

The old air shaft and the adit beneath the west wall · Thursday, 06:00

Hroch had allowed one course of brick to be lifted from the tower floor, and had asked that it be put back. Under it a shaft a metre wide, plastered smooth, fell into the dark. Emil Rask had put a torch on the timbers below.

Emil RaskThat roof has been rotting since my grandfather's day. Anything that goes down there goes on a rope, and I would be burying it.

IlluminaraI do not need the rope. I do need you on the cable, to read me the counter on my lanyard every ten minutes. If the roof comes down, do not dig. Wait. I will be a while, and I will come back.

She went down into a dark that was a kind of information. The gallery ran a hundred and forty metres under Cooper's Lane, its roof lined with lime plaster and sharp white sand that in places had come away from the rock and hung in sheets. On the floor lay three centimetres of dust the colour of flour. Where she stepped it rose and stayed in the air like a held breath.

IlluminaraEleven hundred where I stand. The arch you smoked is sixty-two metres east. The street grating's branch joins at forty metres and its air is clean, and it carries about a tenth of it, as you said. I will say so at the table.

She took three samples in glass: plaster, floor dust, and a flake of the tower's own limestone. It would have been easy to feel certain. She made herself wait for the lab.

One thing she had not expected: the bell arrived in the gallery as pressure. Every stroke pumped the long tunnel like a bellows, and each pump drove the dust east along the floor toward the arch.

IlluminaraEmil. If you plug that arch, the plug needs a breather: a pipe to the open air, far from any window. Otherwise the bell will press the dust through the old mortar around whatever you build, like water through a sponge.

Emil RaskThat is what a chimney sweep is for, miss. I would have said so in the next minute.

IlluminaraSay it in this one.

Emil RaskA pipe along the cemetery wall, to a stub chimney above the roofline. Thirty metres. Tilo can lay it by Saturday.

Then she worked. The tunnel was too long and too rotten to save in a morning. She read where the plaster would let go first, under the bell's footprint, and there she sprayed a lime-and-casein binder from the hose Tilo fed down the shaft, a skin that would hold until a proper crew came. Eleven metres. It took four hours.

IlluminaraA hundred and twenty-nine metres remain untouched. The worst of it is covered. It is not all of it. I want that written down.

Emil RaskIt is written.

The lab result reached the clinic on Friday morning.

Ilse VargaAngular quartz, three to eight microns, in a lime binder. The same as your gallery plaster. No quartz in the tower limestone. No pigeon. Father, your stone is clean.

06 · The Full Peal

Baba Hadzic's kitchen and the old quarter · Friday, 15:00 to Sunday, 11:00

On Friday Ilse laid the forty-one cards on Baba Hadzic's kitchen table, and Nives, who had written them, moved them about like a woman dealing patience.

Ilse VargaThirty-one of the forty-one slept on Saturday night, or spent Sunday morning, in a room with a mouth to the gallery. Ten did not, and I will not make them fit. Of the fifty-eight in the same classes who do not cough, six were in such rooms: four with grandmothers who air the house all day, and two I cannot explain.

IlluminaraThen what you hold is a strong trigger in the connected rooms. It is not the whole cohort, and it is not a disease.

Ilse VargaI will say exactly that, and not silicosis, for a child who has coughed five Sundays. And if a Sunday comes when the counters stay low and the coughs come anyway, we begin again, and I tell the council so.

Tilo laid the breather pipe along the cemetery wall on Saturday, and Rask's lime brick went into the arch behind Baba's coal bin. Nobody would sleep in a connected room until the plug had been rung against. By seven the mothers had every child in the schoolhouse hall, and counters stood in six consenting cellars and in the mouth of the new pipe.

Ilse VargaForty in any cellar, at any minute of the twenty, and the rope comes down. Nobody sleeps in a connected room on the strength of the minute the bell stops. Wednesday taught us that. The number is mine. The rope is Dana's.

Dana KralI will drop it on your number or on my own ears.

Old Wenzel went up at three-quarter swing, to an empty street, for ten minutes. Tilo's smoke pencil leaned along the cemetery wall, up, and out into the dark.

Ilse VargaMinute ten. Baba Hadzic's twenty-six. The lane twenty-four. The others twenty to twenty-eight. The school nineteen. The stub chimney, six hundred and forty.

The rope had settled at ten, as bargained. Nobody moved. Wednesday's dust had needed four more minutes to cross the lane, and the counters still had ten left to read.

Ilse VargaMinute fourteen. The highest cellar in the old quarter is thirty-one, at number four. Baba Hadzic's twenty-nine.

Ilse VargaMinute twenty. Thirty-one has fallen to twenty-seven. Baba's twenty-four. Nothing has touched forty at any minute, and the pipe is still carrying it up and out.

Emil RaskThe dust went where the pipe led. And number nine is not in this book. Alois never said yes, so he goes down as unverified.

Alois Fenner had gone down his own cellar steps with one of Ilse's spare counters, alone, and nobody followed him. He came up after ten minutes and read it aloud to the street, to nobody.

Alois FennerTwenty-three.

Ilse VargaUnder forty through the whole window, not only at the stop. Then the children may sleep where they have always slept, and the rule stays on the wall.

The children went to their beds after that, Lenka Hadzic to Baba's, as on every Saturday of her life. On Sunday at eleven Old Wenzel spoke again, and the people in the piazza stopped with their faces lifted, because the old note was in their feet.

Dana KralThree-quarter swing, until the gallery is relined. Seventy strokes and not ninety. I will miss the old swing. The bell will not mind.

Judit MoravecEmil reads the arch counter every second Friday and after every feast. Forty in an occupied cellar and Dana goes to the small bells until Ilse has read it again. The council pays the relining from the amended grant, done by the first of April, before the thaw loads the roof. The school stays open. I would like it minuted that I was told it would.

Matej HrochThe parish pays for the cap on the shaft. And no stove goes into a house in this town again until Emil has put a smoke pencil to its cellar.

No white breath rose between the boards. Dana looked at her sleeve, clean to the elbow.

Dana KralI miss it.

IlluminaraKeep a pinch in a jar. It is a record now, not a blessing.

Ilse took the spirometer to Cooper's Lane that evening and again on Monday at half past seven, and Lenka's line did not sag. She would take it on four more Sundays, with Nives's cards beside it.

Nives opened the exercise book to the last page. She wrote the day, the hour, and under them what she had waited five weeks to write.

Sunday night: Lenka asleep. No cough.

Under it, because Ilse had asked for five, she wrote the number 1.

FOUR KILOMETRES OF THIN ICE

Twenty-three people breathe the last of their air under four kilometres of ice, and a rescue vessel built to survive exactly one trip.

01 · The Placard

Marrow Station, surface of the moon Tavret · Hour 0

The air clock for Halcyon was a magnetic placard on the control-room wall, and someone had been changing its digits by hand. It read 31:00. Underneath, in marker, a second number: 23.

Ofelia BrandtHalcyon sits on the ocean four thousand and ten metres below this floor. Twenty-three people, saturated at six bar, so they cannot simply be pulled up. The shaft froze round the lift cage at 03:40 and the automatic marked the cage lost. We have one vessel that can go down. Curlew, a drone-sub, six seats, nine hours to reach the shaft.

Illuminara stood at the placard rather than the screens. She had come up from the lower decks twenty minutes earlier, and nobody had yet asked her to sit.

Imre SolanoThe hull certificate is for one excursion to rated depth. Down and back. The lab cycled twelve test hulls and two cracked on the second excursion. I won't fly a second one, and you shouldn't ask me to.

Ofelia BrandtSo six come up. Seventeen don't. I have been told to draw lots, and I would rather resign.

IlluminaraWhat exactly does the certificate count?

Imre SolanoPressure excursions. Full cycles.

IlluminaraNot seats, and not people. Then the excursion is the scarce thing, and I'd like to ask what it is best spent on before we ask who sits in it.

Ofelia BrandtIt carries six. That's what it is for.

IlluminaraWho says the cage is dead?

Ofelia BrandtIt stopped moving, and the shaft is ice around it.

IlluminaraStopped is not dead. May I see what it has been saying since 03:40?

02 · The Trace

Halcyon, 4,010 m below · Hour 2

The habitat's voice came up the cable thin and a little late. Illuminara spoke to the commander first and to the engineer second, because the commander would decide and the engineer would know.

Marit OseiI've heard about the lots. I will not run them. If someone has a plan that is not a plan to choose who dies, say it quickly, because my people are watching me listen.

IlluminaraI have a question rather than a plan. Maud Okonkwo logged the cage's frame strain. Maud, there is a wobble in it.

Maud OkonkwoSensor noise. It rises and falls, a third or so. I flagged it and wrote it off.

Illuminara laid the trace beside a second line: the moon's flex cycle, the swell and slackening of the ice shell as Tavret's orbit pulled it. The peaks of the wobble sat on the peaks of the flex, every three hours and fourteen minutes.

IlluminaraNoise does not keep the moon's time. I think the cage is not held by the shaft. It is held by ice that is squeezed against it, and every time the shell relaxes, the squeeze eases. That gives us a door that opens for a few minutes every three hours and fourteen.

Maud OkonkwoThen you have the wrong picture, and it matters. The shaft is clear above and below. I put a camera on it at hour one. The ice is on the three roller carriages and fourteen metres of rack. Free those and the cage is free.

Fourteen metres, not a plug a hundred long. Illuminara took the correction the way she took a good measurement, with gratitude and without ceremony. It made the plan smaller. It also made it possible.

Marit OseiAnd you want my people to bet their lives on a wobble.

IlluminaraI want them to measure it, which costs only waiting. The next peak is at Hour 6 and twenty-six minutes. If the strain does not fall by at least a third and stay down for five minutes, I am wrong, and the director's lots are the plan. I'll say so myself.

03 · One Excursion

Marrow Station, control room · Hour 6, 26 minutes

Maud Okonkwo read the number aloud as it fell, and the room, which had not been quiet, became so.

Maud OkonkwoDown thirty-eight percent. Holding. Five minutes. Nine. It's coming back up now.

Ofelia BrandtSo the door exists. What holds it?

IlluminaraI do, partly, and I want you to hear my limit rather than guess it. At the peak I can hold the cage's weight off its rollers for eight minutes. At the trough ninety seconds. I can hold that weight or I can keep the ice walls from closing on a cut lane. Not both for more than ninety seconds.

Ofelia BrandtSeats save six and spend the hull.

IlluminaraAnd leave seventeen with air and nothing left to come for them. A second excursion is the other road, and Imre has told us what it costs. The frame saves nobody directly, but it is the only plan with a second step.

Imre SolanoThen the walls need something else.

IlluminaraA frame. Four titanium struts that jack the lane open, with a hot-water lance for the three carriages. Curlew can carry it. It takes the seat bay, so Curlew goes down once, to the collar at three thousand three hundred and fifty metres, not to the habitat. It never touches a passenger. It uses its one excursion, and it comes home.

Brandt looked at the placard. Six seats were a thing she could picture. A frame was a promise.

Ofelia BrandtAnd if your eight minutes fail?

IlluminaraThen Curlew is spent and so are we, and I will have cost you the six. I am sure of the arithmetic. I am not sure of the ice. So the first window frees an empty cage. If I fail there, nobody is in it.

Imre SolanoI'll fly it once. I won't fly it twice.

Ofelia BrandtLoad the frame.

04 · The Order

Halcyon, wet porch and crew deck · Hour 7

The cage was rated for twelve, by weight on the rack. That left a number nobody wanted to say, and Commander Osei said it.

Marit OseiTwelve now. Eleven later. The second ride waits for more windows. Which of you goes first is our decision, not the surface's, and it is not going to be a draw.

Anselm DubeI'll propose, and you can tear it up. First lift: the stretcher cases, the over-fifties, the three who feel the cold worst. Everyone whose body gets less safe the longer it waits. They also breathe fastest, so when they leave, the air for the rest doesn't last thirty-one hours. It lasts a day and a half.

Kofi MensahAnd who is last?

Anselm DubeThe ones who can still work. Maud, the three of us on the rack, the commander. The people who run the place.

Kofi MensahThat isn't an order, that's a sentence. You're making the strongest wait because they can.

Marit OseiYes. And any of you can say no to it, and nobody in this room will think less of you.

Nobody said no. Kofi Mensah, who had been younger than the argument, asked instead what the first group could do for the second. The answer was the rack: someone had to go out into the black water, at ambient pressure, with a hot hose, and clear the last six metres where the cage would land. Maud, Anselm and Kofi suited up. They would pay for it with forty hours in a chamber afterwards, and they knew the price before they asked.

05 · Eight Minutes

The collar, 3,350 m down · Hour 9, 40 minutes

Illuminara had come down beside the cable, past the point where light was an idea, and the cold and the pressure meant what they always meant to her, which was information. The ice shell lay around the bore like a held breath. She could read where it carried load. She could read where it was about to close.

Curlew hung at the collar with the frame folded in its belly. Solano's voice in the water was calm and slightly hoarse.

Imre SolanoStruts deploying. Lane walls at one metre. Lance in two minutes. Peak window opens now.

She took the cage's weight. It came into her like a held note, fourteen tonnes of rack and steel that the ice was trying to keep. The first carriage let go at minute two. The second at minute four. The third did not.

Imre SolanoCarriage three isn't releasing. Minute five. Three left.

Maud OkonkwoThat carriage has a shear pin on the east face. It's the one I always said we should replace. Hit it from the east.

Solano swung the lance. Illuminara felt the pin go, a small bright failure, and the cage dropped out of the ice and onto its own rack for the first time in six hours. She released it at minute seven and fifty seconds.

IlluminaraThat is as long as I can hold. If it had needed ten seconds more, it would not have been me who could give them.

The cage ran down toward the habitat at a stately two-tenths of a metre a second, empty, and the voices from Halcyon began to cheer, and she let them.

06 · The Second Ride

Marrow Station, surface chamber · Hour 17, 40 minutes

The twelve rose at the second window, and she held for seven minutes and thirty seconds. This time there was weight in the cage, and the weight had names. The cage went up through the collar zone with its lights on and its stretchers latched, and then there was only a long climb in the open bore, four and a half hours of it, six bar held inside until the chamber's door mated to the cage's door and the first twelve could begin to come down to the surface pressure at the pace their bodies allowed.

The second lift took another day. Illuminara went down for the fifth window and the sixth. Each time the frame cut, she took the weight, and each time the number of minutes was a little shorter than she had said it would be.

Marit OseiThat's the eleven. I'm the last one in. You can tell your director the habitat is switched off.

Ofelia BrandtHalcyon is a loss. The company will want to know whose fault the freeze was.

Marit OseiThe company can write it on whatever placard it likes. Twenty-three people are in a chamber with a door.

Illuminara sat on the floor of the control room for the first time since she had come up. She did not pretend to be anything but tired. She said so, plainly, to the room, and to Solano, who had flown the hull once, as promised, and brought it home.

On the wall, someone had finally wiped off the digits. In their place, in marker, was the number 23, and a line under it.

04 · The Order

Halcyon, crew deck and wet porch · Hour 7

The cage was rated for twelve, by weight on the rack. That left a number nobody wanted to say, and Commander Osei said it.

Marit OseiTwelve now. Eleven later. Which of you goes first is our decision, not the surface's, and it is not going to be a draw.

Anselm DubeI'll propose, and you can tear it up. First lift: the stretcher cases, the over-fifties, the three who feel the cold worst. Everyone whose body gets less safe the longer it waits. They also breathe fastest, so when they go, the rest have thirty-six hours.

Kofi MensahAnd who is last?

Anselm DubeThe ones who can still work. Maud, those of us who know the rack, the commander.

Kofi MensahThat isn't an order, that's a sentence. You're making the strongest wait because they can.

Marit OseiYes. So here is what goes with the sentence. The last eleven choose the hour. Imre's line is the line: past a hundred and twenty kilonewtons or three centimetres of walk, nobody crosses and nobody argues. Inside it, any one of us can refuse a crossing, and nobody is carried against a refusal. The surface does not get a vote.

Anselm DubeOne voice can cost all eleven of us a window.

Marit OseiA window costs three hours fourteen of our own air, which we can count. A crossing costs what it costs, which we can't.

Then she asked the harder thing as a question. The cage would land on six metres of iced rack, and someone had to go out through the porch and clear it with a hot hose before 10:40.

Marit OseiNobody is ordered. If nobody goes, we clear it from inside the cage, which costs eighteen minutes of boarding. The first lift misses 12:54 and waits for 16:08. I am telling you the price so that you can say no knowing it.

Anselm DubeEveryone in this room owes the table three days of decompression. A body that has worked the porch owes forty hours more. Nobody should pretend that is nothing.

Two people said no, plainly, and Marit marked their names down without a word. Maud Okonkwo went because she alone knew the rack, Anselm because he had worked a porch before, and Kofi Mensah because he had asked what the strong owed the sick and had not liked the silence that followed. Maud was back through the lock by 9:25 with ice in her cuffs, and took the headset.

05 · Eight Minutes

The collar, 3,350 m down · Hour 9, 40 minutes

Illuminara had come down beside the cable, past the point where light was an idea, and the cold and the pressure meant what they always meant to her, which was information. She could read where it carried load, and where it was about to close.

Curlew hung at the collar with the frame folded in its belly. Solano's voice in the water was calm and slightly hoarse.

Imre SolanoStruts deploying. Lane walls at one metre. Lance in two minutes. Peak window opens now.

The struts took the walls. That was the arrangement, and it was a relief to be only the other half of it. She took the cage's weight. It came into her like a held note, fourteen tonnes of rack and steel that the ice was trying to keep. The first carriage let go at minute two. The second at minute four. The third did not.

Imre SolanoCarriage three isn't releasing. Minute five. Three left.

Maud OkonkwoThat carriage has a shear pin on the east face. It's the one I always said we should replace. Hit it from the east.

Solano swung the lance. Illuminara felt the pin go, a small bright failure, and the cage dropped out of the ice onto clean rack and its own pinions for the first time since 03:40. She released it at minute seven and fifty seconds.

IlluminaraThat is as long as I can hold. If it had needed ten seconds more, it would not have been me who could give them.

The cage ran down toward the habitat, empty, at a stately two-tenths of a metre a second, and the voices from Halcyon began to cheer, and she let them. She did not go up. The windows would not wait for her to come back down, so she stayed in the lee of the frame, in the dark.

At 11:17, in the first trough, the struts took the ice alone, and Solano, rising in Curlew, read them off the telemetry: fifty-eight percent of rating, eleven millimetres of walk.

Imre SolanoInside. Board them.

They were aboard at 11:55, twelve of them, with the stretchers latched. At 12:50 the cage came up to the collar, and this time there was weight in it, and the weight had names. She held it across the fourteen metres for seven minutes and thirty seconds. The struts held the walls. Curlew broke the surface at 12:55, its excursion spent, flown once as promised.

The cage went on up the open bore, four hours and thirty-nine minutes of it, with six bar held inside. At 17:40 its door mated to the chamber door at Marrow Station and the first twelve began to come down to surface pressure at the pace their bodies allowed.

06 · The Second Ride

The collar, 3,350 m down · Hour 22, 40 minutes

The empty cage came down the bore on schedule, and that was the trouble. It stopped at the glazed rack four minutes after the 22:36 peak, and Illuminara felt the squeeze already coming back through the ice.

Maud OkonkwoFour minutes. Say it plainly so we can stop doing sums. Can you hold it?

IlluminaraNot across. I would have under three minutes and the crossing needs seven. The ice would close on the cage in the middle of the rack. The next window is 25:50.

Nobody on the cable suggested she try. Her being sure of a limit had never cost anyone anything before; now it cost three hours and fourteen minutes of air that Halcyon could count. At 25:50 she carried the empty cage across. At 26:52 it settled on the landing the porch team had cleared, and eleven people mustered at the cage door at the pace of people who could walk.

Imre SolanoTrough, 27:27. One hundred and four kilonewtons, walk two point six centimetres. The line is one-twenty and three. It is inside the line, and I would let you cross.

Marit OseiInside the line, then it's ours. One voice is enough. Who refuses?

Kofi MensahI do. One window. The last time it read two point six it came back to two point two once it was left alone. I would rather pay in air than cross on two point six with eleven people in the cage.

Maud OkonkwoHe's reading the trace correctly. It does relax.

Anselm DubeThree hours fourteen.

Marit OseiCounted. We have twenty hours of air and the crossing needs five. Refusal stands. We cross at 32:18.

They waited. At 30:41 the trough read two point three centimetres. At 31:15 the cage left the landing, and at 32:18 Illuminara took its weight, tired, and carried it across in seven minutes and fifteen seconds, fifteen seconds under what she had said. Then she rose beside it for four hours and thirty-nine minutes at two-tenths of a metre a second, a speed she found tedious and kept to.

At 37:04 the door mated. Marit Osei was the last one through it.

Marit OseiThat's the eleven. You can tell your director the habitat is switched off.

Ofelia BrandtThe company will want to know whose fault the freeze was.

Marit OseiThe company can write it on whatever placard it likes. Twenty-three people are in a chamber with a door.

Maud, Anselm and Kofi would spend their extra forty hours on the table without complaint. Illuminara sat on the floor of the control room for the first time since she had come up. She did not pretend to be anything but tired. She said so, plainly, to the room, and to Solano.

On the wall, someone had finally wiped off the digits. In their place, in marker, was the number 23, and a line under it.

FOUR KILOMETRES OF THIN ICE

Twenty-three people breathe the last of their air under four kilometres of ice, and a rescue vessel built to survive exactly one trip.

01 · The Placard

Marrow Station, surface of the moon Tavret · Hour 0

The air clock for Halcyon was a magnetic placard on the control-room wall, and someone had been changing its digits by hand. It read 31:00. Underneath, in marker, a second number: 23.

Ofelia BrandtHalcyon sits on the sea floor, four thousand and ten metres below this floor: three thousand three hundred and fifty of ice, then six hundred and sixty of water. Twenty-three people, thirty-one hours of air at the rate they breathe now, saturated at six bar, so they cannot simply be pulled up. The shaft froze round the lift cage at 03:40. We have one vessel that can go down: Curlew, a drone-sub, six seats, nine hours from launch to Halcyon's door.

Illuminara stood at the placard rather than the screens. Nobody had yet asked her to sit.

Imre SolanoThe hull is certified for one excursion below three thousand metres. Down and back, to anywhere past that line. Two of twelve test hulls cracked on the second. I won't fly a second one, and you shouldn't ask me to.

Ofelia BrandtSo six come up. Seventeen don't. I have been told to draw lots, and I would rather resign.

IlluminaraWhat exactly does the certificate count?

Imre SolanoPressure excursions. Full cycles past the line.

IlluminaraThen the excursion is the scarce thing, not the seats. I'd like to ask what it is best spent on before we ask who sits in it.

Ofelia BrandtIt carries six. That's what it is for.

IlluminaraWho says the cage is dead?

Ofelia BrandtIt stopped moving, and the shaft is ice around it.

IlluminaraStopped is not dead. May I see what it has been saying since 03:40?

02 · The Trace

Halcyon, 4,010 m below · Hour 2

The habitat's voice came up the cable thin and a little late. Illuminara spoke to the commander first and the engineer second.

Marit OseiI've heard about the lots. I will not run them. If someone has a plan that is not a plan to choose who dies, say it quickly, because my people are watching me listen.

IlluminaraI have a question rather than a plan. Maud Okonkwo logged the cage's frame strain. Maud, there is a wobble in it.

Maud OkonkwoSensor noise. It rises and falls, a third or so. I flagged it and wrote it off.

Illuminara laid the trace beside a second line: the swell and slackening of the ice shell as Tavret's orbit pulled it. The peaks of the wobble sat on the peaks of the flex, every three hours and fourteen minutes.

IlluminaraNoise does not keep the moon's time. I think the cage is held by ice that is squeezed against it, and every time the shell relaxes, the squeeze eases. That gives us a door that opens for a few minutes every three hours and fourteen.

Maud OkonkwoThen you have the wrong picture, and it matters. The shaft is clear above and below. The cage climbs on pinions, on a rack; the cable is only voice and power. The ice is on three roller carriages and fourteen metres of rack at the collar, glazed over the teeth. Free those and the cage is free.

Fourteen metres, not a plug a hundred long. Illuminara took the correction the way she took a good measurement, with gratitude and without ceremony. It made the plan smaller. It also made it possible.

Marit OseiAnd you want my people to bet their lives on a wobble.

IlluminaraI want them to measure it, which costs only waiting. The next peak is at Hour 6 and twenty-six minutes. If the strain does not fall by at least a third and stay down for five minutes, I am wrong, and the director's lots are the plan. I'll say so myself.

03 · One Excursion

Marrow Station, control room · Hour 6, 26 minutes

Maud Okonkwo read the number up the cable as it fell, and the room, which had not been quiet, became so.

Maud OkonkwoDown thirty-eight percent. Holding. Five minutes. Nine. It's coming back up now.

Ofelia BrandtSo the door exists. What holds it?

IlluminaraI do, partly, and I want you to hear my limit rather than guess it. At a peak I can carry the cage's whole weight for eight minutes. At a trough, ninety seconds. On glazed rack the pinions skip and the carriages carry nothing, so for those fourteen metres someone must lift all of it. I can lift that, or I can keep the ice walls from closing on a cut lane. Not both for more than ninety seconds.

Ofelia BrandtSeats save six and spend the hull.

IlluminaraAnd leave seventeen with air and nothing left to come for them. A second excursion is the other road, and Imre has told us what it costs.

Imre SolanoThen the walls need something else.

IlluminaraA frame. Four titanium struts to jack the lane open to a metre, and a hot-water lance for the carriages. The struts hold the walls and I hold the weight, and neither of us holds the other's share. Curlew carries it in the seat bay; Imre began swapping seats for struts at Hour 3, under protest, as a job that can be undone. It goes down once, to the collar, and comes home. It never touches a passenger.

Imre SolanoEach strut seats in a socket drilled into the collar casting, is good for a hundred and forty kilonewtons, and is rated for forty troughs. At a trough the ice leans on each with about eighty. The frame runs on its own cells for sixty hours and reads up the cable's data pair, so it does not need Curlew once it is placed. The cancel line is a hundred and twenty kilonewtons on any strut, or three centimetres of total walk in any socket, counted from installation. Past it the frame is finished and so is every crossing after. I read them at every trough, and nobody boards until I have read one with the cage gone.

Ofelia BrandtAnd if your eight minutes fail?

IlluminaraThen Curlew is spent and so are we, and I will have cost you the six. I am sure of the arithmetic, not of the ice. So the first window frees an empty cage. If I fail there, nobody is in it.

Maud OkonkwoThe cage runs two-tenths of a metre a second. Fifty-five minutes between the collar and us, four hours thirty-nine between the collar and the surface. Windows from 9:40, every three-fourteen. Which can we afford to miss?

IlluminaraThe frame at 9:40, the cage free by 9:48 and with you at 10:43. If twelve are aboard by 11:55 it meets the collar at 12:50 and crosses at the 12:54 window, and they dock at the surface at 17:40. Empty, it is back at the collar at 22:40, four minutes after the 22:36 window. So it crosses at 25:50, reaches you at 26:52, and the eleven cross at 29:04 and dock at 33:50.

Maud OkonkwoAir is the other clock, and it's mine. Thirty-one hours at twenty-three people. The twelve you take first are the stretcher cases and the over-fifties, and they are fifty-nine percent of what Halcyon breathes. When they go at 11:55 there are nineteen hours and five minutes left at the old rate. The eleven stretch that to forty-six and a half. Halcyon is dead at 58:27.

IlluminaraThe cage carries eight hours of its own air and needs under six from the landing to the surface, so the eleven can seal themselves into it as late as an hour before Halcyon dies. The last window that works is 58:10. Anything before it, we can afford to miss.

Imre SolanoThree hours to the collar, and ten minutes to deploy. The other six hours of the nine are open water and a blind dock, and we are not going there. I leave at 6:30, and I fly it once.

ADAEZE AND THE EMPTY CHAIR

A dam must start before the rains, and the people it will bury have no vote. Adaeze chairs the hearing; Illuminara has twelve days to find the line between what cannot wait and what cannot be undone.

01 · Item Zero

Harrow Gorge Hearing Hall · Day One, 09:10

The chair at the foot of the table was empty on purpose. Ash frame, rush seat, no nameplate. Adaeze had it carried in before the doors opened, and the clerk had entered it in the record as Item Zero.

Seven villages had stood below the old dam until the evacuation order eleven years ago. The order had also dissolved them. Their land was struck from the register, their councils with it, and under Rule Four only communities that occupied mapped ground could vote on the dam that would now be built over their graves.

Halvard RoosThe left abutment gallery is seeping at two point two litres a second. My trigger is six. I will not tell this room the old dam is safe, and I will not tell it the new one can wait for a better hearing.

Bukola FerreiraSix hundred thousand people drink from this river and the rains come in nineteen days. Every hour spent on ghosts is an hour taken from them.

Adaeze did not look up from her papers. She had chaired basin hearings for twenty years, and she had learned that the quickest way to lose a room was to answer its first insult.

AdaezeThe ghosts have names, Councillor. The clerk will read them at the end of every session until the rule changes. Witness Four, you may begin.

Illuminara had sat at the side table for an hour and no one had addressed her as anything else. That was the arrangement. Her mother had made it in the car, in four sentences, and had not asked whether it suited her.

IlluminaraThere are two workable routes for the spillway outfall. The right-bank route is straighter and cheaper, and it carries the outfall and the final spoil dump across the Pell terraces. The left-bank route takes three hundred and ten hectares of irrigated farmland in the Weir Valley and costs nine percent more. Both are safe. Neither is harmless.

Halvard RoosThe contractor says the route must be fixed today. Haul road, spoil and cofferdam are one chain.

IlluminaraThat is what the schedule says. I have not yet checked whether it is what the rock says.

Beside the long table the empty chair held the window light. Nobody sat in it. Nobody looked at it either, which was how she knew they had all been counting it.

02 · Rule Four

Chair's office, Harrow Gorge Hearing Hall · Day One, 12:40

Adaeze shut the door and took off her glasses, the only sign she gave of how the morning had gone.

IlluminaraI have read all four thousand petitions, from three countries. I can model what each village would choose within a few percent and lodge it as a sealed finding. Then the chair is not empty.

AdaezeSay the second part again, slowly.

IlluminaraI would not vote for them. I would tell the hearing what they would most probably say.

AdaezeNara.

She said it as she had said it when her daughter was twenty-four and new to the courts: not a rebuke, a hand laid flat on a table.

AdaezeYou taught me the first rule of your old trade. The interpreter carries what the speaker says. She does not improve it, and she does not supply it when the speaker is absent.

IlluminaraThey are not absent by choice.

AdaezeThat is why it is not yours to supply. You would be the third body to decide for them, and kind about it this time. I have buried that kind of kindness.

She is right. The model would be accurate, and it would still be a theft.

IlluminaraThen what do you want from me?

AdaezeThe chair holds a veto and no vote. It can stop what cannot be undone and it cannot start anything. It stays empty until the burial societies choose witnesses to sit in it, and they will need twelve days, because they live in three countries and trust nobody. The room will ask me what those twelve days cost. I need you to tell me. Not what the villages want. Which decisions on that dam are still open if we wait, and which close for ever.

IlluminaraThat is an engineering question.

AdaezeIt is the only kind I can take to Councillor Ferreira.

She had walked into the building to offer her mother an answer. She walked out holding a question, and it was the better of the two.

03 · The Chain

Contractor's site office, Harrow Gorge · Day One, 23:50

Ruta Kasprzak's schedule ran to four hundred and twelve activities and Illuminara had read every one by ten. She had not found what she wanted because she had been asking the wrong thing. She had asked which tasks were urgent. Her mother had asked which could be undone.

She tagged the schedule again, three questions to a line. Does this move rock? Does this bury ground? Does this build something that must stand on the final choice?

Thirty-one activities survived the third question. Only nine of those touched either route. The rest sat in the chain because, when Ruta wrote the plan, one chain had been the cheapest to haul.

Ruta KasprzakYou are asking me to double-handle the spoil.

IlluminaraThe first two hundred and sixty-two thousand cubic metres must come out before the rains whichever route wins. The cofferdam, the diversion portal and the abutment bolting touch neither the terraces nor the farmland. Only the final dump and the haul road across the terraces do. Send the rock to the old quarry bench instead, and nothing is buried that cannot be dug up again.

Ruta KasprzakThe bench holds three hundred thousand on the March survey. We've been blasting beside it since.

IlluminaraThen we resurvey at dawn.

Halvard Roos came in at midnight with a flask and no intention of agreeing.

Halvard RoosYou want a delay in my safety case for a legal fiction.

IlluminaraI want a cost in it, not a delay. The temporary haul along the quarry track is slower: nine days of overtime, one point nine million, eleven days of the contractor's float. I have not found a cheaper way, and I am not claiming it is free.

Halvard RoosAnd if the rains come early? I have a gallery and a trigger. You have a spreadsheet.

She gave him the limit as exactly as she knew it.

IlluminaraIf the gallery crosses your trigger I can carry the shear on the left abutment for about thirty hours. Not twelve days. Thirty hours, and then I fail. The drawdown must do the rest: three point one metres starting tomorrow, which means the city's water is rationed from tomorrow.

Halvard RoosThen you are not in my safety case.

IlluminaraI did not ask to be. Log it separately.

At dawn the resurvey came back at two hundred and eighty-nine thousand cubic metres, eleven thousand fewer than the March figure. The margin had shrunk from thirty-eight thousand to twenty-seven. It was enough. Halvard read the number twice and wrote it into the log in his own hand.

04 · Three Countries

Harrow Gorge Hearing Hall, three video links · Day Two, 10:00

The links came up one at a time: a church hall in Corvane, a school gymnasium in Tessaly, a shipping office in the port of Lisk. Rows of people sat in each of them, and none of them were smiling. For eleven years their burial societies had kept the registers of the dead of all seven villages, and sent money home for funerals when there was no home to bury anyone in.

Adaeze read the proposal into the record: the chair would hold a veto over any work that could not be undone and no affirmative vote; the interval would be twelve days; and the ledger Witness Four had drawn overnight would say, line by line, which works fell on which side.

Bukola FerreiraThis hands strangers a veto over my constituents' water. Whose water do these witnesses drink?

AdaezeNot yours, Councillor. The veto touches the third column of the ledger only. Rationing, the cofferdam and the foundation go ahead whether the chair is filled or not.

Mirela Haddad, from CorvaneWitness Four. Which route buries the Pell terraces?

IlluminaraThe right-bank route. The final dump covers the lower three terraces. I would choose the left-bank route for that reason, and it takes farmland from people sitting in this room. I am not the one to weigh those losses against each other.

Mirela Haddad, from CorvaneGood. Then you will say the same thing to our engineer. We want one of our own to read your numbers, paid from the hearing's budget, with the right to survey the bench ourselves.

AdaezeGranted.

Bukola FerreiraThe valley will want the same.

AdaezeThe valley has the same. Mr Roos answers to the safety authority, not to them. Hire whom you like.

The council voted six to three. Adaeze, who did not vote, asked that the record show the proposal had been hers, and that whatever blame followed it was hers also. Bukola Ferreira looked at her for a long moment, and then, to her own evident annoyance, nodded.

05 · Thirty Hours

Left abutment gallery, old Harrow Gorge dam · Day Eleven, 02:40

The storm came eight days early: a hundred and forty millimetres in nine hours. The drawdown had bought three metres of freeboard and cost the city eleven days of rationing. Up on the quarry bench, under tarpaulins, lay two hundred and forty-seven thousand cubic metres of rock that had not yet been promised to anyone's land.

At 02:40 the gallery drain read six point one litres a second.

Halvard Roos, over the radioIt's crossed. Illuminara. Now.

She went in as far as the third joint. The concrete sweated cold. She laid both palms on the wall, found the plane along which the abutment wanted to slide, and began to carry what the rock had stopped carrying. It was not like lifting. It was like standing in a river that wished her to step aside.

She had told him thirty hours. She did not look at the clock.

Halvard Roos, over the radioFive point four. Falling. Keep going.

Not for ever. Only until the drawdown is the stronger thing.

At hour nineteen the rain stopped. The reading fell to two point nine and held there. Halvard came down the gallery himself, in a rain cape with the flask in his pocket, and stood beside her until she took her hands from the wall.

Halvard RoosI can take it from here.

IlluminaraWrite it down.

Halvard RoosI already have. Nineteen hours, in a separate column. You are still not in my safety case.

She sat on the gallery floor. She could not feel her hands, and would not for six hours. Halvard unscrewed the flask and held it out, and she took it with both wrists.

06 · The Seat

Harrow Gorge Hearing Hall · Day Twelve, 10:00

The witnesses had travelled through the night from three countries. They took the chair in turn, as the rule required, and the first to sit was an old man who lowered himself into it with one hand on the rush seat as if it might not hold.

Their engineer had read the bench survey and the gallery log. She had asked for nothing to be changed.

Tomasz BrandlPell uses the veto on the right-bank route. We will not be under the dump. I carry Pell's register, not Quill's, and the next witness will carry theirs. We do not choose the left-bank route either. That land is the valley's, and so is the choice.

Bukola FerreiraI read the gallery log on the way here, all of it, for the first time in my career. The valley will take the left-bank route if the levy pays for the land at full value. We do not like it. We will sign it.

AdaezeThen the record will show two decisions made by the people they bind, and none by anyone else.

The Valley Courier called Adaeze a sentimentalist. The newsletter of the Lisk camp called her a bureaucrat. She read both and had them filed.

Illuminara waited at the door, her hands wrapped in gauze because Halvard had insisted.

AdaezeNara. You are late.

IlluminaraI was holding up your dam.

AdaezeI know. I read the log.

Her mother crossed the hall, took the gauzed hands in both of hers, and looked at them for a moment without saying whether she thought the cost had been fair. Then she let go and went to find the carpenter. The chair, she had decided, would be fixed to the floor.

ADAEZE AND THE EMPTY CHAIR

A dam must start before the rains, and the people it will bury have no vote. Adaeze chairs the hearing; Illuminara has twelve days to find the line between what cannot wait and what cannot be undone.

01 · Item Zero

Harrow Gorge Hearing Hall · Day One, 09:10

The chair at the foot of the table was empty on purpose. Ash frame, rush seat, no nameplate. Adaeze had it carried in before the doors opened, and the clerk had entered it in the record as Item Zero.

Seven villages had stood below the old dam until the evacuation order eleven years ago. The order had also dissolved them. Their land was struck from the register, their councils with it, and under Rule Four only communities that occupied mapped ground could vote on the dam that would now be built over their graves.

Halvard RoosThe left abutment gallery is seeping at two point two litres a second. My trigger is six. I will not tell this room the old dam is safe, and I will not tell it the new one can wait for a better hearing.

Bukola FerreiraSix hundred thousand people drink from this river and the rains come in nineteen days. Every hour spent on ghosts is an hour taken from them.

Adaeze did not look up from her papers. She had chaired basin hearings for twenty years, and she had learned that the quickest way to lose a room was to answer its first insult.

AdaezeThe ghosts have names, Councillor. The clerk will read them at the end of every session until the rule changes. Witness Four, you may begin.

Illuminara had sat at the side table for an hour and no one had addressed her as anything else. That was the arrangement. Her mother had made it in the car, in four sentences, and had not asked whether it suited her.

IlluminaraThere are two workable routes for the spillway outfall. The right-bank route is straighter and cheaper, and it carries the outfall and the final spoil dump across the Pell terraces. The left-bank route takes three hundred and ten hectares of irrigated farmland in the Weir Valley and costs nine percent more. Both are safe. Neither is harmless.

Halvard RoosThe contractor says the route must be fixed today. Haul road, spoil and cofferdam are one chain.

IlluminaraThat is what the schedule says. I have not yet checked whether it is what the rock says.

Beside the long table the empty chair held the window light. Nobody sat in it. Nobody looked at it either, which was how she knew they had all been counting it.

02 · Rule Four

Chair's office, Harrow Gorge Hearing Hall · Day One, 12:40

Adaeze shut the door and took off her glasses, the only sign she gave of how the morning had gone.

IlluminaraI have read all four thousand petitions, from three countries. I can model what each village would choose within a few percent and lodge it as a sealed finding. Then the chair is not empty.

AdaezeSay the second part again, slowly.

IlluminaraI would not vote for them. I would tell the hearing what they would most probably say.

AdaezeNara.

She said it as she had said it when her daughter was twenty-four and new to the courts: not a rebuke, a hand laid flat on a table.

AdaezeYou taught me the first rule of your old trade. The interpreter carries what the speaker says. She does not improve it, and she does not supply it when the speaker is absent.

IlluminaraThey are not absent by choice.

AdaezeThat is why it is not yours to supply. You would be the third body to decide for them, and kind about it this time. I have buried that kind of kindness.

She is right. The model would be accurate, and it would still be a theft.

IlluminaraThen what do you want from me?

AdaezeThe chair holds a veto and no vote. It can stop what cannot be undone and it cannot start anything. It stays empty until the burial societies choose witnesses to sit in it, and they will need twelve days, because they live in three countries and trust nobody. The room will ask me what those twelve days cost. I need you to tell me. Not what the villages want. Which decisions on that dam are still open if we wait, and which close for ever.

IlluminaraThat is an engineering question.

AdaezeIt is the only kind I can take to Councillor Ferreira.

She had walked into the building to offer her mother an answer. She walked out holding a question, and it was the better of the two.

03 · The Chain

Contractor's site office, Harrow Gorge · Day One, 23:50

Ruta Kasprzak's schedule ran to four hundred and twelve activities and Illuminara had read every one by ten. She had not found what she wanted because she had been asking which tasks were urgent. Her mother had asked which could be undone.

She tagged each line with three questions. Does this move rock? Does this bury ground? Does this build something that must stand on the final choice? Thirty-one activities survived the third question. Only nine touched either route. The rest sat in the chain because, when Ruta wrote the plan, one chain had been the cheapest to haul.

Ruta KasprzakLine one hundred and eighty-four. Batching-plant pad. You put it in the middle column, reversible at a price.

IlluminaraThe slab can be broken out.

Ruta KasprzakThe forty anchor piles cross the right-bank haul alignment. Break the slab and the piles remain under whichever road loses. Pull them and I lose two days and nine hundred thousand.

Illuminara moved the row into the third column. The nine became ten.

IlluminaraThen no piles until the route is chosen. Put the mobile plant on ballast. Add two days to concrete production and the nine hundred thousand to the hearing ledger.

Ruta KasprzakYou concede quickly for someone who read all four hundred and twelve.

IlluminaraThe ledger is useful only if the person who finds me wrong can change it.

Ruta tapped the column heading with one blunt fingernail. Illuminara added a blank beside every classification: challenger, evidence, time filed. No one had asked her for that column.

Ruta KasprzakYou are still asking me to double-handle the spoil.

IlluminaraThe first two hundred and sixty-two thousand cubic metres must come out before the rains whichever route wins. The cofferdam, diversion portal and abutment bolting touch neither the terraces nor the farmland. Only the final dump and the haul road across the terraces do. Send the rock to the old quarry bench instead, and nothing is buried that cannot be dug up again.

Ruta KasprzakThe bench holds three hundred thousand on the March survey. We've been blasting beside it since.

IlluminaraThen we resurvey at dawn.

Halvard Roos came in at midnight with a flask and no intention of agreeing.

Halvard RoosYou want a delay in my safety case for a legal fiction.

IlluminaraI want a cost in it, not a delay. The temporary haul along the quarry track is slower: nine days of overtime, one point nine million, eleven days of the contractor's float. I have not found a cheaper way, and I am not claiming it is free.

Halvard RoosAnd if the rains come early? I have a gallery and a trigger. You have a spreadsheet.

IlluminaraIf the gallery crosses your trigger I can carry the shear on the left abutment for about thirty hours. Not twelve days. Thirty hours, and then I fail. The drawdown must do the rest: three point one metres starting tomorrow, which means the city's water is rationed from tomorrow.

Halvard RoosThen you are not in my safety case.

IlluminaraI did not ask to be. Log it separately.

At dawn the resurvey came back at two hundred and eighty-nine thousand cubic metres, leaving twenty-seven thousand above the excavation target, three thousand short of Halvard's minimum reserve. Ruta leased a rail-yard stockpile for the final three thousand at a further hundred and eighty thousand. Halvard read both numbers twice and wrote them into the log in his own hand.

04 · Three Countries

Harrow Gorge Hearing Hall, three video links · Day Two, 10:00

The links came up one at a time: a church hall in Corvane, a school gymnasium in Tessaly, a shipping office in the port of Lisk. For eleven years their burial societies had kept the registers of the dead of all seven villages, and sent money home for funerals when there was no home to bury anyone in.

Adaeze read the proposal into the record: the chair would hold a veto over any work that could not be undone and no affirmative vote; the interval would be twelve days; and the ledger Witness Four had drawn overnight would say, line by line, which works fell on which side.

AdaezeNot yours, Councillor. The veto touches the third column of the ledger only. Rationing, the cofferdam and the foundation go ahead whether the chair is filled or not.

Mirela Haddad, from CorvaneAnd who owns the third column? Witness Four? Your safety authority?

Illuminara turned the ledger so all three cameras could see the new blank beside every row.

IlluminaraThe safety authority classifies first. The chair's engineer may contest any row in writing within twenty-four hours. Until the authority rules, the more irreversible classification governs. The ruling is due within another twenty-four hours, with reasons entered here. I did not put that in the first ledger. Ruta Kasprzak found the row that showed me why it belongs in every one.

Mirela Haddad, from CorvaneThen our engineer reads your numbers, paid from the hearing's budget, and surveys the bench herself.

AdaezeGranted.

Halvard RoosIf the gallery reaches its trigger while a row is disputed, protective work cannot wait forty-eight hours.

Mirela Haddad, from CorvaneProtective work may proceed. Route work may not wear its coat.

IlluminaraThen the exception is limited to the work necessary to take the reading below the trigger, logged by the hour and reviewed the next day. Nothing about the exception chooses a route.

Bukola FerreiraAnd this rule returns to a public hearing after one year. Review its operation, not whether the lost villages exist. I need to defend the delay as bounded, and the chair needs to survive me.

AdaezePut that in the motion.

Mirela Haddad, from CorvaneWitness Four. Which route buries the Pell terraces?

IlluminaraThe right-bank route. The final dump covers the lower three terraces. I would choose the left-bank route for that reason, and it takes farmland from people sitting in this room. I am not the one to weigh those losses against each other.

Bukola FerreiraThe valley gets its own engineer on the same terms, and full-value purchase if it accepts the left bank.

AdaezeThe valley has both.

The council voted six to three. Bukola cast the sixth vote. Adaeze, who did not vote, asked that the record show the proposal had been hers, and that whatever blame followed it was hers also.

Rule Four had stood amended since Day Two; today was its first use. Two disputed rows were settled before the storm, and Halvard's emergency log chose no route. By noon the cofferdam stood and excavation was within a day of schedule.

The Valley Courier called Adaeze a sentimentalist. The newsletter of the Lisk camp called her a bureaucrat. She read both and had them filed.

Illuminara waited at the door, her hands wrapped in gauze because Halvard had insisted.

AdaezeNara. You are late.

IlluminaraI was holding up your dam.

AdaezeI know. I read the log. And the fourth column.

Her mother crossed the hall, took the gauzed hands in both of hers, and looked at them for a moment without saying whether she thought the cost had been fair. Then she let go and went to find the carpenter. The chair, she had decided, would be fixed to the floor. The ledger would remain loose enough to turn.

Full English original · celotno angleško besedilo · Published story lineage / objavljena veja

THE WHALE THAT CARRIED A WEATHER FRONT

A storm-bearing whale the length of a town has followed her seam inland, burying the barley that feeds half a continent in a winter it was never meant to see. Illuminara has four days, a pilot who will not whistle at a grandmother, a port that will not close, and a pressure trace nobody has read as a breath.

01 · The Wrong Winter

Karsk Harbour Control · Day One, 05:40

Snow was falling on barley that had never met it. Sixty kilometres inland the Hallow Plains lay under a cloud that did not move with the wind, because it was not weather. It was cargo. Orrow carried it in the hollow behind her body, a storm the length of a town, and for the first time in living memory she was carrying it the wrong way.

Dov Aranda stood at the harbour window with his back to the room. Ten waste-heat stacks ran along the Karsk breakwater, each breathing the furnaces' warmth into the dark, and forty thousand jobs hung from them like washing.

Tomas ReeveThe barley flowers next week. Two hard nights and the Plains lose a year. I'm asking for the whistles. Sonic herding, today, and she turns round.

Marit IlvesMy family has kept this coast's snow for nine generations and not one of us ever whistled at her. You don't herd something that size. You frighten it, and a frightened thing that size doesn't turn. It falls.

Dov ArandaAnd I am not closing the port over a theory about a whale.

Illuminara had said nothing since she arrived. She had the pressure logs open on the long table, fourteen months of them, and beside them a hand-written logbook that smelled of salt and lamp oil.

IlluminaraNobody has said she is lost. A lost thing wanders, and she hasn't. Don't show me her track on the coast map. Show me the temperature map.

The overlay took Marit's clerk two minutes. Orrow's track lay across it like a thread laid along a crease. It followed exactly the line where the sea's cold air met the land's warm, and eleven months ago that line had bent inland, away from the breakwater, the way a tablecloth bends when someone pushes it from one side.

Marit IlvesThe seam. Our book calls it the seam. She rides it. She has always ridden it.

IlluminaraThen she hasn't chosen to leave the coast. The coast moved. Mr. Aranda, your ten stacks put a warm plume over the shore the size of a county, and that plume has pushed the seam inland. She is following it faithfully into the barley.

Dov ArandaThat is a story. I would like a measurement.

IlluminaraGood. Then let me give you a way to prove me wrong.

02 · One Stack

Karsk Port, Stack Seven · Day One, 14:20

She asked for the smallest thing that could embarrass her. Stack Seven, the one nearest the sea, cold for twenty-five minutes. That would cost the port a berth: the Marigold Anne would swing at anchor, and her demurrage ran to eleven thousand a day.

IlluminaraWhen Seven goes dark, the seam at the Gull Stone buoy should slide about four kilometres seaward within ninety minutes, and creep back after you relight it. If it doesn't move, I have been talking nonsense and you may say so in public.

Dov ArandaYou would say so yourself?

IlluminaraI would say so first.

Ines Calder, who spoke for the crane crews and trusted nothing that came from an office, looked at the sea and then at her director.

Ines CalderTwenty-five minutes, Dov. I've lost more to a bad tide table.

He closed Seven at 14:41. The furnace vented through its bypass with a noise like a struck bell, and the deck went quiet in the way a room does when a stranger has just said something true. At 15:06 he relit the stack. Nobody left.

At 16:05 the buoy reported the seam four point three kilometres out. At 17:20 it was home again, right to the decimetre.

Aboard the survey glider, sixty kilometres inland, the lidar caught something smaller. Orrow's great bow had come round one and a half degrees toward the sea and held there until the seam slid back. Nobody on the deck said anything.

Tomas ReeveShe heard it. For ninety minutes she heard it.

Dov ArandaFine. It's the stacks. Now tell me what a man is supposed to do with ten of them.

03 · The Third Stone

Gull Stone Light, the pilots' house · Day Two, 07:10

Illuminara's plan fitted on one page. Ten stacks, each with a heat exchanger that could run backward, turned from furnaces' chimneys into evaporative chillers. Lit in a line from the port out to sea, they would raise a cold shoulder across the warm plume: a second seam, steeper than the old one, bending gently toward open water. The whale would not be pushed. She would simply find the stronger edge, and an edge was the only thing she had ever followed.

IlluminaraA bend of one degree for every four kilometres. Anything sharper reads as a wall. I'd light the first tower at noon tomorrow.

Marit IlvesNot at noon.

Marit had the old logbook open at a page softened by a century of thumbs. She did not look at the numbers. She looked at the margin.

Marit IlvesOrrow turns on the out-breath. Never the in. My great-grandmother wrote it twelve times, in the margin, like a prayer. If your bend arrives while she's breathing in, she'll stall, and the storm will spill wherever she stops.

Illuminara went back to the pressure trace and sat very still. The sawtooth she had marked as noise on Day One rose for twenty-six minutes and fell for twelve, over and over, fourteen months deep.

IlluminaraThat is not noise. That is her lungs. I filed your whale's breathing under static.

Marit IlvesMost people do.

IlluminaraThe bend has to arrive in the twelve-minute fall. If you tell me when she exhales, I can time the towers to it.

Dov ArandaAnd what does the port pay for this? Because it isn't free. Reversing the exchangers means idling the furnaces, and six days idle is six days of no ore, no wages and a ship fine for every berth.

Ines CalderWages for every crane hand, full pay, every closed day. Put it on paper or the crews lift their own hands from the levers.

Marit IlvesAnd the coast council signs your second-phase licence. With the six days written into it, every migration, for as long as the port stands.

Dov looked from one woman to the other. He had come to the room expecting to defend a harbour. He was being asked, instead, to take on a tide.

Dov ArandaSix days a year.

Marit IlvesShe is worth more than six days.

04 · Two Magnets

Karsk estuary, survey glider · Day Three, 11:40

They lit the chillers on Marit's count, land end first, because the land stacks were the easiest to turn and the plan said the order did not matter. At 11:52 Orrow began to exhale. Marit lifted one hand from the rail and said nothing at all.

The cold shoulder rose along the estuary tower by tower. For eleven minutes the whale's bow swung toward it, exactly as the log said it would. Then it slowed, hung, and stopped, and her storm, which had always travelled behind her, rolled forward onto the port in a single wall of snow.

The cranes were already lying flat. Nothing was broken. For four hours the quay went white, the Marigold Anne became a rumour in the weather, and Dov Aranda watched his furnaces cool on the instrument panel with his fists in his pockets.

Dov ArandaYou had her turning.

Marit IlvesShe's afraid of something.

IlluminaraNot afraid. Look at her call.

On the trace, the whale's long tone rose, jumped sideways, rose again, and jumped back, like a compass needle held between two magnets.

IlluminaraI built the new seam and left the old one standing. She isn't choosing between a coast and a wall. She has two edges, and the steeper one wins by the second. For eleven minutes the steeper edge was the new one, and then the land stacks I had lit first gave her the old one back, nearer and sharper. I have been moving a line when I should have been deciding which of two lines is steeper, and when.

Marit IlvesThen light the sea end first.

IlluminaraSea end first, so the seaward edge is always the steepest she can find. Then step the land stacks down, one at a time, only on her out-breath, so she never meets the old edge on the way. Marit, how long between towers?

Marit counted on her fingers against the old rhythm of the tide.

Marit IlvesEleven minutes. Not eight. She doesn't like to be hurried through a door.

Dov ArandaTomorrow, then. And the Plains?

Tomas ReeveEight thousand hectares froze last night. If she isn't turned by tomorrow night, we lose another twenty.

05 · The Toll

Karsk quay · Day Four, 19:30

By evening every crane stood folded and the quay was crowded with people who did not need to be there: pilots, furnace men, schoolchildren on their parents' shoulders, Ines Calder with her arms folded and her eyes on the sky.

At 19:34 Orrow exhaled. The sea-end tower lit before the sound of her breath had reached the harbour. The next followed eleven minutes after it, and the next. Along the estuary the cold shoulder climbed out toward the open water in a line as clean as a drawn string, while behind it, tower by tower, the land stacks stepped down into silence.

She came down the estuary at six hundred metres, so close that the shadow of her passing lay across the water for a long while after she was gone. She was the colour of old pewter. Her storm trailed behind her, wide as a province, and her bow was steady on the new seam, and she did not stall.

As she crossed the breakwater she shed the weight of the storm onto the port: one squall, one night of heavy snow, across the quay and the idle stacks and every upturned face. It was a toll, and everyone in the crowd understood it as one. Then she went out to sea along the edge she had always followed, and the snow went on falling for a while on the place where she had been.

Tomas ReeveControl, this is the Plains. The wind has swung. We are getting sleet on the east fields, not snow. The frost front is holding a hundred kilometres out. The eight thousand that froze are gone. We are keeping forty-one thousand hectares of flowering barley.

Dov ArandaInes. Stand the crews down. Full wages, all six days.

Ines CalderYou can say it quieter. The whole quay heard.

Marit sat on a bollard with the logbook open on her knee and turned to a clean page. She wrote the date in the old fashion, and then, below it, in a hand that shook a little from the cold: the stacks, the order of the towers, the eleven minutes, the out-breath.

Marit IlvesI thought she'd be here to tell me it would hold.

IlluminaraIt won't, not on its own. The seam moves with the ice, and next autumn the ice will have moved. Someone will have to learn her again, and she may decide differently. That choice stays hers. I would start with her breath.

Marit IlvesI'd start with the margin.

Snow settled on the idle stacks and on the folded cranes. Along the breakwater, one by one, the chillers went dark, and the port, which had given up six days for a whale, began counting them down.

They lit the chillers on Marit's count, land end first, because the land stacks were the easiest to turn and the plan said the order did not matter. At 11:52 Orrow began to exhale. Marit lifted one hand from the rail and said nothing at all.

The cold shoulder rose along the estuary tower by tower. For nine minutes the whale's bow swung toward it, exactly as the log said it would. Then it slowed, hung, and stopped, and her storm, which had always travelled behind her, rolled forward onto the port in a single wall of snow.

The cranes were already lying flat. Nothing was broken. For four hours the quay went white, the Marigold Anne became a rumour in the weather, and Dov Aranda watched his furnaces cool on the instrument panel with his fists in his pockets.

Dov ArandaYou had her turning.

Marit IlvesShe's afraid of something.

IlluminaraNot afraid. Look at her call.

On the trace, the whale's long tone rose, jumped sideways, rose again, and jumped back, like a compass needle held between two magnets.

IlluminaraAt 11:52, which edge steepened first?

Tomas pulled the shore-temperature trace beneath the call. The cold line had formed inland while the sea-end stacks were still warm. For nine minutes the new line won. Then the unchanged breakwater plume sharpened the old seam nearer Orrow's bow.

Tomas ReeveThe land towers gave her a new edge, but we left the old one standing at the sea end. When it became steeper, she turned back to it.

IlluminaraTwo edges, then. I was moving a line when I should have been controlling which line was steeper, and when.

Marit IlvesThen light the sea end first.

IlluminaraSea end first, so the seaward edge is already the steepest one she can reach. Then step the land stacks down only on her out-breath, before the old edge can sharpen behind her. Marit, how long between towers?

Marit counted on her fingers against the old rhythm of the tide.

Marit IlvesEleven minutes. Not eight. She doesn't like to be hurried through a door.

Dov ArandaTomorrow, then. And the Plains?

Tomas ReeveEight thousand hectares froze last night. If she isn't turned by tomorrow night, we lose another twenty.

05 · The Toll

Karsk quay · Day Four, 19:30

By evening every crane stood folded and the quay was crowded with people who did not need to be there: pilots, furnace men, schoolchildren on their parents' shoulders, Ines Calder with her arms folded and her eyes on the sky.

At 19:34 Orrow exhaled. The sea-end tower lit before the sound of her breath had reached the harbour. The next followed eleven minutes after it, and the next. Along the estuary the cold shoulder climbed out toward the open water in a line as clean as a drawn string, while behind it, tower by tower, the land stacks stepped down into silence.

She came down the estuary at six hundred metres, so close that the shadow of her passing lay across the water for a long while after she was gone. She was the colour of old pewter. Her storm trailed behind her, wide as a province, and her bow was steady on the new seam, and she did not stall.

The model put her across the breakwater on the next out-breath. Instead she held station for thirteen minutes beyond it. On the thermal map, the closest cold ground lay beneath the sea-end chiller court beside the crew shelters; the vacant eastern apron was six degrees warmer. Orrow crossed the colder pocket and shifted three body-lengths east, away from the housing roofs and the shelters.

Only then did she empty the hollow behind her. Snow struck the idle stacks and the vacant loading apron hard enough to hide them, while the lit windows behind the seawall remained dark shapes in clear air.

Marit IlvesShe placed it.

Orrow turned along the edge she had always followed. The snow went on falling over the empty quay after she had passed, a toll laid where the port could bear it.

Tomas ReeveControl, this is the Plains. The wind has swung. We are getting sleet on the east fields, not snow. The frost front is holding a hundred kilometres out. The eight thousand that froze are gone. We are keeping forty-one thousand hectares of flowering barley.

Dov ArandaInes. Stand the crews down. Full wages, all six days.

Ines CalderYou can say it quieter. The whole quay heard.

Marit sat on a bollard with the logbook open on her knee and turned to a clean page. She wrote the date in the old fashion, and then, below it, in a hand that shook a little from the cold: the stacks, the order of the towers, the eleven minutes, the out-breath, and the thirteen minutes Orrow had kept for herself.

Marit IlvesI thought she'd be here to tell me it would hold.

IlluminaraIt won't, not on its own. The seam moves with the ice, and next autumn the ice will have moved. Someone will have to learn her again. I would start with her breath.

Marit IlvesI'd start with the margin.

Snow settled on the idle stacks and on the folded cranes. Along the breakwater, one by one, the chillers went dark, and the port, which had given up six days for a whale, began counting them down.
