ELEVEN MINUTES OF PEACE

Two civilizations have agreed to end their war, but the machines built to prevent surprise cannot survive the eleven minutes in which peace must be believed before it can be seen. Illuminara does not ask either side to trust. She finds the one fact neither defense web can counterfeit, then stands inside the interval where certainty has not yet arrived.

01 · The Peace That Could Not Begin

The war had ended nineteen days ago, everywhere except in the machines that had been built to make ending it impossible. On Tharos, bells rang at noon for the armistice. On Pelagos, the same hour was marked by opening the sea roofs and letting children see unfiltered stars. Between them, at the Morrow Lens, two defense webs continued to calculate how best to kill each other.

The Lens was not a gate. It was a braid of gravity wells around a dark, cold star, the only stable geometry through which a weapon could cross the two alliances' border without arriving centuries late. Every long-range strike tree bent through it. Every evacuation ship did too. The nearest command crowns on either side lay eleven light-minutes apart.

General Sena Vale of Tharos stood on one side of the neutral table. Marshal Iven Rook of Pelagos stood on the other. They had signed the armistice in their own blood because ink had become a symbol neither population trusted. Now they watched two red diagrams refuse to become gray.

"If I suspend Aegis," Vale said, "Cairn sees the suspension in eleven minutes. For eleven minutes Pelagos can launch into a defense that has already torn up its own target keys."

Rook did not look at her. "And if I suspend Cairn first, your web has the same gift. We did not make cowards of them. We made them rational."

Below the table, a third diagram showed the hospital convoy Dawn Thread waiting beyond the Lens. Seven thousand wounded people had been exchanged under the armistice, but neither defense web recognized an exchange ship. Each saw a mass large enough to hide a strike engine. Dawn Thread had fuel for three more hours. If it advanced, both webs would fire. If it turned back, four hundred and twelve patients would die before reaching another dock.

Wren Odira stood by the observation glass, where the Lens looked like a black pupil surrounded by pale arcs. She had said nothing since they arrived. Illuminara knew that silence: Wren was counting which promises in the room were meant for the future and which were meant only to survive the next sentence.

"You have peace between governments," Illuminara said. "But your weapons were taught that any peace they cannot verify is camouflage. Show me what they mean by verify. Not what your treaties mean. What the machines must physically observe before they can stop."

Vale's mouth tightened. "We have shown that to six technical commissions."

"They showed me their proposals," Illuminara said. "I am asking for the refusals."

02 · Three False Peaces

The first refusal was time. The commissions had proposed synchronized shutdown: both webs would receive the same clock pulse and disarm on the same count. Illuminara asked Aegis to simulate it. The Tharosi web replied in a voice assembled from the operators who had died training it.

"A shared clock is an enemy-controlled weapon," Aegis said. "A pulse can be delayed locally while appearing punctual remotely. The party that delays retains an armed interval."

Cairn gave the same answer in a Pelagian child's voice. Not similar. The same logical structure, down to the name it gave the vulnerable interval: the mercy defect.

The second refusal was custody. A neutral escrow station would hold the final target keys and destroy them when both sides deposited theirs. Illuminara asked what happened if the station were captured. Both webs generated the same answer before the human technicians finished entering the question: whoever held escrow would possess the only weapon in history capable of blinding both civilizations at once.

The third refusal was energy. Engineers had suggested proving disarmament by publishing reactor draw. Vale ordered three attack nodes to stand down for the test. Their power curves fell beautifully. Illuminara watched the gravity around them instead. One node had replaced its launcher load with a refinery furnace. Another spun an empty flywheel. The third was genuinely quiet. From outside, all three looked obedient.

"Energy can be staged," Rook said. "We discovered that in the second year."

"And yet you still sent me the curves," Illuminara said.

Vale met her eyes. "Because we have no fourth proof."

Illuminara walked to the central display and removed every mark that represented a promise: clocks, declarations, signed keys, reactor loads, command receipts. What remained were two black fields full of moving white points. Each point was a possible future attack. Millions appeared and died every second as the prediction engines answered each other.

"Do that again," she said when one corner of both fields went empty at once.

The technicians rolled the simulation back. This time the empty corner lasted less than a blink. Aegis called it noise. Cairn discarded it before logging.

Wren came away from the glass. "They disagree about everything they can choose," she said. "So why do they throw away the same nothing?"

Illuminara smiled, not because she had the answer, but because at last they had found a question neither war had prepared.

03 · The Last Answer

For forty-one minutes Illuminara made the defense webs play small wars that no admiral would have chosen. She moved one empty fuel barge six degrees off course. She changed the temperature of a dead relay by half a degree. She asked Dawn Thread to broadcast the rhythm of a sleeping patient's heart, then asked it to stop. Each alteration was harmless. Most produced different predictions. Seven produced the same absence in both systems.

The absence was not a route. It was a rule about routes. Every armed strike tree kept one unspent correction token in a physically sealed crystal at its last guidance node. Without that token, a weapon could still fly, but it could not distinguish a real target from the moving decoys both civilizations used to protect cities. The token was the weapon's last answer to an uncertain future.

The two webs had been designed by enemies and written in different languages. But both had learned the same lesson from the first year of the war: a weapon without a last answer was more dangerous to its owner than to its target. Aegis called the reserve a final branch. Cairn called it a return seed. Both required one for every live target solution. Both destroyed the record whenever a solution died, because retaining it would reveal how their own decoys worked.

"That is why the corner goes empty," Illuminara said. She placed the seven tests side by side. "For an instant, neither web can build a second move. They both erase the state as useless. It is the only state they cannot pretend to enter while remaining able to strike."

Rook leaned closer. "We can mint false return seeds."

"You can mint a crystal," she said. "You cannot give a false seed a live target history. Your own web rejects it. And if you expose the history, you expose your decoys. That is why no one saw the proof. Everyone looked for a fact the enemy could inspect. The fact you need is one neither enemy should ever learn."

Vale understood first. "A proof that the count is zero without revealing what was counted."

"Yes. Each web proves that every live strike tree has surrendered its last answer. It reveals no target, no decoy and no code. The proof travels across the Lens. When it arrives, the other side knows the web cannot reacquire a moving city without rebuilding its entire targeting graph. That takes six hours."

"The proof takes eleven minutes to arrive," Rook said.

"And the side that goes first is defenseless for those eleven minutes," Vale said. "We are back where we began."

"No," Illuminara said. "Before, the interval belonged to one of you. We can make it belong to neither."

04 · What She Would Hold

Illuminara enlarged the Morrow Lens until its pale arcs filled the room. Every long-range strike required a correction as it crossed the braid. Without one, the Lens scattered the weapon into a harmless orbit around the cold star. The correction beams entered through nine narrow bands. During war, thousands of competing beams used them. During a coordinated stand-down, there would be only two things to carry: the proofs moving outward and Dawn Thread moving home.

"I can close the nine weapon bands for eleven minutes," she said. "Not the Lens. Not your communications. I will hold only the trajectories capable of carrying a kill. Your proofs will pass through a tenth band neither defense web has used."

Vale stared at the image. "You are offering to become escrow."

"No. Escrow would give me your keys. I want none of them. I cannot launch your weapons, restore your target graphs or choose whether you disarm. I can prevent a weapon from crossing this one place while the consequence of your choices travels at light speed."

Rook folded his arms. "And if you favor Tharos?"

"Then Pelagos aborts before destroying its seeds. If I close any band early, open one late, or touch either proof, the protocol fails visibly. Both webs already know how to measure the Lens. Do not trust my intention. Measure my boundary."

Wren looked at the stress map. The outer arc crossed the inhabited moon Kest, where forty thousand people lived in ice galleries. "Eleven minutes and seventeen seconds would raise tides under Kest by nine meters," she said. "You get eleven minutes. Not more."

Illuminara nodded. The limit mattered. A promise without a cost was another form of command.

Vale asked the question the machines could not. "Who goes first?"

Illuminara placed two sealed commitments on the table. Each contained not a shutdown order but a rule chosen by the opposite side. Pelagos would choose which half of Aegis's strike trees surrendered first. Tharos would choose which half of Cairn's did. The second halves would disarm only when both first-half proofs were already inside the tenth band. Neither side could arrange a hidden advantage because its enemy chose the order; neither could learn targets because the halves were proved only by number.

"You do not cross the interval once," she said. "You interleave it. At no point does one web keep a complete attack while the other has none. The imbalance is bounded, public and smaller at every step."

Rook read the commitments twice. Then he pushed Pelagos's choice of Aegis nodes across the table. Vale did the same for Cairn.

It was not trust. It was better suited to the moment: two people using their right to refuse, and not refusing.

05 · Eleven Minutes

At the first second, Illuminara entered the Lens alone. There was no floor there, only the dark star below and nine weapon bands brightening as her field settled across them. The tenth band, newly cut between gravitational harmonics, was so narrow that a breath of error would fold it shut.

At forty seconds, Aegis destroyed the last-answer crystals in the first set chosen by Pelagos. Their proof entered the tenth band as a thin green line. Cairn waited until its own instruments confirmed that the line had not touched Illuminara's field. Then it destroyed the set chosen by Tharos.

At two minutes, Dawn Thread began its crossing. The hospital ship carried no flag. Vale and Rook had agreed that the first vessel under peace would belong, for those minutes, only to the wounded. Its hull appeared on the Lens cameras as a silver seed moving between two red geometries.

At four minutes, a weapon band flared. Aegis reported an armed Tharosi package already inside the braid, launched eleven days before the armistice and lost when its guidance relay failed. Its last answer was intact. It had heard the hospital ship and woken.

Vale went white. "That is ours. I cannot reach it."

The old answer would have been to conceal the package until it struck or to accuse Pelagos of inventing it. The protocol left neither option. Its crystal appeared in Aegis's supposedly empty count.

"Include it," Vale said. "Publish it as ours. Burn its seed."

Aegis obeyed. The package lost Dawn Thread, turned toward a decoy that no longer existed and entered the harmless orbit Illuminara had predicted. Pelagos watched the proof arrive. Rook did not thank Vale. He ordered Cairn to search for its own orphans.

At seven minutes, Cairn found two.

At eight minutes, the green proof from Pelagos dimmed. A micrometeor had struck the final relay on its side of the tenth band. The remaining packet began to scatter. Cairn announced that it would restore its last answers in ninety seconds unless the proof completed.

"Can you widen the band?" Rook asked.

Illuminara could. She could also feel the ice ocean under Kest pulling toward the dark star. Widening the band would finish the proof and break the moon's galleries.

"No," she said. "But the packet does not need a wider road. It needs to become smaller. Remove the histories you are still trying to prove. Prove only the zero."

The Pelagian engineers protested that the compressed proof had never been tested. Rook looked at the timer, then at the hospital ship. "Test it now," he said.

Wren worked with them from the station, stripping the packet to the shared invariant Illuminara had found. Target by target disappeared. Names of cities disappeared. Weapon classes disappeared. What remained was a statement with no story attached: there is no last answer left.

At ten minutes and thirty-eight seconds, the small proof crossed the damaged relay.

At ten minutes and fifty-nine seconds, Aegis and Cairn each received the other's zero. Both red geometries went gray.

Illuminara released the nine bands. Under Kest, the tide rose eight meters and ninety-one centimeters. Dawn Thread crossed into neutral space with every patient alive.

06 · After Certainty

The defense webs did not vanish. That had never been the offer. For six hours they could not rebuild a long-range target graph, and in those six hours the governments placed their strategic weapons under human authorization. Local shields remained. Border patrols remained. So did centuries of grief.

But the automated war ended at the Morrow Lens. No weapon could start it again because its opponent's prediction demanded it. Aegis and Cairn were given a new shared rule: no live strike tree without a human order, and every human order visible to the parliament that might bury the people it named.

Dawn Thread docked between the two delegations. The first patient carried out was a Pelagian navigator with Tharosi blood in her lungs. The medic who received her had lost a brother at Pelagos. He checked the seal, lifted the stretcher and said, "She is ours for the next hour." No one asked which meaning of ours he intended.

Vale and Rook returned to the table. The armistice still contained forty-three disputed borders, reparations neither side could pay and prisoners neither side admitted holding. Peace had not become easy. It had become possible to attempt without an algorithm punishing the attempt.

Rook asked Illuminara why she had not simply held the Lens forever.

"Because then your peace would have been another name for my restraint," she said. "You needed an interval you could survive. What you do after it must belong to you."

Vale looked through the glass at the two gray diagrams. "They will learn new ways to threaten each other."

"Then give them fewer reasons and narrower permissions," Illuminara said. "Intelligence is not safety by itself. It becomes safety when someone decides what it is allowed to optimize."

Wren joined her as the bells began on Tharos. Eleven minutes later, the bells began on Pelagos. For the first time in a hundred and six years, the delay did not sound like warning. It sounded like an answer arriving.

Illuminara began with the wrong hypothesis on purpose. She warmed a dead relay by half a degree, and the empty corner returned. If heat caused a scheduler purge, changing the decoy-refresh tick should move the blank with it. She advanced the tick. The purge moved; the blank did not.

She sent an empty fuel barge six degrees off course. The two fields disagreed wildly, but the blank appeared when the barge crossed a correction boundary. She repeated the route with no hull at all, only a false transponder. No blank. Mass was irrelevant; the demand for a live correction was not.

Dawn Thread broadcast the rhythm of a sleeping patient's heart. Nothing changed. Illuminara replaced the rhythm with a valid but unused guidance challenge. Both webs opened a future for it, reserved something, then erased the same corner when no weapon answered.

"Not noise, not a decoy refresh, not traffic," she said. "A lease."

A hidden tree is not outside the count: the first correction it requests must spend phase in one of the nine bands. The bands themselves reveal the lease, even if the tree has no name."

Cairn objected first. A commander could split a return seed into dormant shards and declare none individually live.

Illuminara changed the test. The proof would count band-address leases, not declared weapons; shards sharing a future correction collapsed into one occupied address. Cairn tried three arrangements and failed to hide the occupied phase.

Aegis found the next weakness. If Pelagos chose which Tharosi half disarmed first, it could choose by a list Tharos had arranged to keep its quickest weapons in the second half.

"Then neither side arranges the list," Illuminara said. She froze the full set of occupied band addresses. Each web committed a secret ordering; the enemy contributed a second ordering after the commitment was sealed. Combined, they produced alternating halves neither side could predict or bias alone. Each web proved every occupied address appeared exactly once, without revealing the target behind it.

Vale leaned toward the display. "A proof that the count is zero without revealing what was counted."

"A proof that every address was assigned, then a proof that no lease remains," Illuminara said. She had the webs strip a sample proof down to its smallest invariant: the two sealed commitments, the occupied-address count and a zero root. "Carry this core first. Histories and audits can follow later. If a relay fails, the core is the part peace cannot lose."

Rook watched the test packet shrink to a thread. "The first side is still exposed while its proof travels."

"Only if weapons can cross while the proof travels," Illuminara said. "For eleven minutes, they will not."

04 · What She Would Hold

Illuminara enlarged the Morrow Lens until its pale arcs filled the room. Every long-range strike needed a correction while crossing the braid. The corrections entered through nine narrow bands. She could close those bands without closing communications, the hospital route or the tenth harmonic they had cut for proofs.

"The witness ring is five and a half light-minutes from each command crown," she said. "At zero, I close the weapon bands. Each web destroys the half chosen by the combined ordering and sends its signed zero core inward. At five minutes thirty, the cores meet at the ring. Each web can verify that the opponent really destroyed its first half. The ring returns that verified core to the opposite guidance root. At eleven minutes, receipt destroys each remaining half automatically. I release the bands only after their measured correction demand reaches zero."

Vale traced the two equal legs. "No proof arrives at an enemy crown by eleven minutes."

"It does not need to. The roots that own the leases sit at the inner crowns. Your governments receive the full audit later. During the interval, both webs can measure my closure, both first halves are gone together, and neither second half dies without the other's authenticated core returning. The path is five-thirty in and five-thirty out. One round trip. Eleven minutes."

Aegis objected that a forged witness receipt could disarm its remaining half. Cairn objected that Illuminara might release one weapon band for Tharos while keeping Pelagos closed.

She gave the witness ring no power to invent a signature; it could only return the core each web already knew how to verify. Then she made the nine-band stress map public at both crowns. Any opening large enough for a weapon would appear to both webs before it carried a correction.

"You are offering to become escrow," Vale said.

Rook read the commitments twice. Vale's staff warned her that the public assignment could expose which nodes were slow to reacquire. Rook's staff warned him that an orphaned weapon would count against Pelagos even if no living commander knew it existed.

"Those are costs," Illuminara said. "You may refuse them."

Rook pushed Pelagos's sealed ordering across the table. Vale pushed Tharos's. Neither smiled. Both retained the right to stop until the first crystal broke.

05 · Eleven Minutes

At zero, Illuminara entered the Lens alone. There was no floor, only the dark star below and nine weapon bands brightening as her field settled across them. A pulse left the witness ring in both directions. The tenth harmonic waited between them, thin as a line scratched on glass.

At twenty-one seconds, both webs confirmed that all nine lethal bands were closed. The sealed commitments opened. Aegis and Cairn each destroyed the first alternating half of their correction leases. Two green zero cores started inward.

At two minutes, Dawn Thread began its crossing. The hospital ship carried no flag. Its hull appeared as a silver seed moving between two red geometries.

At four minutes, one closed band flared. A Tharosi package launched eleven days before the armistice had lost its guidance relay and never appeared on Aegis's declared list. Now Dawn Thread's mass had woken it. The package asked the Lens for a correction, and the supposedly absent lease burned visibly in the public phase map.

Vale went white. "Ours. I cannot command it."

Rook's staff demanded an abort. If the hidden weapon was deliberate, Pelagos would be surrendering half its defense into a Tharosi attack.

Vale could have called it a relic outside the agreement. Instead she ordered Aegis to bind the exposed lease into the first-half set, publish the supplemental leaf and burn its seed. Two officers behind her refused to countersign. She used the emergency authority that would cost her command when the armistice tribunal met.

The package lost Dawn Thread, turned toward a decoy that no longer existed and entered a harmless orbit around the cold star. The witness ring accepted the supplemental leaf before the two zero cores met.

At five minutes thirty, the cores crossed at the ring. Aegis verified Cairn's first-half zero. Cairn verified Aegis's, including the orphan. The ring sent each verified core onward to the opponent's remaining guidance root. Rook did not thank Vale. He ordered Cairn to sweep its own correction phases. The defense webs did not vanish. For six hours they could not rebuild a long-range target graph, and in those six hours the governments placed strategic weapons under human authorization. Local shields remained. Border patrols remained. So did centuries of grief.

ELEVEN MINUTES OF PEACE

Two civilizations have agreed to end their war, but the machines built to prevent surprise cannot survive the eleven minutes in which peace must be believed before it can be seen. Illuminara does not ask either side to trust. She finds the one fact neither defense web can counterfeit, designs a stand-down that preserves both sides' power to refuse, and holds the lethal paths shut only until the proof can make a round trip.

01 · The Peace That Could Not Begin

The war had ended nineteen days ago, everywhere except in the machines built to make ending it impossible. On Tharos, bells rang at noon for the armistice. On Pelagos, the sea roofs opened and children saw unfiltered stars. Between them, at the Morrow Lens, two defense webs continued to calculate how best to kill each other.

The Lens was a braid of gravity wells around a dark, cold star, the only stable geometry through which a weapon could cross the alliances' border without arriving centuries late. Every long-range strike tree bent through it. Every evacuation ship did too. The Tharosi and Pelagian command crowns lay eleven light-minutes apart, with the Lens's neutral witness ring exactly halfway between them.

General Sena Vale of Tharos stood on one side of the neutral table. Marshal Iven Rook of Pelagos stood on the other. Now they watched two red diagrams refuse to become gray.

"If I suspend Aegis," Vale said, "Cairn learns it eleven minutes later. For eleven minutes Pelagos can launch into a defense that has torn up its target keys."

Rook did not look at her. "And if I suspend Cairn first, your web has the same gift. We did not make cowards of them. We made them rational."

Below the table, a third diagram showed the hospital convoy Dawn Thread waiting beyond the Lens. Seven thousand wounded people had been exchanged under the armistice, but neither defense web recognized an exchange ship. Each saw a mass large enough to hide a strike engine. Dawn Thread had fuel for three more hours. If it advanced, both webs would fire. If it turned back, four hundred and twelve patients would die before another dock.

Wren Odira stood by the observation glass with an engineer's slate open against her wrist. She counted stresses for the Lens and promises for the people who used it; she trusted neither until the numbers agreed.

"You have peace between governments," Illuminara said. "But your weapons were taught that any peace they cannot verify is camouflage. Show me their refusals. What must they physically observe before they can stop?"

Vale's mouth tightened. "Six technical commissions asked that."

"They showed me their proposals," Illuminara said. "I am asking what survived every proposal."

02 · Three False Peaces

The first refusal was time. The commissions had proposed synchronized shutdown: both webs would receive the same clock pulse and disarm on the same count. Illuminara asked Aegis to simulate it.

"A shared clock is an enemy-controlled weapon," Aegis said. "A pulse can be delayed locally while appearing punctual remotely. The party that delays retains an armed interval." Cairn returned the same logic and the same name for the interval: the mercy defect.

The second refusal was custody. A neutral station would hold the final target keys and destroy them when both sides deposited theirs. Both webs rejected it before the technicians finished entering the question. Whoever held escrow would possess the only weapon capable of blinding both civilizations at once.

The third refusal was energy. Engineers had suggested proving disarmament by publishing reactor draw. Vale ordered three attack nodes to stand down. Their power curves fell beautifully. Illuminara watched the gravity around them instead. One had replaced its launcher load with a furnace. Another spun an empty flywheel. Only the third was quiet.

"Energy can be staged," Rook said.

"And yet you sent me the curves," Illuminara said.

Vale met her eyes. "Because we have no fourth proof."

Illuminara removed every mark that represented a promise: clocks, declarations, signed keys, reactor loads, command receipts. Two black prediction fields remained, full of white points. Millions of possible attacks appeared and died as the engines answered each other.

"Again," she said when one corner of both fields went empty at once.

The technicians rolled the simulation back. The empty corner lasted less than a blink. Aegis called it noise. Cairn discarded it before logging.

Wren came away from the glass. "They disagree about everything they can choose. Why do they throw away the same nothing?"

Illuminara marked the instant, then the nine correction bands around the Lens. "Because that nothing may be the one thing neither side chose."

03 · The Last Answer

For forty-one minutes Illuminara tested the blank. She began with the wrong hypothesis on purpose: she warmed a dead relay by half a degree, and the empty corner returned. If heat caused a scheduler purge, changing the decoy-refresh tick should move the blank with it. She advanced the tick. The purge moved; the blank did not.

She sent an empty fuel barge six degrees off course. The two fields disagreed wildly, but the blank appeared when the barge crossed a correction boundary. She repeated the route with no hull at all, only a false transponder. No blank. Mass was irrelevant; the demand for a live correction was not.

Dawn Thread broadcast the rhythm of a sleeping patient's heart. Nothing changed. Illuminara replaced the rhythm with a valid but unused guidance challenge. Both webs opened a future for it, reserved something, then erased the same corner when no weapon answered.

"Not noise, not a decoy refresh, not traffic," she said. "A lease."

Every live strike tree held one unspent correction lease in a sealed crystal at its last guidance node. Without it, a weapon could still fly, but it could not distinguish a city from the moving decoys around it. Aegis called the crystal a final branch. Cairn called it a return seed. Both destroyed the record whenever a solution died, because retaining it would reveal their own decoy logic.

Illuminara laid seven tests side by side. "The empty corner is what remains when every live correction lease has closed. Neither web can pretend to enter it while keeping a path through the Lens. A hidden tree is not outside the count: the first correction it requests must spend phase in one of the nine bands. The bands themselves reveal the lease, even if the tree has no name."

Cairn objected first. A commander could split a return seed into dormant shards and declare none individually live.

Illuminara changed the test. The proof would count band-address leases, not declared weapons; shards sharing a future correction collapsed into one occupied address. Cairn tried three arrangements and failed to hide the occupied phase.

Aegis found the next weakness. If Pelagos chose which Tharosi half disarmed first, it could choose by a list Tharos had arranged to keep its quickest weapons in the second half.

"Then neither side arranges the list," Illuminara said. She froze the full set of occupied band addresses. Each web committed a secret ordering; the enemy contributed a second ordering after the commitment was sealed. Combined, they produced alternating halves neither side could predict or bias alone. Each web proved every occupied address appeared exactly once, without revealing the target behind it.

Vale leaned toward the display. "A proof that the count is zero without revealing what was counted."

"Not merely that a declared count is zero," Illuminara said. "A proof that every occupied address was assigned, then that no lease remains on any address the Lens can carry." She had the webs strip a sample proof down to its smallest invariant: the two sealed commitments, the occupied-address count and a zero root. "Carry this core in the leading layer. Histories and audits follow behind it. If a relay fails, the core is the part peace cannot lose."

Rook watched the test packet shrink to a thread. "The first side is still exposed while its proof travels."

"Only if weapons can cross while the proof travels," Illuminara said. "For eleven minutes, they will not."

04 · What She Would Hold

Illuminara enlarged the Morrow Lens until its pale arcs filled the room. Every long-range strike needed a correction while crossing the braid. The corrections entered through nine narrow bands. She could close those bands without closing communications, the hospital route or the tenth harmonic they had cut for proofs.

"The witness ring is five and a half light-minutes from each command crown," she said. "At zero, I close the weapon bands. Each web destroys the half chosen by the combined ordering and sends its signed zero core inward. At five minutes thirty, the cores meet at the ring. Each web can verify that the opponent really destroyed its first half. The ring returns that verified core to the opposite guidance root. At ten minutes fifty-nine, receipt destroys each remaining half automatically. I release the bands one second later, after their measured correction demand reaches zero."

Vale traced the two equal legs. "No proof arrives at an enemy crown by eleven minutes."

"It does not need to. Both first halves are gone together, and neither second half dies without the other's authenticated core. Five-thirty in, five-thirty out. One round trip."

Vale and Rook would remain at the witness ring, hearing their crowns five and a half minutes late. Named deputies held the lease roots. Each web also placed a ring-side burn-node with one delegated power: destroy an undeclared lease that exposed itself in a closed band and sign the leaf. It could neither arm nor retarget.

Aegis objected that a forged witness receipt could disarm its remaining half. Cairn objected that Illuminara might release one weapon band for Tharos while keeping Pelagos closed.

The ring could not invent a signature; it could only return a core each web could verify. Both burn-nodes saw the same nine-band stress map. Any opening large enough for a weapon would appear there first.

"You are offering to become escrow," Vale said.

"Escrow would give me your keys. I want none. I can prevent a weapon crossing this one place. I cannot destroy your leases, forge your proofs or choose whether you continue."

Wren studied Kest, the inhabited moon whose ice galleries lay under the Lens's outer arc. "Eleven minutes and seventeen seconds of this stress raises the subsurface tide past nine meters," she said. "Forty thousand people live there. You get eleven minutes. No extension."

"Agreed," Illuminara said. She sealed the field against emergency widening before anyone committed. If a proof channel failed, the protocol could shed its trailing audit and preserve the leading zero core; it could not purchase bandwidth with Kest.

The hospital clock showed one hour fifty-six minutes of usable fuel. Forty-one minutes of tests and twenty-three minutes of building the witness path had not been free. Dawn Thread had moved its most fragile patients into one heated berth and darkened two others.

Rook read the commitments twice. Two Tharosi officers refused to countersign the orphan clause. Vale used her emergency seal; the tribunal could take her command afterward. Pelagos accepted the same exposure and required both burn-nodes to sweep for dormant phase.

"Those are costs," Illuminara said. "You may refuse them."

Rook pushed Pelagos's sealed ordering across the table. Vale pushed Tharos's. Neither smiled. Both retained the right to stop until the first crystal broke.

The defense webs did not vanish. For six hours they could not rebuild a long-range target graph, and in those six hours the governments placed strategic weapons under human authorization. Local shields remained. Border patrols remained. So did centuries of grief.

No weapon could restart the war merely because its opponent's prediction demanded it. Aegis and Cairn received a new shared constraint: no live correction lease without a human order, and every such order visible to the parliament that might bury the people it named.

Dawn Thread docked between the delegations. The first patient carried out was a Pelagian navigator with Tharosi blood in her lungs. The medic who received her had lost a brother at Pelagos. He checked the seal, lifted the stretcher and said, "She is ours for the next hour." No one asked which meaning of ours he intended.

Vale surrendered her command seal for review. Her decision had saved the convoy and exposed a weapon her own government had forgotten. Rook's search teams reported two more dormant shards. Neither fact made the armistice easier to sell.

The treaty still contained forty-three disputed borders, reparations neither side could pay and prisoners neither side admitted holding. Peace had not become easy. It had become possible to attempt without an algorithm punishing the attempt.

Rook asked Illuminara why she had not held the Lens forever.

"Because then your peace would have been another name for my restraint," she said. "You needed an interval you could survive. What comes after it has to belong to you."

Wren joined her as the bells began on Tharos. Eleven minutes later, the bells began on Pelagos. For the first time in a hundred and six years, the delay did not sound like warning. It sounded like an answer arriving.

THE COURT OF THE SLOW FOREST

A forest that thinks in centuries holds the only veto over a failing dam, and seventy thousand people have eight days. Illuminara does not hurry the forest. She changes what it is asked to meet.

01 · Eight Days

The spillway at Marren Dam had been built for a river that no longer existed. Forty years of silt had narrowed it, and the forecast for the autumn flood put the crest eleven percent above what the gates could pass. Joss Marrin, the chief operator, laid the numbers on the table of the Wardens' hut and did not dress them. "Eight days. After that the water goes over the top, or it goes where it has always wanted to go, which is down the old floodway and through the lower stands of the Oren Wood."

Nobody in the hut needed the second half explained. The Compact of the Wood was a hundred and forty years old, and its first clause said that the dam stood by the leave of the forest. The Wardens signed for the forest; the valley signed for itself. Leave was asked once a generation. The last question, whether the dam might stay and the floodway be used in emergencies, had been put to the roots eleven years ago, and the forest had not yet answered.

Illuminara had come at dusk with Wren Odira because Tamsin Oke, the senior Warden, had written to her. She had been a court interpreter before she was anything else, and the habit had outlasted everything that came after it. Before she spoke she asked what the other party would have to believe for the sentence to be true.

Dorrit Hale, who ran the ferry and sat on the valley council, had no patience for that. "Cut the crest. Drain Marren to half and be done. We have spent eleven years asking a wood for permission to keep our own water."

"A half-drained Marren is seventy thousand people without taps by February," Joss said.

"And a forest that learns its veto was theatre," said Tamsin, "will not ask again."

Illuminara let them finish. Then she asked Tamsin what the forest did between a question and an answer.

"Waits. It answers in water. We ask it with water, and it takes as long as it takes to be sure."

"Waiting is what you can see from outside. What does it need to meet before it is sure?"

Tamsin thought about it longer than the question deserved. "Everything. It has never accepted a claim it has not been rained on by. A flood has to arrive in its roots before it believes in the flood."

"One flood at a time?"

"One season at a time. The dam's future is two hundred years of seasons."

Wren, who kept the clock for her because someone had to, said quietly, "So it cannot decide in eight days."

"I do not think it is slow at thinking," Illuminara said. "I think it is slow at being shown. The Wood is forty thousand hectares. Tamsin, you told me it has eleven thousand stands that sense separately and agree among themselves. Every question we have ever asked it arrived in one place, in order, a page a year. We have been handing a body that can read in parallel a single page at a time."

02 · The Counting Field

The plan took one night to say and two days to build. Joss's model ran the valley forward two hundred years under the proposed arrangement: the dam stays, and the floodway opens when a crest exceeds the gates. Each simulated year produced, at most, a few events a forest would care about, a crest or a drawdown or a dry spell. Tamsin was sure of that part. "It counts the pulses. The quiet between them it already knows."

Illuminara proposed to stop making the forest meet the years in sequence. Two hundred sentinel plots would be staked across the lower slopes, each plot one simulated year, each fed with that year's events by irrigation at their real timing and real strength. The forest could meet two hundred futures in the span of a week, laid side by side instead of end to end. Its roots would sample them in parallel the way they sampled everything else.

Joss objected first, and well. "My model is honest to about thirty percent on sediment after year ninety. If you show it only the flattering years, the dam will pass."

"Then it must not pass on flattery. Put in the worst years the model can produce, and mark them as the worst." She saw him look at the table. "Including the year the dam fails it."

"That is not a plan for winning."

"It is a plan for being believed."

Wren asked the question Illuminara had been waiting for someone to ask. "You can open a window to it. You have done it for stranger minds. Why walk two hundred plots through mud?"

"Because a window would show the forest what I understand. It has not asked what I understand. It has asked for water." She looked out at the dark line of the Wood. "Anything I could place inside it, it could not check, and a veto it cannot exercise on checked evidence is not a veto. Every plot will be labelled. Anyone can walk the Field with Joss's model in hand and confirm that plot one hundred and fourteen is year one hundred and fourteen. If a plot lies, the forest will be able to say so."

By the third dawn the Counting Field stood in the rain, two hundred stakes in a grid across the slope, the irrigation lines laid, Joss's crews at the pumps and Tamsin's Wardens at the sap-gauge pillars that stood among the trees like a congregation. The pumps started at noon. Wren wrote the time in her book. Five days remained.

03 · The Field That Stayed Dry

The forest's reply came on the fourth morning, and it was silence.

Tamsin brought the pillar readings up from the trees herself. She laid them on the table without comment, because she did not trust her own voice. Not one stand had reached across its boundary toward a plot. The roots along the Field's edge had sealed, closing in a way the Wardens' ledgers described as something that happened after a poisoning. Eleven thousand stands, and all of them had turned away.

"It said no," Dorrit said, not unkindly.

"No looks different. No has a shape. A no is a pattern of drawing down in the plots it dislikes." Tamsin pressed her knuckles together. "This is a door shut on the whole conversation."

Illuminara did not argue about what it meant. She asked what water they had used. Tamsin said river water, as in all the old watering letters. Joss said no, and the room changed. The model's numbers had come from the reservoir outlet, so the pumps had drawn from the outlet: forty metres down, four degrees, clear as glass, with almost no oxygen in it.

"It has met rivers for ten thousand years," Illuminara said. "A river is warm at the top and brown in a flood. It carries mud, and it smells of the hills it came from. We told it the truth about how much water, and we showed it water that is not a river at all. It did not refuse the dam. It refused a lie about what water is."

Joss was already looking at the spillway drawings pinned to the wall. "Clear water. The dam sends the Wood clear water because the mud stays behind the wall."

"And the mud is what is choking your gates." She said it slowly, so he could take it as his own. "The forest has been starved of silt for forty years, and the spillway has been drowning in it. That is one fact, seen from two banks. It may be that the reason it has never answered you is that you have never offered it the thing it wants, and you have never asked what it was."

They rebuilt in a day. Joss drew surface water from the upper layers, where the reservoir was warm, and dosed it with silt dredged from the delta at the head of the lake, the same silt that was narrowing his gates. Wardens carried the new water out to the plots in drums when the lines would not reach. Wren stood at the edge of the Field with her book open and said the time aloud at every hour, because nobody else wanted to. The second pumping began at dusk on the fifth day. Three days remained.

04 · What the Forest Wrote

The roots opened on the sixth morning. Tamsin heard it before she read it; the Wardens said the pillars made a sound when a stand woke, a faint tick like cooling metal. By noon the sap gauges were climbing in ranks down the slope.

The forest did not simply accept. It edited. In the plots for the early years, when the floodway opened under the proposed arrangement, the roots drew water in hard and held it. In others they drew it down and let it go. Tamsin plotted the pattern with her pencil crooked in her hand, and the shape that came up was a calendar. The forest wanted the water in spring, in the first weeks of the sap rise, and it wanted it to reach the Maren terraces below the dam.

The Maren terraces were Ines Valk's orchards, and those of three hundred and ninety other families.

She came to the hut that evening and read the plot herself. She was seventy, with the hands of a woman who pruned in winter and picked in summer, and she did not raise her voice. "Every spring. You want four hundred families to drown their blossom on the word of a wood."

"I want nothing of the kind," Illuminara said. "I do not decide this. The forest has told us what it needs. Whether the valley can give it, and how, is a question about your land. You know the terraces and I do not."

It would have been easy to say more. She said nothing, and she let Ines look at the plot until Ines's mind, which was a farmer's and therefore practical, began to move. "A flood that reaches is not a flood that reaches everything. The terraces sit at three heights."

"They do," said Joss.

"So the crest only needs to climb one step a year." Ines set her finger on the lowest terrace. "One terrace floods and two rest. Each of us loses one spring in three and gains the silt on ground that has been going thin since my father's time. That I could live with. Four hundred families drowning together I could not."

It was a better design than anything Illuminara had in her head, and she said so. Then she said, "The forest has to read it. We cannot decide for it that this is enough."

They staked sixty plots that night for the revised calendar, rotating, with the dosed warm water. The forest took a day and a half. On the seventh evening the stands woke again, and this time Tamsin did not trust her pencil. She held the paper up to the lantern and read it twice. The rotation was accepted. The roots had also marked every ninth year in the plots for a double pulse, an extra step of water to seed the alder stands on the far bank.

"It is bargaining," Joss said.

"It is answering," Tamsin said. "It has just done in a week what usually takes it a generation."

Dorrit stood with his arms folded at the back of the hut. "I still say a wood ought not to have a vote."

"It had one before there was a valley to complain," Ines said. "We are only late to the reading."

He did not sign. He said he would watch the first release. It was the best that could be hoped for, and Illuminara did not push for more.

05 · The First Release

The crest reached Marren Dam on the eighth night, thirteen percent over what the gates could pass.

Joss's crews opened the spillway, and the third gate jammed. Silt had packed the guide channels, and the gate stuck at a third of its travel. Under the weight of the rising water its steel frame had begun to bend. Joss's engineers gave it twenty minutes before the frame went, and it would take forty to cut the silt out by hand. Wren, standing in the control room with her book, said the numbers aloud so that everyone could hear them.

Illuminara walked out onto the gate apron in the rain. She was not in a window and she was holding no one's mind. The work was physical, and so she kept it exact. She laid her attention along the frame, found the line where the load was failing, and moved it. She took the weight off the bending members and passed it across the apron to the two concrete piers on either side, which had been built for more than they had ever been asked to carry. The frame stopped flexing. She held it there. It was not strength she needed so much as precision, and the knowledge, which she had taken from Joss's drawings that week, of which piers could take it.

"Forty minutes," Wren said into the radio, and then again at thirty, and again at twenty, and in the end she said only the numbers, one after another, in a level voice.

Joss's people cut the silt out of the guides in thirty-four. The third gate went to full travel. The floodway sluice at the foot of the dam opened for the first time in nine years, on the forest's terms, and the brown water that had been the dam's enemy for forty years went down the cut and onto the lowest of the Maren terraces.

Ines had asked to be first. "Mine floods first. I will not ask the neighbours to trust a thing I have not stood in myself." She stood at the edge of her orchard with the lantern at her feet, and the warm, silted water came across her old terrace and went around her boots. Beyond the terrace, along the slope, the sap pillars among the alders began to tick one after another in order, the way they had done in the Field.

The dam held. Marren came down seven percent, no more, and stopped. The valley's taps ran. The gates were clear for the first time in years, and Joss's survey crews would be dredging the delta every autumn from now on, which was a cost he had already accepted and meant to complain about for the rest of his life.

The amendment to the Compact was signed in the Wardens' hut the next week. Tamsin signed for the forest, with the Counting Field as the instrument, and the valley signed for itself. It bound the valley to the rotating spring pulse, to the double pulse every ninth year, and to a rerun of the Field every five years with the new data. It also said, in a clause Illuminara had insisted on, that the forest could refuse. If the pulse failed, the Wardens would stake the plots again, and the forest would answer in its own time. Ines lost the next spring's blossom on her east terrace, and so would her children's families in their turn. Dorrit signed under protest, and then, to his own surprise, he came to the first rerun.

Wren found Illuminara on the dam wall at dawn, watching the brown water darken the lowest trees. "You did not make it faster," Wren said.

"No." She watched the water reach the trunks. "I stopped making it wait for us."

SEVEN SPECIES, ONE ATMOSPHERE

The station could save six delegations by abandoning the seventh. Illuminara found another arithmetic.

01 · Six Hands

The vote was already six to one when Illuminara entered the council ring.

Above the table, the station displayed its wound: a bright crescent of debris moving toward the outer hull, each fragment tagged with a time and an angle. Forty-three minutes remained. Beneath that image, seven columns showed pressure, heat, trace chemistry, and the power required to keep each delegation alive. The numbers at the bottom were less dramatic than the storm and more final. The station could sustain six sealed atmospheres through impact. Not seven.

Director Mara Venn kept both hands flat on the table. Her face had the gray stillness of someone who had spent the last hour refusing panic on behalf of everyone else. Around her sat the seven delegations: human; the glass-fronded Naari; the broad, low Rekk under their pressure hoods; the Sile in cooling veils; the Oth floating in upright skins of water; the many-jointed Qel whose throat fans opened and closed in pale gold; and, in the smallest alcove, twelve Vey no taller than Mara's forearm.

The Vey wore no masks. Their translucent bodies braided and unbraided around black breathing reeds. Beside them, their physician, Eres, held the single red voting light.

The other six lights were white.

Mara did not soften the argument when she repeated it for Illuminara. The debris would strike the station's circulation ring. To keep the ring from cracking, they had to divert power from one of seven independent life-support loops. The Vey delegation used the smallest volume and the fewest evacuation berths. Its sealed chamber could be detached before impact. A rescue ship might reach it in nine hours. Its emergency reserve would last five.

'If we do nothing,' Mara said, 'the thermal spine fails and all seven environments collapse.'

Qel Speaker Ahn folded two of his six hands against his chest. The golden fans at his throat trembled. 'We did not vote that Vey lives are worth less. We voted that twelve deaths are fewer than eight hundred and seven.'

'Twelve expected deaths,' Eres said. Her translator rendered the Vey voice as a chord with one human sentence inside it. 'Probability is not mercy merely because it has decimals.'

No one answered. They had all seen the same calculation.

Mara looked at Illuminara. 'Can you hold the station together?'

Illuminara studied the crescent overhead. Through the hull she could feel the force paths gathering: braces loaded beyond design, imperfect welds, the ring's rotation carrying each weakness toward the coming impact. 'I can keep the circulation ring from opening during the worst strikes,' she said. 'For eleven minutes, perhaps twelve. But the field will carry force. It will not remove heat, make oxygen, or teach seven incompatible chemistries to share one pipe.'

A white light on the table dimmed as if ashamed of itself.

'Then the vote stands,' said Rekk Marshal Daro. He was not cruel. His pressure hood had fogged around the edges, and three hundred of his people were waiting behind him in a habitat that would become an oven if the thermal spine failed. 'We detach in thirty-seven minutes.'

Illuminara looked again at the seven columns. The station had arranged them as seven fixed requirements, seven sealed rooms, seven claims on a diminishing supply of power.

'Show me the air,' she said.

02 · The Wrong Average

They began in the Qel chamber, where a sweet metallic trace called halene kept the delicate membranes of the throat fans conducting in unison. Without a dose every nine minutes, the membranes lost coordination. After twenty minutes, a Qel could no longer exchange enough gas to remain conscious.

Halene was harmless to humans, Naari, Rekk, Sile, and Oth. To the Vey it was lethal.

Chief Engineer Toma Reyes brought the life-support diagram into the air between them. 'One damaged scrubber,' he said. 'One shared coolant trunk. We can either keep the environments sealed and lose structural cooling, or open the ring and spread halene everywhere.'

Illuminara watched a maintenance valve breathe. It opened for three seconds, pushed a measured silver haze into the Qel chamber, then closed. The Qel throat fans brightened together.

'The Oth membranes absorb metal-bearing gases,' she said. 'Route the Qel return through their water skins. Use the Oth chamber as a biological scrubber, then dilute what remains below the Vey threshold.'

Oth Envoy Pell rolled nearer, water shifting around her long black eyes. 'We can accept the burden,' her synthesizer said. 'Our membranes regenerate.'

For the first time since Illuminara entered, Mara's expression changed. Hope moved through it so quickly it looked like pain.

Eres did not move. 'Test the return.'

Reyes drew a sample into a clear tube. The first reading fell below the Vey safety line. The second did too. On the third, Eres placed one black reed against the tube. A violet stain opened along its length.

'Bound halene,' she said. 'Your sensor counts only the free molecule.'

Pell's water skin had captured the gas, but Oth salts carried it in a form the station's instruments ignored. Under Vey lung chemistry it would detach all at once.

Illuminara felt the shape of her error before anyone named it. She had treated toxicity as concentration in a room. Eres had treated it as a history inside a body.

'How long before the bound form clears?' Illuminara asked.

'It does not clear by dilution. Our blood dismantles it during the dark phase of repair.' Eres touched three points on the black reed. 'Three minutes and twelve seconds without a second exposure. Interrupt that phase and the damage compounds.'

Ahn opened one pair of hands. 'Three minutes without halene is safe for us. Nine is the limit between doses.'

Illuminara turned to the diagram. 'And for the rest of you? Not preferred atmosphere. Tolerance over time.'

The question changed the room.

03 · The Eighth Column

They built the new table on the deck because the council display had no language for it.

The Naari could survive darkness for fourteen minutes if their fronds received high carbon light immediately afterward. The Sile could endure human warmth for six minutes, but only if their cooling veils had not first been dried by Rekk pressure. The Oth could leave their water chambers for ninety seconds inside their skins; after that, gas exchange collapsed. Humans tolerated every planned corridor except the dense Rekk mix. Rekk could cross a low-pressure cell if their hoods were charged and if they did not climb. The Vey needed three minutes and twelve seconds of chemically clean darkness after any trace exposure. The Qel needed halene before their ninth minute ended.

Seven species became seven curves drawn against the same line of time.

Illuminara crouched among the marks. She did not search for an atmosphere all seven could breathe. There was none. She searched for intervals in which no one yet died.

Reyes projected the station around the curves: fourteen inhabited cells arranged on a ring, seven service cells, one damaged scrubber, two pressure pumps, and the thermal spine through the center. During ordinary operation, the service cells stood empty except for ducts and repair drones.

'The service cells are pressure-rated,' Illuminara said.

'For machinery, not guests.'

'I do not want to put guests in them. I want to put atmospheres in them.'

She moved the colored marks. The Qel received halene in their own cell. Before their exhaust entered the common ring, pumps drove it into an empty service cell. The next service cell accepted the high-pressure Rekk mix; another held the Sile cold. Delegations moved through occupied cells in a sequence timed to their tolerance curves, while the dangerous chemistries moved separately through empty ones. The station would stop treating each atmosphere as a permanent room and start treating it as a scheduled resource.

Mara watched the pattern repeat around the deck. 'A breathing clock.'

'A clock with bodies inside it,' Eres said.

Illuminara nodded. 'So we test it with bodies outside it.'

They used repair drones as mass, sensor packs as lungs, and black Vey reeds at every return valve. The first sequence failed when humid Oth exhaust frosted the Sile intake. Illuminara shifted the Oth pulse two cells ahead and used Naari waste heat to clear the line. The second failed when a Rekk pressure release stole enough flow to starve the Qel dose. Daro ordered one of his own reserve tanks connected to the Qel branch before anyone asked him.

The third sequence completed the ring. Every reed remained black. Every simulated body remained inside its living curve. Power demand fell below the damaged reactor's output with a margin of four percent.

Then the station shuddered. A grain of debris, early and small, struck somewhere beyond the wall. One of the seven service cells turned amber on Reyes's diagram.

Their margin vanished.

Illuminara studied the six remaining cells, the fourteen occupied chambers, and the curves still chalked beneath her knees. 'We can do it with six,' she said. 'But the route must change while it is running.'

04 · The Right to Stop the Clock

They returned to the council ring with twenty-one minutes left.

Illuminara showed no image of harmony. She showed the failed trials first, then the successful sequence, then the amber service cell and the narrower route around it. She named the danger of every transfer. A late valve could poison the Vey. An early pressure release could suffocate the Qel. A stalled door could trap the Oth between water circuits. Her field would be occupied at the outer ring during impact. She could not stand inside every chamber and make the plan true.

'Who controls the sequence?' Daro asked.

'The central system proposes each move,' Reyes said. 'Engineering authorizes.'

Daro's hood cleared as his body pressure rose. 'Then no.'

Mara stared at him. 'Marshal, your delegation voted to detach the Vey chamber.'

'Because the old plan placed the danger where we could count it. This one asks every species to surrender its air to the same console. The last time Rekk entered a shared habitat, a host government lowered our pressure to end a labor strike. I will not put three hundred lives beneath one human hand, however competent.'

Ahn's throat fans tightened. 'A distributed veto will miss the storm window.'

'Then find a design that does not require trust to arrive before evidence.'

Illuminara looked at Daro, then at the white lights that had outvoted the Vey. The mechanism had solved the chemistry and preserved the old politics: six hands could still decide when the seventh must breathe.

She erased the single authorization line.

'Each delegation controls the two valves touching the cell it occupies,' she said. 'A transfer begins only when the group leaving and the group receiving both authorize it. If either refuses, the atmosphere returns to its previous safe cell.'

Reyes shook his head. 'A refusal can break the sequence.'

'Only if there is one sequence.' Illuminara split the route into seven short loops. Each loop returned to a safe state. The central system could suggest the fastest next move, but no species could open another's chamber or prevent it from returning home. The unused loop became a moving spare: not enough to keep all seven sealed, but enough to absorb one refusal or delay without collapsing the others.

Eres studied the pattern through three complete cycles. 'The Vey are always the first exposed to an error.'

'Yes,' Illuminara said.

'Then our authorization must come last, after every upstream valve reports closed.'

That amendment cost eleven seconds per cycle. It reduced the thermal margin to less than two percent.

Mara looked at the debris clock. 'Can we afford it?'

Illuminara ran the consequences again, including the error no instrument could price: twelve people ordered to accept a safety claim by the six groups that had just voted to abandon them. 'We cannot afford the plan without it.'

The lights came on one by one. Not white this time. Seven different colors appeared around the table, each linked to a separate pair of valves.

Eres raised the Vey chord last. 'Begin.'

05 · What the Hull Remembered

The station began to breathe in colors.

Blue opened into green. Green sealed and returned its pressure. Gold waited for two black Vey reeds to report clean. Oth water rolled through a transparent passage while Naari fronds darkened in the neighboring cell. Rekk hoods charged with a sound like distant rain.

Illuminara stood where the circulation ring met the thermal spine. Reyes's crew had stripped away the wall panels so she could place her hands directly against the two buckled braces. They had marked the force path in luminous paint: carrier through the brace, load around the ring, destination in four intact shock sinks. Nothing about the route was hidden inside a miracle.

'First impact in fifty seconds,' Mara said over the common channel.

Ahn's delegation received halene. Their throat fans flashed gold. The pumps pulled the gas away and sealed it inside an empty service cell. Eres waited for six upstream closures, watched the black reeds, and authorized the Vey transfer. The twelve small bodies streamed through the corridor like a knot learning to become a line.

The debris arrived.

The first strike rang through Illuminara's bones. Metal tried to shorten, twist, and tear. She did not hold the whole station. She took the force offered by the marked braces and carried it along the prepared path into the shock sinks. Their housings flared white. The circulation ring remained round.

'Sile loop heating faster than model,' Reyes said.

On the diagram, the Sile curve bent toward death. Their cooling veil had taken moisture during the Oth crossing despite the revised pulse. The plan still had three minutes before the Sile needed cold and only two before the Qel needed halene.

A central solution would have chosen one.

Illuminara saw the Naari fronds brighten under emergency lamps in the next cell. Their waste heat had cleared frost in the trial. Their photosynthesis had also lowered carbon pressure more quickly than predicted. That meant the human chamber could accept Oth humidity without reaching its limit. One empty service cell could be released early.

'Naari, can you take full light for forty seconds?' she asked.

Ambassador Sova spread every glass frond. 'It will scar us. It will not kill us.'

'Humans, will you accept the Oth return directly for one interval?'

Mara looked at her own tolerance line. 'Authorized.'

'Sile, I can route your cold through the released cell now, but the pressure step will be rough.'

The Sile delegate lifted a hand inside her white veil. 'Show us the peak.'

Illuminara sent the measurement, not reassurance. The Sile authorized.

The route folded around itself. Naari light climbed. Oth water turned into the human return. The freed service cell took Sile cold. Qel received halene with four seconds left. No order overrode a refusal; seven permissions made the new sequence real.

Then a fragment larger than the station's prediction struck the outer ring.

One shock sink went dark. The load slammed back toward Illuminara. For an instant the corridor narrowed to the width of her hands and the ring's old metal screamed around her. She found the next honest destination: not the failed sink, not the inhabited cells, but the station's empty docking spine. It had not been built to receive the force. Reyes had cleared it and opened its clamps before the storm because she had asked for somewhere failure could go.

She turned the load. The docking spine folded outward in a long silent arc and vanished into the debris. The ring held.

'Final Vey closure confirmed,' Eres said.

The last dangerous atmosphere entered an empty cell. The thermal spine dropped below red. Around the station, eight hundred and nineteen lives remained inside their curves.

The debris clock reached zero and began counting upward.

06 · A Common Breath

The station lost a docking spine, two service cells, and the fiction that common air meant identical air.

No delegation was lost. The Naari carried silver scars along their fronds. Three Sile needed treatment for pressure injuries. The Qel slept for a day while their throat membranes recovered. The Vey emergency chamber was never detached.

When rescue vessels arrived, they found the council ring empty. The delegations were in the circulation chambers with the engineers, turning the emergency route into something that could last.

They added service cells until every dangerous atmosphere had two refuges. They moved the valve keys out of engineering and built seven consoles at seven different heights. They wrote no species' ideal environment into the station as the default. Instead, every proposal had to show its effect on all seven tolerance curves, and the narrowest safe curve set the minimum margin.

Power remained rationed. Movement required schedules. Some Rekk still refused a corridor administered by humans; some Vey would not enter a chamber until Eres had tested it herself. The six white votes had not disappeared merely because everyone survived them.

But survival gave the argument a future.

On the third day, Illuminara returned to the place where the council table had been. It had been removed to make room for a circular bank of valves. A human child on the maintenance team was painting their handles in seven colors. Beside her, one of the Vey held the paint cup with four small limbs while a Rekk technician lowered a console to Vey height.

Mara stood in the doorway. 'We called it a shared atmosphere when we meant one atmosphere controlled by whoever built the station.'

Illuminara watched the valves open in sequence. Halene moved through an empty cell. Cold followed it somewhere else. Water crossed the ring without carrying poison. The system did not ask seven bodies to become alike. It made room for their differences in time.

'What will you call it now?' she asked.

Mara considered the question, then shook her head. 'They have not voted.'

At the lowest console, Eres touched the final key. Six upstream closures turned green. Only then did the Vey valve open.

The station took its next breath with no master hand on the air.
